. A LANGUAGE of the sole—Creaking boots. A UNIVERSALLY-LIKED gallant—A rain-bow. WHAT most helps and yet most retards a pilgrim? A Bunyan (bunion.). WHY should a blockhead be proinoted 7 Because he is equal to any post. READING by lamplight probably accounts for the different "shade. 3 of opinion." To dream of a bear betokens mischief, which your vision shows you is a bruin. WHEN does: a rogue think he gets "a drop too much ?" When he gets the hangman's. THE road to success is open to all, but too many Want to get there without tha trouble of going. CHAMPIONSHIP eating matches ought to be for large steaks.—Rochester Post,Express. A scHOOl., GIRL, on being told to compare the adjective little, said, "Little, small, nothing at all." LITTLE three-years-old was out in the fields the other day, and came running in with, "I saw a pansy and I was going to pick it, and it was a butterfly and it flied away." DENTIST, kindly—" Now, does that hurt?" Patient —"I don't mind your working on the tooth so much, but. if you will just take your sleeve-button out of my right eye, I shall be obliged. WHEN a young lady dreams of a coffin, it betokens that she should instantly discontinue tight stays, and always go warmly clad in cold weather. ON TICK.—Why wouldn't you sell anything to a man in bed? Because cash business is best, and it is evident that he would be buying on tick. THE VILEST CONUNDRUM EVER SEEN.—At what time should an innkeeper visit an iron foundry? When he wants a bar made. "WHISKY lowers the man and raises the devil," said a revivalist preacher, as he was making a fervid appeal for temperance. WHEN a fashionable young lady dreams of a fil- bert, it is a sign that her thoughts are running on the colonel (kernel). THE best way to get along with people who are "set up by pride" is to upset their pride and them, tOO. WITH the dishonest, money will do almost anything. Philip of Macedon said: "Send an ass laden with gold into a city, and all the sentinels will run away." "IT was not the dhrop I had taken," said a Kerry peasant, charged with being drunk and dis- orderly, "but I had a shmoke, out of a neighbour's pipe, and that leaned upon me." A YOUNG politician once told Abraham Lincoln, that he was going to set up as "The Poor Man's Friend." "I am afraid," replied Mr. Lincoln, "that you will make some expensive acquaintances." "FOOL OF THE DEEPEST DYE.—" Do you see that man there ? " "Yes. What of him?" "He's a fool of the deepest dye." "How so? " " Why, he's over seventy, has magnificent white hair, and beard, and yet dyes them to a muddy black." Miss DELLA. CREME, wearily: "I known every- thin we eat is adulterated; but what can we do, Reginald? We must trust our grocer." Mr. Reginald Creme, drearily: " Ah, yes, Della, very true; and if—oh, if—our grocer would only trust us!" THE Duke of Wellington, in a certain debate in the House of Lords, stated that two Irish clergymen had been murdered. •A noble Lord exelaimed, "No, no • only one." Whereupon the Duke rejoined, "If I am mistaken, I am sorry for MAMMA—" Did you have a nice time at the party, Harry ?" Harry—" Oh, yes, splendid! I had five kinds of cake. First I had some sponge cake and chocolate cake, and then I had jelly cake and cre.asn cake, and then I had the stomach-cake." PalleaiT—" Doctor, I can't sleep at night. I tumble and toss until morning." Doctor—" H'm, that's bad. Let me see you tongue. (After diag- nosis.) Physically you are all right. Perhaps you woay, over that bill you've owed me for the past two years." MESSRS. HUNTER, JONES or Co. are building a gigantic flume, or otherwise a narrow passage con- fining water to turn a mill wheel. A Californian editor wrote a notice of it, and the compositors astoonded and delighted Italian opera-goers with the news that the firm in question were "construct- ing a. great flute two miles long." , • A FELLOW lately started a store in Kansas. The following was the sign he hung out :--•• Dry goods, by John Smith, who wishes to get married.' The sign drew all kinds of custom. The single ladies went, of course, and the married men told their wives to go under the impression that they could easily cheat so great a simpleton. H:USBAND (airily—they had just returned from their wedding-trip)—" If I'm not home from the club by—ah—ten, love, you won't wait—" Wife (with appalling firmnesa)—" No, dear; I'll come for you I" He was back at 9.46 sharp. ;SOCIAL VICE.—" Drunkenness and extravagance In dress are the most common socialvices," said the Rev. Dr. Teaser. "I beg your pardon, uncle, but I think there is a social vice far more common than either of 'em, and one to which you are yourself _much addicted," responded his nephew Tom. " Name it," said the uncle, aghast. "Ad-vice," responded the audacious Tom. A SCHOOLMASTER, on inquiring of a delinquent - pupil how many lines of a rather extensive holiday imposition he had written out, was met with the answer, "I can only tell you in round numbers, sir; bat, if you will wait a little, you shall have it exactly." "Thank you," replied the pedagogue, sternly; "I will do so. I prefer square numbers to roultd ones." TkAIIP (to Editor, who is hurrying past)—" Say, couldn't you help me a little, please? I gave you a, boost once." Editor—" What do you mean, . fellow!" Tramp—"Ton't you remember that bur- glariy- by Jim Crackitt and his pals some years *or Editor—" Yes." Tramp—" And how your • repette of it just set the Howler's circulation a- boomin' 7" • Editor—" Yes." Tramp=" Well, I'm - Jim I" MRS. BLANK (to her husband)—'; Do you remem- ber, that before we were married you always offered Me your left arm ?" Mr. Blank—" Yes,; I wanted to have my right hand free. You see, I had a lover's fear that some one would try to take you away from me, and I always kept it in readiness for defence." Mrs. Blank—" How sweet I But how is it that now you generally offer me your right arm ?" Mr. Blank —"Well, I are not so afraid of losing you as I was." • WHAT'S IN A NAME T—A few week ago a pas- from Holyhead to Dublin in one of the North =boats was surprised at seeing a number of caroasses of cattle on board bound for Ireland. He inquirill, %atilt kind of beef it was. "Well, Colonel," "was the reply, "these carcasses were American " beef the day before yesterday; yesterday they were English beef; to-day they are Irish!" A LA/E Judge, whose personal appearance was as urprepossessing as his legal knowledge was pro- .fon.scd and his intellect keen, interrupted a female witness:—" Humbugged yoli, •rov rod woman. ,What do you mean by that ? " he Ada iarn.l7. my Lord,",_ xeplied. the woman, "I don't know how to explain it alik,tly ; but if a girl called your Lordship a handsome man she would be hum- bugging you.' A LADY took her son, of some five years to church. Aker the minister had been preaching about half , an hour the little fellow grew sleepy and began to acid. The mother roused him into attention several times by pushing; but, as it seemed a hopeless case, ; she concluded to let him sleep undisturbed. After a little while the little fellow had his nap out, and saw the minister still holding-forth. He looked up In his mother's face and innocently asked, "Mother,- Is this Sunday night, or is it next Sunday night ? " THE VERDICT OF EXPERTS.—"Fetch in the " body," ordered the foreman of a Texas coroner's jury. The body was laid before them. The jury made a careful examination, and questioned the attending surgeon.. " Whar wa,s he shot ? " "Square through the heart." "Dead in the centre?' "Right in the centre." "Who shot him ? " "Jake Daniels." A dozen witnesses declared that Jake fired the shot, and Jake himself admitted it. The jury consulted softly for some time. "Well, gentlemen of the jury," said the coroner, "what is your verdict? " " Waal, Jedge, we've come to the conclusion that Jaka Dan- iels is the dandiest shot in .these parts, and don't you forget it I" "CLARA,' said the old man from the head of the Stairs, "say to that young fellow that a storm ia coming up," "All right, sir; thanks," responded the young fellow himself, "I hadn't noticed it. I think I'll wait and see if it doesn't blow over."

Dom Pedro, the ex-King of Brazil, is translating the "Thousand and One Nights" from the original Arabic into Portuguese. It is said by those who see him daily that he is much happier thus employed than he was in governing Brazil.

Mr. Sexton, M.P., has been invited to. undertake the political direction of the new Irish Nationalist journal. Mr. Sexton's acceptance of this post, how- ever, would not involve his residence in Dublin during the sitting qf Parliament.

I am informed that the very beautiful painting by Gainsborough of "-Eliza Ann Linley, Mrs. Sheridan, and 'her Brother" (No. 167) now being' exhibited at the Guelph Exhibition in the New Gallery, has been sold by its owner, Lord Sackville, for the enormous sum of twelve thousand guineas. The purchaser is Mr. Alfred de Rothschild. The size of the canvas is twenty-six and a half by twenty- three inches.

The Registration Bill to which Mr. Gladstone alluded in his letter to Mr. Farness is Mr. Stans- feld's. Mr. Gladstone describes it as" a Bill to clear away the obstacles which hinder or delay qualified voters from coming on the register, and to limit, on the register, every single citizen to a single vote." The Bill is quite ready, though it has not yet been printed.

Mr. Christopher Furness, the Liberal candidate for Hartlepool, was born -in West Hartlepool in 1852, and at the present 'day he is probably the mast remarkable figure in its history as a port and an industrial centre. He is the foinder and guiding spirit of the great Furness line of steam- ships, which trade to all parts, of the world; and some idea of the resources of the line may be gathered from the fact that the total dead-weight carrying capacity of the steamers running under the Furness flag represents no less than sixty thousand I tons.

Mr. Furness is eminently a self-made man and a man of the people, with the inbred lore of democracy from his youth ; and his public life hitherto has shown his sturdy capacity and fitness for the political arena. He enjoys the confidence and respect of his constituents alike on the Durham County Council and the West Hartlepool Town Council; and in the first contest of the former governing body. be defeated the strongest candidate that the Tortes , could put into the field—viz., Colonel Cameron, a local brewer and county magis- trate.

Hertford has set an example which might be ad- vantageously followed by other towns which have a river near at hand. With the permission of the lessee of the Towii Mill two of the extensive Castle meadows have bPen flooded, and thus magnificent and perfectly safe skating pound has been formed, which was opened on Monday. A charge will be made for admission, and the proceeds are to be added to the fund which is being raised for the benefit of the poor of the neighbourhood, who are suffering from the long continuance of intense cold.

I have obtained a clue to Mr. Tim Healy's mean- ing when he said the other day that further revela- tions might be forthcoming from Mrs. O'Shea's pro- bate suit. My information is that Mr. Parnell will be called as a witness in the suit. You probably know that the dispute is between Mrs. O'Shea and her brother, Sir Evelyn Wood. and his sister, as to the will of old Mrs. Wood. It would be improper to suggest what part Mr. Parnell-will play in the wit- ness box, nor is it necessary to suggest; but I imagine the great difficulty will be to get Mr. Parnell into the box.

Mr. Plimsoll is in New York gathering facts re- I garding the " cruelty and danger of the Atlantic I live cattle trade," and he reports that public opinion in America is strongly against it. Revolting des- criptions are given of the torture inflicted upon the poor animals, packed in three tiers so closely that they cannot lie down, aboard vessels that are com- pared tobicycles, being only steady while going on, and liable to topple over at once if brought to a stand. Attempts have been made to check these practices, but they have broken down on the tech- nical rule of law, that people can only be punished for offences committed and not for those which they are about to commit.

While on this side of the Atlantic Dr. Koch's discovery is regarded as still in the probationary stage. Dr. Austin Flint, an eminent medical writer in the United States, bids us look forward to the discovery "in the near future " of a' whole series of curative lymphs. Among these he enumerates the typhoid lymph, the diphtheritic lymph, the lymph for measles, that for scarlet fever, and so on. They will, he tells us, promptly arrest these dis- eases, and save patients from tbe degenerations and the accidents which are liable to occur when mor- bid processes are allowed to run their course. As Dr. Flint observes, "This would truly be a revolu- tion in medicine," but he assures us that it is one 'which" now' seems to be impending."

-- - The Indian papers publish numerous details of the arrival of the Czarewitch in Bombay. He is des- cribed as a etrongly-built„ broad shouldered youth, of about five feet eight inches in height, With sharp black eyes, contrasting with the fairness of his complexion and his light brown moustache. When he landed in company with Prince George of Greece and the officers of his suite on the stepa of the Apollo Bunder, lie was attired in the quaint uniform of the Hussars of the Imperial Guard, con- sisting of a black bearskin busby surmounted by a. tall, white aigrette, a short red tunic, with close- fitting trousers of dark blue elaborately embroidered in gold lace, and Hessian boots. here he was re- ceived by the high officers of State, the foreign Consuls being also grouped around.

Truth says :—A certain peer, recently on a visit 1 to Constantinople with his daughter, had the honour of being entertained at dinner by the Sul- tan, on which occasion the lady in question sat be- tween the Grand Vizier and another high official of State, both of whom were singularly assiduous in their attentions. The Sultan remarking this, and 'desirous of setting his distinguished visitor at ease, sent a message round to explain that the Giand Vizier already had three wives, and the other offi- cial was more blest with four, adding in all serious- ness, "You need not, therefore, be in the least alarmed, as I do not intend permitting them to add further to the number." The simplicity of Eastern matrimonial etiquette is somewhat embarrassing to our more InattcT-of-fact Western minds.

Who has said that an oyster has "'lO feeling"? Whoever he may have been, he is justly rebuked by an Essex man, who assures us that the Essex oysters at least feel the cold quite as much as we bipeds do, in proof of which many thousands of Colchester natives have fallen victims to the severe frosts of the last seven weeks. From Burnham, in East Essex. it is reported that the Roach River Company find their oysters, both in the pits and in the river, weak from the extreme coldness of the water, though as yet they have not suffered any serious loss. The report of the Crouch river dred- gers is similar. At Tollesbury the frost has com- pelled the dredger men to suspend. operations, though the company are inundated with orders. On the other hand the fall of spat on the Edon oyster ground this year has been better than any that, has occurred since the memorable season of 1881. '

By the death of the Duke of 'Somerset, which took place at 28, Berkeley-square on Saturday, the dukedom passes to the last of three sons of the eleventh duke, all of whom will have succeeded to their father's title. The duke best known in our times, the 8.G., who died in 1885, was married to the granddaughter of Richard Brinsley Sheridan, and had two sons who both lived to man's estate, but he had the misfortune to lose them both. The younger, Lord Edward Percy St. Maur, who was in i the diplomaiic service, died n 1865, and the heir to the dukedom, Earl St. Maur, died four years later. Both young men were unmarried. Their father was accordingly succeeded by his brother. Lord Archi- bald Henry Algernon, the duke whose death is now announced. Ile has died, like his elaer brother, in his 81st year. The third brother, who now becomes Duke of Somerset, was born in 1813, and married in 1845, Horatio, Isabella Harriet, daughter of the late Mr. John Philip Morier, her Majeysty's Minis- ter at Dresden. He was formerly Captain in the Royal Horse Guards. He has four sons, of whom two are twins, but as they have an elder brother, the question of their priority will probably never excite the curiosity of the general public.

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
Apropos of vegetarianism in politics, a correspon- dent writes to suggest that its members might be called the" Peas at any price" party.

Dr. Magee is distinguished by his wit and elo- quence. There is a good store of racy stories about him. One of the most characteristic of these is the spade and shovel -story. Although pretty well known it is worth reviving. One day, at:Petert borough Station, Dr. Magee heard a wicked peer scolding a porter in language of a decidedly unpart liamentary character. The peer ultimately took a seat in the same compartment b.s the bishop. Dr: Magee took the opportunity of dropping a word in, sewn as to the impropriety of using profane lan,. guage, and particularly the bad example that was set by a person in the exalted position of the pee; using such language. Now the wicked peer was one who prided himself upon the cultivation of a bluff and hearty manner Hence he replied to the bishop in an airy manner, "Well, you know, I always call a spade a spade." "Quito so," replied the bishop, with a bland smile, "but that is no Bea- son why you should call it a-shovel."
THE EXAMINER, SATtRDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891.

div.head: MICROBES IN THE AIR.
div.p: MICROBES IN THE AIR.

Some interesting experiments were made on this point a short time ago by Dr. P. F. Frankland. The air was tested at different places and under differ- ent circumstances. It was found that the number of organisms present in the atmosphere differed at different seasons of the year, the largest pioportion being found during the summer months. In a cer- tain volume of air (two gallons) collected on the top •of the science and art department buildings at South Kensington, 105 of these micro-organisms were found to be present. This was in the month of August. Indoors, of course, the numtier is very much greater. Thus, in a similar ,quantity of air collected at the rooms of the Royal society during a conversazione, no fewer than 452 were found to be present, while another experiment showed that from the air of a third-class railway carriage con- taining ten people no fewer than 3,120 microbes fell per minute on a square foot.

div.head: " OTHELLO AND DESDEMONA."
div.p: " OTHELLO AND DESDEMONA."

• A German contemporary has the following: A I Berlin merchant, one Herr 8., With his wife and I daughter, visited a relative in Chicago a little while ago. While there the daughter fell in love with "a man of colour" employed in a merchant's office. Theparents, discovering this, shortened their stay in Chicago, and returned to Berlin. Letters passed, and ten days ago the young Othello arrived in Hamburg, whither his fair Desdemona had fled, taking with her a grandmotherly' portion in the shape of 7,000 marks in paper money. While there , the coloured man made the acquaintance; of .a Gil;r- man-American,. who kindly offered to cosh the paper. He left the hotel for that purpose, but never returned. In this strait there was nothing left but to communicate with the young lady's father, who speedily arrived on the scene. Herr B. took his daughter back to Berlin, and packed off his would- be son-in-law to Chicago. No tidings, however, ,have yet been heard Of the 7,000 marks. P

div.head: BISHOP VA.UGHAN AND LICENSING.
div.p: BISHOP VA.UGHAN AND LICENSING.

The Roman Catholic Bishop of Salford makes an ' eanest appeal to all parties to unite on a common basis in order to bring about a settlement of the licensing question. Dr. Vaughan states that besides the Catholic children in workhouses it his diocese, they have now over thirteen hundred children in Industrial schools and homes here and in Canada. Ile is looking anxiously to the time when the number 'will diminish and disappear ; but of this experience tells him there is no hope "so long as that corrupter and destroyer the drink shop is systematically established within the sight and hearing of almost every poor man's house, while perhaps the poor, man's iionse is unEt for hitnaan habitation." If, satys this active philanthropist, "it be folly to quarrel and wrangle as to the mode and 'measure of defence while the enemy is thundering at the gate, how fatal and suicidal to do so when hale actually Withisthe walls,slaying the population by thousands!'

div.head: AFRICAN KING AND THE DOCTOR.
div.p: THE AFRICAN KING AND THE DOCTOR.

—Prince Bismaick lately, in epeculcing FuLat. I 'African affairs to a newspaper. TO rrespondent, incidentally told tNe following story: When the well-known African traveller, Dr.. Robert Felkin, was staying with the blood-thirsty King Mtesa of Uganda many years ago, the King out of gratitude for his visitor's medical treatment, wished to out off his head. On Felkin representing that the treatment was not finished, and that if interrupted it would cause Mtesa's death, the latter granted him a reprieve until he was quite recovered. Then bGw- eyer nothing availed, and the execution was deter- mined upon. Emin Pacha, who was, a friend of Dr. Felkin's, had instructed him most accurately about the state of affairs in Uganda, and the Court of King Mtesa, and had revealed to him an impor- tant State secret,. namely, where Dltesa'S powder store was hidden. Dr. Felkin remembered this at- the right moment and as a last resort threatened that if Mtesa killed him he would bring down a flash of lightning upon his powderstore. Mtesa re- plied incredulously, "Tell me where it is; " where- upon Dr. Felkin whispered in his-ear, "It is con-, cealed under your harem." Mtesa, turned pale, and allowed Felkin and his companions to. live. The " lightning maker's authority increased when next day a flash of lightning 'happened to strike near the harem.

div.head: NEW ARCHBISHOP OF YORK,
div.p: THE NEW ARCHBISHOP OF YORK,

Dr. Magee, Bishop of Peterborough, who has been appointed Archbishop of York, is the most eloquent member of the Church. Dr. Magee'a appointmeat will be received with general satisfaction. Ile is Vone of the ablest men on the Episcopal Bench, and 1, the only one that can make a speech worth listening to in the House of Lords. , Dr. Magee is an Iriehman, and began his clerical career with a Dublin curacy. In 1848 he was a curaZe at Bath,. and during- the nine years which he spent in that town distinguished himself as a valiant defender of the State Church. In 1856 he came to London and took up the charge of Quebec Chapel, and four years later returned to Ireland ae the rector of Inniskillen. After a sojourn at Cork he became Bishop of Peterborongh in 1868. As a controversialist Dr. Magee has few, if any,., equals in the Church ; he is a brilliant orator, and as a writer of nervous and forcible English has few' equals. He may justly be regarded as one of the great intellectual forces of our time. His opinion.e: are moderate, and he signalises himself by entering fiercely into conflicts from which his colleagues hold aloof. Ile recently declared that there was no sin; in gambling, and his historic saying that he would. I rather see England free than sober is still the r311y,-1 ing cry of many a fierce wordy war. The Bishop of Peterborough's oratory is still one' of ,the traditions of the House of Lords. It is. not over sympathetic, but it is powerful. suggutive, and bears the stamp of the vigorous personality from which it proceeds. The new Archbishop's' square, strong face, with its heavy underjaw,is still fairly familiar in the lobbies of the Lorda. and Commons, and last session it was more than:usually conspicuous during the debates on the Protection, of Children Act, which he piloted though the Lords in his usual vigorous fashion. On what one may call the more spiritaal. side of Christianity the Archbishop represents no force at all, lie is a vigorous exponent of Butlerian and Paleian common sense. He is an Anti-Socialist, and will find little in common either in doctrine or practical work with his neighbour the nevt Bishop of Durham. But, he will do the business part of Archbishop's duties admirably, and as his tongue has had the sharp edge taken off, it ol late will probably make no mistakes.—Star.

div.head: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
div.p: RHYMES IN THE DIALECT.
A TWICE-TOLD TALE.

BY WATCHMAN. To write under the heading I have adopted is plainly to indicate there is not much freshness in our thoughts. Were it not that so many people listen without hearing, and look without seeing, it would be waste of time and effort to multiply our lessons. That the conditions in which men are placed will frequently alter very materially their point of view and give sight to the blind as well as ears to the deaf, lends some hope, however, to men who repeat occasionally a "Twice-told tale." There are certain things in every man's life that never happen twice, and we cannot afford to sleep, not even while the clouds roll by. There may be in the most unpromising circumstances gleams of sunshine and it is the trial of our faith that worketh patience, and patience experience, and experience hope. To- ' sit down and cry about it may bring tears, but never treasure. To so about with our hands in our pockets, exclaiming, "Who will show us I any. good." is, if not an improvident position, 'an impertinent one Why be so unself-reliant and I maundering, hanging about, and loafing at eorners I where currents meet and traps are set. Then it is ! that men are driven like chaff before the wind, and I there it is that the wicked do not live out half their I days. "Darkest England,'.' as given to us by Gen- eral Booth, is a marvellous compilation, and terrible record, and he has found, as every man will find who cares for what is honest and true, that the sub- merged millions he has brought to the surface and I is now gibbeting before the eyes of the nation, are in the main, the dregs of the liquor shop, and are now, and will for ever be so, so long as the cause remains a festering sore and a polluting and pauperising source. This drainage from the public-house is not conveyed as in our ordi- nary sanitary arrangements in sealed pipes and trapped boxes but is left on the surface to distribute itself in its seething mass of foulness and impurity amongst tens of thousands of wretched and helpless victims. Talk of infections. There is no disease so infectious as the drinking disease, and there are but few, if any, families that escape its terrible ravages. The question often occurs to one's mind how far it can be wise or safe to have near re- lationship with medical men who are so constantly in the habit of touching and treating such cases, but that these gentlemen do most assuredly, and sadly too often, convey the drinking infection amongst those who are too ready to seek an excuse foreelf-indulgence,and a dangerous practice is mani- festly true. Whisky for gout and port wine for rheu- matism are about as conducive to health as smoke is to the purity of the atmosphere. That we can live despite offending chimneys and doctors' folly there is no doubt, but we should live better and longer if we were not effected by either. Doctors, Magistrates, Ministers, Judges, Members of Parliament„and Peers of the Realm are all alike tainted and troubled by this one, this universal plague., General Booth's cab horse may be got up and his John Jones have his dinner, and the sooner thebetter :: and we bless every man, and any man, who gives a helping hand tin such matters, but unless we mend our ways I another horse will be down, and another John Jones I will be without his dinner. There are two short cuts out of this" Darkest England?' One is to take men from the drink, the other to take drink from the men. The money that is taken to the liquor shop by men in rags and women•offensive in filth t and foulness is a disappointing and sad spectacle. ' What condition can their homes be in, and! what a prospect their poor children have';, and what a dire necessity when any decent young woman has to , stand behind the bar and breathe such foulnese and touch such impurities I It it be undesirable to give ' postmen drink at Christmastide, is it wise to give postmen or anybody else drink', at any, time'?. Are we never to have done with this-danger 7 If our Government have not sense to stay% tnis enemy, and t the publican the wisdom to shuthis door,, there is a door every man can shut—the one under his own nose.—From the "Scarborough Mercury.'!" div.head: POEICEMANS CALL
div.p: THE POEICEMANS CALL
THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;

" I strongly suspect that 'twas this same gun-maker that led to the investigation of that medicine; and if it was him, then you will be more quickly sus- pected than I shall." "Ha! Why think ye so ?" "Because he is a fellow of wondrous wit and in- telligence, and can see without being told. lie has had several conferences here, and it was from here that he went direct to the count's residence. lie knows by this time why the:kluel was hatched up, and if he has half the mind T give him credit for. he will know that your are at the bottom of the poisoning business. lam sure of this." "By heavens, yo & are right, Savotano. Let him die " I had thought myself that would be the best way; for if he were at large you would not be safe:, "Yon can have him killed without noise or turbance ? " I think so," replied the priest, with a wicked smile. "At all events, his noise would not hurt any' one, for he is rather too far away from the world to make himself heard." " Where is he." " Why—where you recommended: In the furthest vault beneath your old bathing-house; and that's a place where he cannot be readily found." And what disposition can you make of the body. after the work is done ?" "Why—that is simple. It ean be hidden in the. old conduit. You know the conduit still exists there, and probably in some places between there and the river it is perfect; but near the building it is all in ruins. The body can be hidden .so far in that no stench can come from it in summer time even to those in the vault itself. So you see that 18 easy." "Then let the work ..be done at once—say to- night." "To-morrow night, my lord, will do as well,ior- am engaged to-night." "very well—Let it be to-morrow night. But mind —this is settled. There is no more question about this affair. When I, see you again I. trust you will have no reason to offer why Ruric Nevel has not been disposed of." "You need have no fears on that head, my lord. YOumay consider that the gun-maker .is dead." " Right ! So let it be." And thus did tne wicked duke dispose of Ruric' Nevel ! Again Olga took a turn across the room, and when he stopped there was a dark cloud upon his brow:

" Savotano," he said, "there is one more man whom I at least would be assured is not in my way. I mean that infernal monk." " I saw him this morning, my lord, and I am sure he is watching me. And he is not alone. Hellas others with him. I have been followed, and one a my men—the one who, entrapped Nevel—told me, not two hours ago, that he knew his steps had been followed." "And do you think this monk is at the bottom of it ?" asked the duke, with some uneasiness. "I know it, for I have seen him when I knew he was watching me." BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER XIII. THE PLOTTERS AT WORK.

The Count Conrad DaMorioff was able to sit up. Ile was in a great stuffed chair, playing with a fa- vorite dog, while near by him sat Stephen Urzen. Th e young nobleman had gained rapidly since the visit of Itnric, for the antidotes he had taken had proved efficient, and he soon came back to the point he had reached before the administering of the poison. " Stephen," lie said, pushing his dog gently from him, "has anything been heard yet from Runic Navel?" • "Not that 1 know of," returned Urzen. "Oh, I wish I were able to assist in the search. But have you heard anything of what suepicions may be afloat ?" "Only that the humpbacked priest is looked upon by some as having had some hand in it." "Ea—and how does suspicion point towards him ?" " Why—in no dixect way, I believe. I can, not understand it. All I know is, he is suspected." The count pondered a few moments, and he thought he could see it. Urzen did not know the secret of his friend's strange relapse, for that had been kept private; so he had no clue to the priest's true character such as the count possessed. " Lbelieve the fellow is a villain," Urzen resumed, "lie is surely a villainous-looking man." , "So he is,' responded the count. " 1 never saw such a wicked look before in any human face." " Ahruttered a voice close by the door.. "Who comes inter the flattering remark, my friend ?" Both the count and Stephen turned, and the humpbacked priest himself stood in their presence. " lla ! ,r he utteied, as he noticed the position of the invalid. " Up? By the holy Virgin, you are recovering.?" "Ay," returned Conradr" I am gaining fast now, as you may see." The priest struggled hard with his feelings, and 1 at length he managed to conceal the deep disap- pointment he felt. That is—he hid it from Ste- phen's eyes, but the count knew him too well. "You have not been very punctual of late, father," the latter said, also trying to conceal his real feelings. "No—no," returned Savotano in a perplexed manner ; " I admit it; but the fact is, I have been called away. Let's see—l have not been here since the evening on, which I found a stranger sitting by your side while you were asleep." " Who was title stranger I.t.'"' " 1 don't, know. I think I never saw him before. lie was a good-looking young man. Perhaps he was some relative of yours." This downright falsehood—so bold and flagrant— astonished even the count, for he knew the conver- sion which the priest had held with Runic on that occasion. As- quick as lightning, too, went the thought to the sick man's mind that this was to hide the probability of his being suspected in con- nection with Rune's disappearance. " I thought you knew that man," the count said, looking the priest sharply in the face. "No. I may have seen him before, but I did not surely recognise him then. I asked him why he was here, but he would not answer me save by urg- ing me to silence. Who was he, my son ? " The count was at first notinclined to answer,but he thought better•of it, and finally told the priest that it was Runic Nevel. The villain seemed much surprised at this, and professed to wonder why the fellow should come to t.tt place. Urzen, who knew nothing of the falbehood which rested under all this questioning, went- on and explained the nature of Buries mission) . and its results. And , thereupon Savotano expressed a wondrous degree of joy and gratification; .and he presumed even to bless God that such a reconciliation had taken place. " And now," the prioet named. after this mat- ter had been disposed of, "'how happened this Eud- den change in your disease i: my son? The doctors thought were were dying when I was here last." " Yes—l know," answered the count, still hiding the deep disgust that moved within him : " but a new physician was called in, and he prescribed a new medine. lle said the medicine I had been taking was unsuited to m.y,case,so he gave me new. You can see the result." " Yes—llsee," was the reply - "and as you seem to have very good company Illta'ke my leave. I have several calls to make before night." i The Count made no reply to this, and as the priest I. found th he was not urged to remain he arose at ' once. Ile stopped twice before he reached the door, but in neither case did he speak. As soon as he gained the street he turned: towards the upper part of the city, and he stoppednot until he had reached the palace of the Duke of Tula. The old porter ad- mitted him without qucation, and he made his way at once ta, the hall, where he inquired for the duke. One of the servants wont in search of his master, and when he returned , he- bade the priest follow him. _

The (hike was in his arivate room, and as soon as the servant had withdrawn he bade his visitor take I a seat„ "Now, Savotano, how is it ?" he asked. " Have you seen the count ? "Aye'-1 am from there now. By all that's bad, my lord, the villain :a-gaining." "Gaining ?" repeated Olga, with surprise. "But you assured me he waaweal-nigh gone.. "So he was—so he. was. But he is recovering now',, "But bow is it? "Why—he tells me. he hacks new physician, ana thati the old medicine was all condemned, and an entire new course prescribed." "-Anal under thia..new treatment ha is recovering, ehl!" "Yes." "-Well—have yam.: not taken some measures toASx this- new medieine ? By the god 4 Savotano, you must not let hirnaslip nova" "Ala, my lord,. I have only.toldlou how he-ex- the matter.. I have another explanation." " What is it, sir priest ? " Why—they,simply know thate someone ha a at- temped to 'poison the count." "-Ha! Did they' say anything "No—there,was no need. I know that tharnedi- eine he wee- taking before waa the right !rand of medicine, so ;Zer as it came from the hands. of the 'surgeon. Arad, tlabn there is another thing: The count must have had some powerful antidote on purpose fceltias poison." ' "flow tha,you know that ? "Simply, because he would not have now been alive had not such been the ease. You may be sure, my lord, that they know poison has been adminis- tered. They have discovered it in some way, and taken the-most effective and: speedy method to over- come it. lb know this." "And., do you think thay, suspect you.?" the duke asked, with some show of uneasiness. "1 don't know, but I fear they do. However, that; amounts-to nothing—only to prevent me from work,- ing any farther at present in the same direction.. L have not laid myself open to detection in any avay.. By heavens, 'tis too bad!: In four-and-twenty hours more he would have been a dead man." "hen you know when the discovery was "Mes—on the afternoon before auric Nevel,was captured. I was there just befor,e night, and, the gun-maker was then, there, and I noticed that the phials were gone from the table„though I gave no signs of having noticed it. They had even, then commenced some•treatment for his cure, foe L could see that the appearance of his. skin had changed. Y,ou must not lalameme "I do not, Sayotano. But there may be a. 7 r left yet." "Oh, yes ; there are a hundred ways in which we can dispose of him. But I may find same-way yet before he gets- out.' "Look ye," the duke said; after a short pondering over of his own thoughts You m-ast watch every chance. Something may turn up in our favour, You may find some opportunity to finish him yet. I wish you could." "1 will do all I can; be sure of that.. I shall watch narrowly. And now about tho other one. Young Nevel is safe,and can .be disposed of at any moment. I have let him live thus far, because I had no orders otherwise." a Aye—that was right," replied Olga; and as he did so he arose and commenced to pace the room, The priest followed him with his eyes,but said noth- ing. At length the duke stopped and looked Savo- tano in the face. "It would not be a difficult case to kill him," he uttered in a IJW whisper. "Not at all. Nothing could be more easy,' "And could detection ensue ?" "In no possible way.* "Then—" "Listen !" spoke the humpback, as Olga hesitated

div.head: COLLISION IN THE FIRTH OF
div.p: COLLISION IN THE FIRTH OF
FORTH.

- TWO STEA.MERS SUNK AND 13 LIVES LOST. ' In the Firth of Forth, on Sunday, a collision occurred between two steamers, which, in addition to the sinking. of the steamers, resulted in the loss of 13 lives. One of the vessels is the Britannia, 359 tons, of Leith, belong- ;.l,ag. to Messrs. James thirrie and Co., and the other the near, about the same tonnage, belonging to Grange- mouth, and owned by George Watson, Glasgow. The catastrophe happened off St. Abb'S Head, about half- Past three, while the Britannia was on her way to New- castle, and the Bear proceeding to Grangemouth from Middlesbrough with a cargo of 660 tons of pig iron. From the general account supplied it appears that both vessels saw the lights of each other, The night was dark but clear, with little or no sea. The Britannia Ported her helm, indicating the movement by a blast from the whistle, while the Bear blew two successive blasts, notifying that she was starboarding, but almost immediately after the second warning the Britannia crashed into the Bear amidships, and the latter vessel sank in a few seconds. A boat was launched from the Britannia as promptly, as possible, but only succeeded in rescuing two out of a crew of' 14, viz., the second mate and a lamp trimmer, who was at the wheel when the collision occurred. The bow of the Britannia was Rflocked completely out of her, and she filled with water in the fore cabin. While floating in this helpless con- dition the steamer Thames; of Grangemouth, hove in Sight, and, in response to a signal for assistance, came ,sloogside and took off the Britannia's passengers, num- "cring 45. A hawser was attached to the Thames with the object of towing the disabled steamer back to Leith, but she had only got about. two miles west of Fidra Is- land when the connection snapped, causing the Britan- nia to heel over and disappear under water. Her crew were left thundering in the water, all, however, having taken the precaution to provide themselves with life- belts, so that their rescue was rendered a comparatively easy task. Before 'however, the chief engineer, David Etterbanks, could be reached, he' disappeared. The Others, with the exception of the first mate, David Wil- son, who swam to the Thames, were picked up by the Yorkshire Lass, of Alloa, who were coming up the, Firth: The Thames proceeded to Leith, which was reached about seven o'clock in the evening, and where the pas- sengers and rescued members of the respective crews Were housed in the Sailors' Home. All the men lost were married, and a number of them leave families.

div.head: IRISH DIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.
MR. DILLON'S RETURN.

Mr. John Dillon alled from New York for France on Saturday for the purpose of conferrin2; with Mr. O'Brien and others ot the majority ot the Irish Parliamentary party on the crisis brought on by the Leadership ques- tion. He had telegraphed asking that the O'Brien-Par- nell negotiations should not be closed till after he had had an opportunity of taking part. Meanwhile, con- ferences have again been taking place at Boulogne be- tween Messrs. M'Carthy, O'Brien, Sexton, and Condon. The discussions are described as animated. One sitting 'lasted fromafter supper on Friday night till past four on Saturday morning. Messrs. M'Carthy, Sexton, and 'Condon returned to London on Saturday night, but declined to say anything respecting the conferences. They said, however, that Mr. O'Brien had no intention of coming to England for thepresent. MR. PARNELL AT LIMERICIt. Mr. Parnell opened his political campaign at Limerick on Sunday, when be addressed a meeting of twenty thousand of the men of North Munster. It is more than ten years since his last visit to Limerick, and those who witnessed Mr. Parnell's reception then and now say that, taking the altered circumstances in consideration, Sun- day's meeting did not compare unfavourably with the Previous one. , There attended the Mayor of Limerick, some half- nesen members of the Limerick Corporation,and perhaps ▪ docen other representative men, with a crowd of many bheusands of labourers and artizans and a limited number of farmers and shopkeepers. The Roman Catholic clergy were absent, except one or two of the innior city curates, who certainly did not attend out of IsTrapathy for Mr. Parnell, but on the platform and in r•ne procession the absence of many of the leading Natienalists of the locality was very noticeable. Accord- ing to arrangement, Mr. Parnell left Dublin by train on Saturday. On the way from Dublin to Limerick Mr. Parnell made Several carriage-window speeches at stations where stop- Pages were made, and generally was well received. At Monastevan, however, there was a fight on the platform betweenthe rival partisana, and at Oola a hostile demon- stration. In the course of his Limerick speech Mr. Parnell criti- tiaed the action of the bishops, and denied that their interference was on the question of morality. Respect- ing the Boulogne conference, he was perfectly satisfied With what had been done. Mr. O'Brien and himself o• und themselves so far in agreement, and they fully recognized that, pending the resumption of negotiations, steps would have to be taken by men who were certainly not under his (Mr. Paanell's) control, upon whom a very great responsibility would rest if Mr. O'Brien and he were not able to resume their conference withthe assured hope of success. If a solution of the Irish question such as the Irish people expected could be assured from Eng- lish Liberals, he would retire from the chairmanship of a party which he scarcely cared to lead so long as it retained its present composition. Later in the day a deputation waited on Mr. Parnell and asked his interference in the 'case of John Daly, the convict; and Mr. Parnell afterwards delivered a speech in the market field to a mass meeting. Mr. Parnell left Limerick on Monday morning for Dublin, where he is expected to take part at a meeting of the National League. He also expects to speak on the 18th at Tralee ; on the 25th at Waterford; and on the Ist of February at Ennis.

- MR. PARNELL AND THE NATIONAL LEAGUE. Mr. Parnell returned from Avondale to Dublin on Tuesday, and in the afternoon presided at the fortnightly Meeting of the Central Branch of the National League. Mr. Parnell said there existed a conspiracy of lying Which, next to Billingsgate, seemed to be one of the pro- ulinent characteristics of his opponents' resources and arguments. It had been sought to contradict his state- Ment at Limerick that Mr. Justin M'Carthy conveyed an outline of his "interview manifesto" to Mr. Gladstone. Ile communicated to Mr. M'Carthy an outline of what a'S known as the four points—namely, the questions !egarding the Constabulary the Judicial Bench, dl,e Land, and the Retention of Irish Members. Mr. 'l'oarthy went to Mr. Gladstone with that information, and admitted it on two subsequent occasions. The 'lairesto was read by him (Mr. Parnell) to Mr. M'Carthy In the presence of Mr. John Redmond before it was corn- ,TUnicated to the newspapers, and Mr. M'Carthy there- "Pon said, "Well, all I can say is this, that, as I have already told you, Mr. Gladstone intends to deny every 1311 e of these statements point blank." The subscriptims ‘0 the National League showed that members were not going to desert that organisation for mongrel committees 1103a,inly composed of expectant lawyers. In view of the exing up of the reserve funds in Paris through the aetion of Mr. M'Carthy, it was important that every exertion be made for the evicted tenants, who were I,Potinded soldiers of the war against landlordism. Mr. arnell returned to Avondale in the evening.

MR McCARTHY AND MR. PARNELL. Mr. Justin McCarthy writes :—Mr. Parnell and Mr. John Redmond have attempted to contradict my state- Inert that I did not inform Mr. Gladstone of the contents °f Mr. Parnell's intended Manifesto. On that point I an not merely the best, but the only, authority. I did not inform Mr. Gladstone of the contents of Mr. Parnell's Manifesto. I was asked to call on Mr. Gladstone and to *lf'equest from him certain assurances with regard to the uture measure of Home Rule. Mr. Gladstone gave me an account of his opinions, his wishes, and his willingness cn the subject. From what he told me I was able to °Press to Mr. Parnell my conviction that if the manifesto 'were published Mr. Gladstone would be in a pcsition to Rive certain of its statements a fiat contradiction. That 4. the whble story. BANKRUPTCY OF AN IRISH M.P. The failure has been announced at the London Bank- Court of Garrett Michael Byrne, M.P. for Wick- .(llY? County, and described as of 21, Parliament-st., "estminster. The petitioning creditor is a Mrs. Hatch, °f Birkdale, Lancashire. The bankruptcy of Mr. Byrne, ;410 is a supporter of Mr. Parnell, will create a vacancy °r !Vest Wicklow, for which he was returned on the 4th December, 1885. In 1880 he was elected for county _oxford, but resigned his seat in 1883. Mr. Bryne was "gaged in business in Liverpool for many years as an :abate agent and mortgage broker, and at one time took considerable part in local municipal affairs.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on: Wednesday morning .A lderman Harrison presided, and there were also present the Revs. G. F. Roberts and E. C. E. Carleton, Messrs. Blackhurst, Ratcliffe, T. Jones, Heaton, D. Jones, Davies, Aukland, Jolley, Balharry, W. -Houghton, Clarke, Smith, Turton, Humphries, Warburton, Dobson, Hood-Wright, Owen, Eilshall, J. Houghton, Hibbert, Swinton, J. C. Sutton (clerk). S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of the Padgate Schools.) TOWNSHIPS IN ARREARS Tile CLERK reported that the total of the cheques that were to be paid at that meeting was £1,900, while the treasurer only had in hand £1,700. He supposed that he would, therefore, have the approval of the Board to pro- ceed against any of the townships which were in arrears with their calls. This suggestion was agreed to by the Board. Mr. R. OWEN subsecidently asked which of the townships were in arrears.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said his township had paid its call that morning.—The CHAIR- MAN : You have saved your reputation. (Laughter.)— The CLERK said Rixton had not yet paid its first call, which was due on the 9th October, and Southwcrth- with-Croft was also in arrears with its first call.—Mr. OWEN said he was not surprised that Croft or any other country township was in arrears. He was afraid they should not be able to pay the call, especially if those salaries went on increasing. (Laughter.)—The CLERK said Burtonwood had already paid its third call, which was not yet due. The townships which had not yet paid their second call were Grappenhall, Penketh, Great Sankey, Winwick, and Woolston. THE 'WORKHOUSE. The House Committee through its minutes thanked the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton for performing the duties of chaplain during the vacancy of the office. The Work- house Master acknowledged gifts to the inmates from the following :—Mr. S. Parsonage, Winwick-road ; . Mr. Pritchard, Horsemarket-st. : and Mr. B rierley, Sankey-st.

SCHOOL FEES. It was reported that school fees had been allowed in 94 cases, 68 of which were old cases and 26 new. THE CHAPLAINCY OF PADOATE SCHOOLS. A letter was read from the Rev. J. J. Langhana, vicar of Padgate, thanking the Board for his appointment to the chaplaincy of Padgate Industrial Schools, and en- closing the permission of the Bishop of Liverpool to hold the office.

THE GUARDIANS AND THE WARRINGTON INFIRMARY.— LETTER FROM THE HOUSE SURGEON. The CHAIRMAN said that with regard to some remarks made at the previous meeting of the Board he had re- ceived the following letter from Dr. J. Turville Smith, the senior house surgeon at the Infirmary :—" A report having appeared in the Warrington papers on Decem- ber 20th last, of a meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, at which a most unjust attack was made up3u the Infirmary and its officers, allow me to correct some of the reckless and grossly misleading statements made by certain members at that meeting7With regard to the case of Robert Murray, who was said to have been "turned out" of the Infirmary, I beg to say (1) That Murray was not" turned out but left the hospi- tal by his own desire and against advice. (2) That a cab would have been sent for, as in other cases, had he asked for one; he did not ask. (3) That crutches were lent to him, and the porter had orders to go with him and see him to his destination. Murray, however, would not wait till the porter was ready to go, but went off on the crutches by himself. The crutches were not returned. Statements were made to the effect that patients were turned out of hospital after the usual six weeks' treatment and no further interest taken in them. Those statements, for which the persons who made the m could have no authority, are unjust and contrary to facts. It was also stated" that two men, a short time ago. had been turned .out of the Infirmary, and brought to the Workhouse door and then left." That statement is not in accordance with the facts,which are as follows: —The two men referred to were discharged when fit to leave the hospital, and as they had no means of getting away, cabs were taken for them, and they were driven, at their own request, to the Workhouse. The porter went with them to look after them, as he invariably does when patients need looking after, and their friends have not come to take them away. When a patient is fit to leave this hospital he is discharged. If he has a home to go to, he goes there and is treated as an out-patient if necessary; if 'he has no home he naturally goes to the workhouse. He is not sent there; he is simply told ha can be kept here no longer, the • number of beds in this Infirmary being iar too small to admit of any cases being kept in hospital after the necessity for their staying here has ceased."— The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Harbourne told him that before a patient was turned out of the Infirmary hospital if he was a fit person to go to the workhouse he (Mr. Harbourne) always got an intimation from the house surgeon to go and fetch the patient. It seemed as though they had been rather hard on the Infirmary, and it was a pity, because it was one of the best institutions Warrington could boast of, and there were always people who took advantage of the smallest circumstance to excuse themselves from contributing to the Infirmary.— Mr. HEATON said the remarks of Dr. Smith did not really affect the case. He told them the porter was to go with the man, but admitted that the porter did not go.—The CHAIRMAN: That was the patient's own fault.—Mr. JOLLEY : The man tells us different.—Mr. HEATON said he had every reason to believe that it was the patient's own fault to a certain extent, but the case came before the Board in such a way as almost to compel them to make the remarks they made. When these cases came before the Board time after time and they had evidence before them he for one should never stand there and keep his mouth closed as to what he believed to be correct. The patient referred to left the Infirmary, and after walking about 200 yards to Froghall bridge he fell down and had to be brought to the workhouse. He con- sidered it was a disgrace to the Infirmary.—The CHAIR- MAN : He left the Infirmary against advice. —Mr. HEATON said he did not believe the man was taken by the shoulders and pushed out of the Infirmary, but he con- sidered a cab might have been sent for, and if it were thought necessary that the porter should go with the man it was the duty of the house surgeon to see that he did go. Seeing that the man had £3 in his pockets it was the least they could have done at the Infirmary to send for 'a conveyance to fetch him to the workhouse so that he should not fall in the road. Complaints of that sort caused the institution to lose pound -after pound, because it gave people the impres- sion that if a man 'was poor he was pushed out or the infirmary into the streets.—The CHAIRMAN said that was a false impression. He knew it was the wish of the governing body that everybody should be treated in the most humane way.—Mr. HEATON said that poor people who had to make use of the institution had got the im- pression that they were put out as soon as they could be got rid of, and it prevented them from subscribing. He had spoken to men who had been in the institution, and that was their impression; he did not say it was his.— The CHAIRMAN said the Infirmary Management were not at all responsible for erroneous impressions.—Mr. DAVIES said he was surprised at Mr. Heaton' as nobody was more ready to tell them to pay no heed to outside statements. He (Mr. Davies) did not believe the Infirm- ary was a bit to blame in that case.—The CHAIRMAN said it appeared to him that Dr. Smith's letter was a full and absolute answer to the complaints made, and he thought that in justice to the Infirmary they ought to take a vote upon the question as to whether they were satisfied.— Mr. HEATON thought the matter ought first to be thoroughly investizated.—The CLERK suggested that he might write to the Infirmary stating that they had re- ceived the explanation and that there were circum- stances in the explanation of which the members had not before had any knowledge, and also pointing out that where a man had sufficient means to provide lodgings for himself, and was sufficiently well to be discharged from the hospital, the proper thing to do was to endeavour to arrange for his admission to some home where he could be treated.—Mr. BLACKHURST thought this was the proper course to adopt, and the CLERK'S suggestion was agreed to.

THE CHAPLAINCY. The appointment of a chaplain to the Workhouse was the next business to be considered. Applications for the appointment were read from the following clergymen : Rev. J. G. Richards, vicar of St. Ann's, Warrington; Rev. G. F. Allton, vicar oi St. Barnabas's, Warrington ; Rev. T. Rigby, vicar of St. Peter's, Warrington; Rev. I. Philips, vicar of Orford; and the Rev. H. V. Pigot, vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington.—Mr. Donsos moved that Mr. Pigot be appointed, and he mentioned that at present the inmates of the Workhouse who attended church went to St. Paul's as also did the officers.—Mr. D. JONES, in seconding this proposition, pointed out that although the seats of St. Paul's were not free seats nothing was charged for the pews occupied by Workhouse inmates.— Mr. .Tonx HoxrcarroN proposed that Mr. Rigby be ap- pointed.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON supported the nomination Of Mr. Pint, and remarked that St. Paul's was nearer to the Workhouse. than St. Barnabas's.—Mr. T. Jotsips seconded the proposal to appoint Mr. Rigby.— The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS said his inclination was ratber to 'support those whom he knew He therefore spoke in favour of the appointment of Mr. Rigby, the Rev. I. Philips living rather far away from the Workhouse for practical purposes.—Mr. BLACKHURST also supported Mr. Rigby's nomination.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. HOOD-WRIGHT seconded, the appointment of Mr. Philips. On a first vote being taken there were fourteen votes each given for Mr. Pigot and Mr. Rigby and 'eight for Mr. Philips. A deciding vote between Mr. Pigot and Mr. Rigby was then taken, and fourteen vote'd for Mr. Pigot and only nine for Mr. Rigby. Mr. Pigot was declared elected. -

div.head: PAYMENT TO A CATHOLIC PRIEST.
div.p: THE PAYMENT TO A CATHOLIC PRIEST.

The CHAIRMAN, in accordance with notice of motion, moved that £2O a year be paid to the Rev. Father Feeney, of St. Alban's Catholic Church, for his services at the Workhouse, in place of the £lO previously fixed upon.—Mr. BLACKITHRST seconded the proposal.—Mr. T. JONES said he understood, that the matter was thrashed out and settled at a previous meeting,and he deprecated the bringing of it forward a second time.—Mr. DAVIES said that on the previous occasion he had moved that the payment to the Catholic clergyman be 45, and not £lO, and he should move an amendment to that effect

now. The Roman Catholic inmates of the Workhouse never numbered more than a third, and if if+ paid eo to the Catholic priest, it would be more in proportion than they were paying their own chaplain.—Mr. RAT-- CLIFFE seconded Mr. Dasie,s's amendment.—Mr. HIBBERT supported the proposition to give £2o.—Mr. ilsa-Torr proposed that the sum remain at £lo.—The Rev. E; O. E. CARLETON regretted that the matter should have been re-opened.—Mr. R. OWEN said that the work for which the chaplain was appointed used to be all done for £5O 'a year,but if they made that increase they would now be paying £lOO. Ho considered that was the best Board that had ever existed in Warrington for raising salaries,l and if he were an officer he would always b 3 wishing for October to come round that he might make an applica- • tion for an increase of salary, as he would be sure to get it. (Laughter.)—S Member having remarked that the Catholic clergy were quite satisfied with the sum of £lO that had been already fixed upon, Mr. Hoop- WRIGHT replied that Father Lennon, of Newton, had said to him that £lO was a paltry sum and would ' pro- bably not be accepted.—Mr. HEATON : I believe Father Feeney has expressed himself satisfied.—The CHAIRMAN said that Father Feeney had expressed himself in the most gracious manner to him, but at the same time he (the Chairman) could not help thinking that he-would have been better pleased if they had made the sum larger. (Laughter.) The Chairman added that, with the consent of his seconder, he would withdraw his motion in favour of Mr.Davies's amendment.—On a vote being taken there were fourteen votes in favOur of £lO being the remuneration of the Catholic priest, and six for £l5. The,former sum was therefore agreed to. The relief cases were then taken.
ANNUAL DINNER OF THE BLUE COAT BROTHERLY SOCIETY.

The annual dinner of the Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society, was held at 019 Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., on Monday evening. Mr. William Sharp, one of the patrons of the society, presided, and Mr. Edward Rose, head master of the Blue Coat School, occupied the vice-chair. The Chairman was sup- ported by the Mayor (Aid. Francomb), the Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, vicar of Holy Trinity Church, Alderman Sutton, Alderman Jos. Davies, Mr. P. Davies, Mr. W. Owen, Mr. F. Monks, Mr. John White, Mr. Thos. Morris, and Mr. H. Greenall. The Vice-Chairman was supported by Mr. F. W. Gilbert, Mr. T. E. Hughes, Mr. W. J. Freeston, secretary of the society, and others. The speeches were interspersed with songs, by Messrs. Rose, Forshaw, and Allen, a eupho- nium solo by Mr. Andel-ton, and a pianoforte solo by Mr. Lane, who was the accompanist during the evening. There were about 60 guests present. The usual loyal toasts having been honoured with due fervour and the accustomed vocal accompaniments, Alderman JOSEPH DAVIES proposed the toast of "The Church," coupling with it the bishop, and the clergy of the diocese, and the ministers of all denominations. In the course of a lengthy speech, Mr. Davies said he had, more especially as he had grown older, observed that there was a very wide gulf between the clergy and the laity in these days, and he thought neither the clergy nor the laity were entirely to blame for this. .But a great revolution had since taken place in the cause of Christianity in England. When the Hon. and Rev. Horace Powis came to Warrington there was a great revolution there. He wasvery ably assisted by his curate, the Rev. Frank Gregg Hopwood, who became rector of Winwick, He (the speaker) was pleased to think that the clergy during the last 10, 20, or even 40 years, had been striving to the best of their ability to help the laity in their endeavours to overcome the evils we had to con- tend with. He believed the present rector of Warring- ton was a man whose heart was entirely devoted to his work. (Applause.) He (Ald. Davies) was quite pleased to hear the applause at that, becaugt he had seen the in- fluence of the rector's work operating in the town. (Ap- plause.) His friend Mr. Carleton—(applause) he (the speaker) knew had worked hard in the town for some time, and was, in a quiet manner, trying to do his best in Trinity parish. He (Mr. Davies) believed the clergy of all denominations in Warringtonwere doing their hest, and that the Dissenting ministers and the Catholic clergy of the town had a better feeling towards the ministers of the Church of England than had ever existed before (renewed applause) and he was pleased to believe that in the town of Warrington, through the exertions of these gentlemen there was more of Christianity than there had ever been before.

The Rev, F. W. WILLIS in responding said the company had been drinking prosperity to the church, and he urged that among essentials to the promotion of that prosperity were the realisation of the divine nature and spiritual constitution of the church, a knowledge of its historic continuity, and that external unity which was in accord- ance with the will of Jesus Christ, the material support of the Church, its schools, and charities,and the mainten- ance of spiritual life by the constant and right use of all the means of grace. The rev, gentleman expressed his acknowledgement of the courtesy and kindness of the present bishop of the diocese, and congratulated his (the speaker's) late bishop on his elevation from the bishop- ric of Peterborough to the archbisopric of York, Deal- ing with the subject of the emoluments of his (Mr. Willis's) living he said that the nominal value was £1,500 a year, but this was subject to deductions of £3OO in tithes, £3OO for rates and taxes and collection of tithes, and £3OO for the stipends of additional clergy, leaving only £3OO. The Rector also expatiated on the manifold duties a clergyman was called upon to per- form, and said the present number of parochial clergy for the town, 12, was not adequate for the population,

being two to every 4,000, instead of, as it ought to be, two to- every 2,600. , He expressed. his deep pense of gratithde.to the Nonconformist ministers of Warrington for their courtesy to him, and acknowledged their piety and indefatigable work ta which, iies,4l.ad.no doubt, much orthe•good accomplished was due 7. :(Applause.) The Rea. E. C. CARLETON then responded. He re- marked that the Blue Coat Society was an old iiistitution,, and he truited it would long continue to flourish as vigor- ously as now ; and that 'would be the Case so long as it had a body of trustees like the present one, and at it was presided over by such a head master as at pre- sent. (Applause.) The past year had been, he said, an eventful one for the church and not an inauspicious one. The church gained, he thought, in • the estimation of the country. It certainly now got better bishops. Owing to those, in authority understanding and carrying out their .duty better, there never was greater care taken in the selection of indn to preside over the interests of the . church. Mr. Carleton referred to the fact that they were preparing to welcome amongst them a new incumbent in Warrington and trusted that he might find his sojourn there as pleasant as his (the speaker's) had been to him.' (Much applause.) Dr. WHITE proposed "The army, navy; and reserve forces," coupled with the name of Mr. P. DAVIES, who responded at some length, and ,particularly dwelt upon the fact that new inventions, such as the-latest which would mow down whole regi- ments at a time and at a mile and a half distance, were making war more and more terrible. Such inventions, he was afraid were-making it impossible for men to show their pluck and their courage in war. He combatted the idea that the volunteers would not be likely to manifest these qualities in action,and hoped they would soon have a elianbe .of showing whether they would fight or not. (Laughter.) Mr. FORSHAW proposed" The trustees of the Blue Coat School." He said this toast had frequently been pro- posed by Old Blues, and he himself had on many occa- sions had the pleasure of proposing it himself; and he must confess that sometimes it had been very difficult indeed to say somethipg new, but on this occasion, he thought, he should have something new to say in connec- tion with the toast. It was the first time that a lawyer and yet an Old Blue had had the pleasure of proposing it —(applause)—and in the second place, what was more important he had to congratulated the trustees upon the many excellent improvements recently made at the school—(applause)—and also upon the fact that the number of scholars had been increased from 40 to about 60. There was now a very handsome and spacious dining room, and the dormitories were enlarged, and the lava- tories improved. The trustees, while looking after the physical well-being of the children,were also moving with the times with respect to their intellectual culture. Mr. Forshaw then read an extract from the Inspector's re- port on the recent examination, which stated that the school had returned to its normal state of excellence. Mr. Forshaw coupled with the toast the name of the Chairman. (Applause.) Mr. BURGESS endorsed the observations of Mr. Forshaw, remarking that a debt of deep gratitude was due to the teachers for the manner in which they had carried out their work. The CHAIRMAN responded. He mentioned as a re- markable fact that the school, though it had existed 350 years and done such goed work, had never received any addition to its original endowments, except just recently in the foundation of some exhibitions, in one or other of the Universities. The school was so well conducted by Mr. and Mrs. Rose that it was never in a more efficient state than at present. (Applause.) Mr. John WHITE proposed "The Mayor and Corpora- tioa and the town and trade of Warrington," coupling with the toast the Mayor and Mr. Morris. Mr. White expressed the opinion that the Mayor was a worthy successor to those 28 gentlemen who had preceded him in the civic chair of Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. White, referring to the Corporation, mentioned as a ' proof of the labours it performed, that it was divided into 14 committees, these being divided into sub- , committees, many members being on seven committees.' Alderman Burgess, Mr. White took occasion to mention, had been 36 years in the Corporation, Alderman Holmes 34 years, Alderman Harrison 26 years, and Alderman Davies nearly 20 years. (Applause.) Mr. White expressed the belief that if in every ward two members could be nominated for the Corporation, not mere than 500 of the electors wonld go to the poll, not because they were indifferent to, but because they were satisfied with, the management of the town. Mr. White, c dealing with the trade of Warrington, said the town would arrive at a great crisis in its history when the Ship Canal was completed, and hoped that the Corpora- tion and the traders generally would join to make the most of the opportunity that would then be afforded to them. Warrington was, he said,- once one of the great centres of the coaching traffic, and afterwards became one of the places that was touched by the barge canals, it then became the next town after Manchester and Liverpool to which a second passenger railway was made, and now it was to be the first town where the first Ship Canal was to touch, except Runcorn, after it left the sea. The MAYOR, 051 risingto reply, was received with most hearty applause. He said there was no doubt that the members of the Corporation had got a lot of very import- ant work to do • and more than that, they did it. He was sure the older members were mire active in their work than any of the younger ones. He only hoped that as time went on those who were younger would follow in the footsteps of those who had gone before them. The Corporation had at the present time their hands full of work. In' a few months they would have taken over a, very great undertaking, the Water Works, and consider- ing that they had spent about a quarter of a million over that purchase, it would be understood that a very great

responsibility rested upon the Corporation. I.le believed .they felt convinced that they could complete that pur- chase withoutadcling ond penny to the rates at the pre- sent time, and that in the very near future the income derived from that purchase would be beneficial to the ratepayers. The Mayor also referred to the desirability of improved bath accommodation in the town, and to the fact that the subject of the provision of technical education had been broached at the last Council meeting. He believed every reading, thinking, man, must be con- vinced that our artisans and young men must have technical education if we were to hold'our own among , the manufacturing nations of the world. Formerly we had no competition or very little,but newwe had competition from every civilised part of the world. Something was wanted to bridge over the time between leaving school at 13 or 14 years of age and manhood, and he had no doubt that if the intervening years could be spent in attending a technical school the next generation would be much cleverer than the present, and we should have little to fear from the competition of the foreigner. (Applause.) In the course of remarks upon the trade of the district, • the Mayor expressed a wish that each local manufacturer 'could be induced to send to the museum an exhibition case of what he made, so that visitors could form a, better conception of the industries of the town. War- rington, he said, had been second to none in the manu- facture of iron, and he believed stood first in the manu- facture of wire. It had immense foundries, glass works, india rubber .works, potteries, chemical works; and last but not least had arrived at perfection in the matter of Crosfieli's soap ; and if it could get technical education to perfection it would certainly be right. As Mr. Monks had taken the matter in hand perfection might certainly be expected; and it might have. , one of the best technical education establishments lin the country. The Mayor concluded by pointing out that though great things were anticipated from the Ship Canal the rates of the town must not be increased too fast, with the result of deterring manufacturers from , ' coming amongst us, but the object must be to get as Imany manufacturers as possible to come, and then very many advantages would be derived from the canal pass- i ing so near to the town. (Applause.) Mr: MORRIS also replied. He thought that trade gener- ally was prospering very fairly, though, great poverty I had been caused in the town through the stoppage of work by the severe weather. Ironworkers' plates he said were at that time last year £8 ss. per ton, and to day about £6,w,hile ironworkers' wages were about the same, so that the men in the iron trade were getting the best of it. Mr. Morris criticised the McKinley tariff, and expressed the belief that it would cripple the competition of America so much that England would be more pros- perous through it than ever before. The SECRETARY (Mr. Forshaw) read the 36th annual report. This stated that the expenditure for the past year had been £2O Bs. 6d., and that the credit balance was £5O 19s. sd. The Committee always received from employers satisfactory reports of the conduct of the boys sent to them. The Committee had a scheme under con- sideration whereby th 3 Society's operations might be extended to the Sisterly Blues. The Committee deplored the death of Mr. H. Stanton, for many years a valuable trustee and patron. The CirannuAN then proposed, briefly on account of the late hour, "The Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society." He expressed himself very glad to hear the suggestion as to extending the Society to embrace the Sisterly Blues, and pointed out that more subscribers I would be acceptable, alid that to contribute to the4chool was to give money so as to do the maximum of good and F the minimum of harm.
Mr. ROSE briefly replied. The health of the Chairman having been drunk, "Auld Lang Syne " and the National Anthem were sung, and the company dispersed.

The annual tea party took place at the school on Tues- day evening. There was a good attendance of "Old Blues." The rooms were very tastefully decorated for the occasion and a good tea was provided by Mrs. Rose, '•The tables were presided over by Mesdames Rose,Forshaw, W. Richardson, H. Fairclough and Miss Shaw'and Miss Holt. Amongst those present, besidesthe above and the Headmaster and Mistress, were Miss Hedgcock and Miss Smith and Messrs. W. J. Forshaw (Hon. Secretary) Thomas Lane W. Richardson Povey,Crompton and Smith. After tea the children commenced games, and enjoyed themselves thoroughly. Nuts and oranges were freely distributed to them and they partook of cake kindly sent by Mr. N. B. Percival. The "Old Blues" indulged in dancing and dispersed at 10.30, having heartily enjoyed themselves.
