div.head: TEE RAILWAY STRIKE. XOH DEAR DOCTOR, MUST MY X DARLING CHILD DIE.
div.p: TEE RAILWAY STRIKE. XOH DEAR DOCTOR, MUST MY X DARLING CHILD DIE.

At the Glasgow Small Department Court, on Monday, it was agreed to select several cases for trial in February and decide thereby the 228 actions brought by the North British Company against their employes for leaving work without notice.

-On Tuesday the Lord Provost of Edinburgh strove to negotiate with the directors in the hope of bringing about a settlement of the Scotch railway strike. He had an interview with Mr. Harford, who gave him an outline of the men's demands—that they desired a work- ing week of sixty hours, that signalmen and shunters have a workingday of eight hours, that time and a half should be paid for Sunday labour, and time and a quar- ter for week-day nvertime. The Lord Provost then held a consultation with Mr. Walker, the manager of the North British Railway. The interview was private, but it is understood that his Lordship was informed that there was no prospect of meditation, except on the condition that the men returned to work. In that case their demands would be considered. At the men's mass meeting on Tuesday at Edinburgh and Glasgow it wAs stated that the railway companies had been put to great Inconvenience by further desertions and that in all probability the Glasgow and South-Western men would come out. A conference of miners' delegates was held in Glasgow, and a resolution adopted convening a national conference of miners, seamen, dock labourers carters,. and vanmen for Saturday, with the object of voting in favour of a general cessation of work until the railway men have secured a settlement. It is believed there will be a wide response to the invitation to join the strike, and the outlook is now regarded as serious. On Wednesday, the Lord Provost of Edinburgh in- formed a meeting of the railway men on strike that his efforts to bring about a settlement with the manager of North British Railway had been ineffectual. The Lord Provost has called a public meeting of the citizens to consider what steps should be taken to bring the struggle to a close. Statements published on Wednes- day show the traffic decreases on the lines concerned to be enormous.

On Thursday the Citizens' Conciliation Committee at Glasgow met the representatives of the men, but no pro- gress was made towards a settlement, the servants on strike insisting that their Executive should be recog- nised by the directors and that their demands should be conceded before they resume work. Many additional subscriptions have been received on behalf of the men, who are as determined as ever not to retire from the struggle.
THE, LIVERPOOL WATER SUPpLY AND
THE MERSEY AQUEDUCT.

The agitation from outside has at length impelled the Liverpool Water Committee to take action in tilt.) matter of obtaining a temporary supply from Lake Vyrnwy pending the completion of the aqueduct pipe-line under the Mersey near Runcorn Bridge. The discussion in the Council and in the Press has revealed the fact that, in consequence of the corrosion of the pipe lines between Prescot and Rivington, the city is 'only getting 12,000,000 gallons a day instead of 16,000,000, and that there is no prospect of the deficiency being made up flora the Vyrnwy because of the difficulty in carrying the aqueduct beneath the river at Fidler's Ferry. The city has lately been placed on short commons so far as the water supply is concerned, and unless something can be done—and that speedily—it will be farther curtailed. , Under these circumstances, it became necessary to look r about fur some means of supplementing the present service until such time as the Vyrnwy supply may be available. The question was discussed at considerable length at the fortnightly meeting of the Water (Vyrnwy Works) Committee, held on Monday, in the Municipal Offices. Mr. Arthur Holme moved that the engineer (Mr. Deacon) be requested to prepare plans and estimates , for the construction of a temporary pipe-line across the Mersey, either in the bed of the river or at a convenient elevation above the river; and that the Town Clerk be instructed to obtain the sanction of the Mersey Conver- vators, the Board of Trade, and the Warrington Town Council to such an arrangement. Mr. Holm° said that ' such a step was absolutely necessary if a water famine was to be averted. If this pipe-line were provided they would be able to have a supply from Vyrnwy at an addi- tional cost of between £3,000 and £5,000, while the tunnel under the Mersey would be proceeded with in the ordinary course. Mr. Thomas Hughes seconded the reso- lution, remarking that the aotion now taken might have been adopted long since. The resdution of Mr. Holmes was agreed to unani- mously. WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

div.head: TRURSDAY.—Before his Honour, Judge Ffoulkes.
div.p: TRURSDAY.—Before his Honour, Judge Ffoulkes.

A LUNATIC'S PROPERTY.—Mr. A. Browne made an ap- plication, under section 132 of the Lunacy Act, 1890, for an order to vest the property of a lunatic, named William Henry Taylor, formerly a Friendly Society collector at Warrington in the name of Mr. Basil Shearer, collector to the Warrington Board ot Guardians. After an argu- ment, the application was withdrawn, leave being given to renew it at some future date. AN UN-EXPECTED BlLL.—lsaac Haskins, collier, 84, Regent-street, Earlestown, sued Minnie Corlett, domestic servant, Newton, for 235. claim for board and lodgings. From the evidence it appeared that defendant and her sister went to reside with plaintifL and his wife and stayed there nine weeks. Plaintiff said that both defen- dant and her sister had promised to pay him 10s. each as soon as they received their first month's money. The defendant denied her liability, and said she and her sister were invited to a christening, and when they pro- posed leaving plaintiff and his wife persuaded them to stop. Defendant admitted having asked for a bill of what she owed, but said she did this simply out of com- pliment not expecting any charge to be made. She had made three payments on account. A verdict was given for the full amount claimed. APPLICATION FOR THE COMMITTAL OF A LOCAL DOCTOR. —Mr. Benjamin Johnson, coal dealer, applied for a com- mittal order against Dr. C. N. Spinks, of Warrington, for non-compliance with a judgmentbf the court. The plaintiff said Dr. Spinks held an appointment under the Board of Guardians, and could pay off the debt at once. —The Registrar (Mr. Nicholson) : Are there no goods you can take P—The plaintiff: I suppose not. He -added that he believed the effice which Dr. Spinks held under the Board of Guardians was worth £250 a year.— His Honour said there was already a commitment out against Dr. Spinks, and as he had not yet paid off that debt, it looked as though he could not pay.—The Regis- trar said the previous order was mane on the 4th December.--7Hi5 Honour remarked that as the plaintiff in that case was not pursuing his remedy, he might sus- pend that order and make an order on the present appli- cation.—Mr. Longland having come into courthe Regis- trar explained to him that there was now an application for a commitment against Dr. Spinks, but it appeared that there was a previous order of commitment made in favour of Mr. Harrison, a client of Mr. Longland. As no action had been taken under that order, his Honour thought of discharging it as Mr. Longland's client seemed to.be keeping other people out.—Mr. Longland said he did not appear when the order was made, and he had not been in communication with his client since. His client had told him that Dr. Spinks had agreed to pay the debt in a month and the order was made for that time.—His Honour said there did not seem to be any sus- picion of collusion, and he must, therefore, dismiss the present application.—Mr. Longland said he would see his client and see that proceedings were taken. ALLEGED BREACH OF WARRANTY.—In this case Edward ' Wibberley, of 163, Knutsford-road, Latchford, bus pro- prietor and milk dealer, sued Josiah Rollev, Elton,Derby- shire, blacksmith, for a total sum of £l4 17s. Bd., in connection with an alleged breach of yrarranty. Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Taylor, of Bakewell, the defendant. In his opening statement, Mr. Browne said that his client wanting a horse for the purpose of his business as bus proprietor, and knowing that defendant had one Wrote to him asking him if the horse was still for sale and if the horse was , fit for bus work. The letter which was received in reply from the defendant had unfortunately been lost, but ' witnesses would be called to prove that in it the horse was represented as having four good legs and being in sound condition. Plaintiff afterwards went over to Elton,saw the horse and bought it for £B. After the horse was brought to Warrington it was found to be nothing lant a cripple —in fact, a 4, body on four sticks," and Mr. Wibberley had afterwards to destroy it in order to avoid being pro- secuted by an inspector of the R.S.P.C.A. Several wit- nesses were called in support of the plaintiff's case. The defence was that no warranty had been given and that the plaintiff knew the defects of the animal, which were not so serious as had been represented, before he bought it. In giving judgment, his Honour poieted ot that the plaintiff had seen the horse before he bought, and he argued that under the circumstances it was not likely the defendant would give the warranty which it was alleged he had given. A verdict was therefore returned for the defendant.

MORLEY is the fixst Liberal leader filll has addressed a political audience since 61.01 meaning of the.lrish difficulty has become and, as was expected of him, he does r'Pt..:Ql tlO He has not ceased to be a Home Ruler becauc3soo ex-Irish leader has come to think more (4 than of the Irish cause; and he has & clear, 0- $Ol ment to make as to his relations with Mr, 4 rtioo himself. He treats as preposterous the ass° -r of that he offered Mr. PAewELL the secretalri4 Ireland; he is not in the habit,, he
1 i „i,,lii,

that which it is not his to give. As to being party to a plot to undermine the independence of the Irish members, he thinks that it is best answered by the opinion expressed by Mr. JOHN DiLLoN, which was as follows: . .

--- Mr. Parnell's revelation of his conversations with Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Morley is humiliating to every Nationalist. These two for the past five years have to my knowledge fcught consistently and stead- fatly to secure full and genuine Home Rule for Ireland. It is horrible they should be singled out for 0 oss and monstrous insults, and charged with attempts to corrupt the Irish party. If Mr. Glad- stone and Mr. Morley are true friends of Ireland, as I believe, their frequent promises are the best pledges. With regard to Mr. PARNELL'S latest "hallucia- trions" Mr. MORLEY remarks :

I have direct authority to say that after reading that speech Mr. Gladstone maintains that not a single proposal was made at Ilawarden—that is. to say, that no proposition was mentioned to which • assent was asked. The circumstances were these : Mr. Parnell had acted as a warm friend of the Bill of 1886, and he had in 1889, when this interview took place, the confidence of 85 Irish members. So Mr. Gladstone properly and naturally named to him various suggestions. And why? In order to improve his own knowledge of the field within which the ex-Ministers might confer with one another upon those suggestions with the assent of the Irish members. (Hear, hear.) Gentlemen, I have Mr. Gladstone's direct authority to state that neither the constabulary nor the 'magistracy were mentioned, and it was not_proposed to hand over the judiciary to the British Gsvernment either for ten years or for any other period. (Loud cheers.) In view of this explicit and emphatic contradic- tion, Mr. PARNELL will not succeed in convincing anybody that it is Mr. GLADSTONE who is depart- ing from the truth. But if there were a doubt upon the subject that doubt would be resolved by Mr. PARNELL himself, for he has again and again, since the Hawarden interview, expressed his satis- faction with what took place at that celebrated meeting. If, therefore, Mr. GLADSTONE was plott- ing to bring in a sham Home Rule Bill, what are we tb think of the Irish leader who was for twelve months party to that plot? He was a traitor then, if what he now says was true; but nobody believes that Mr. PARNELL was playing false twelve months ago. It fits in with the facts to recognise that he is now a dishonoured and deposed chief, who, out of sheer spite, is doing all the harm he can when he finds lie is no longer trusted as leader of the Irish pecple. Mr. MORLEY sounds the right note as to the future of Home Rule for Ireland by repeating what Mr. GLADSTONE has frequently stated, namely, that no scheme will be satisfactory which is not generally accepted and approved by the people of ;Ireland ; and he adds that "the wider your measure to Ireland is, the fuller it is, the safer it will be." As to the police, he quite knocks all the wind out of the hagglers by the simple statement that "if a community is not fit to have control of its own police, it is certainly not fit to have Home Rule at all." This means that in the next Home Rule Bill, as in the last, provision will be made for giving the people of Ireland control of the police, as soon as it can be done with due re- gard to existing arrangements and existing con- tracts. Indeed it has always been one of Mr. 'GLADSTONE'S strong arguments in favour of Home Rule that, when Irishmen had the management of their own affairs, a substantial saving would be -effected by reducing the large number of police which is deemed necessary in the present unsettled state of the country. But the immediate issue is not this or that detail of the last or of the next Home Rule Bill. The question is whether the Irish as a people are resolved to trust Mr. GLADSTONE to lead them to the promised land, or vliether they will wander in the wilderness along vith Mr. PARNELL. The majority of the Irish larliamentary party have thus far shown splendid ccurage and devotion to the cause; and. we cannot bit think that ere long there will be increasing aigis that the split of which we now hear so much haE, like that amongst the Liberals, become "fine by iegrees and beautifully less." Mr. PARNELL is in eery way so completely in the wi-ong that it is difficrlt to believe he will persist in a wild career whiel must necessarily be one of many kicks and few hdipence ; but, if he do—well, it will be of no great noment if his following be no larger than that oi Lord HARTINGTON as leader of the Dissen- tient :14iberals. Ireland, as represented by the Kilkenny election, has shown that wisdom is still justifik of her children; while, in England, Irish- men hav3 shown themselves just as ready to refuse to commt themselves to a policy which would be alike dsastrous and dishonourable. As Mr. MORLEY remarked, on Tuesday, Irishmen have only to lx true to themselves, and they will find that Englsh Liberals will be true to their pledges. The ternixrary breach must be closed, and when the battle Jot' Home Rule is fought it will be won.

• THERE can be no question that the The Railway Strke. sympathies of the public are with the Scotch railway men who are out on strik€ It is felt that their demands are on the whole fair and reasonable, and, that, as they gave due note of them, and of their intention to strike if they were not taken into account, the Railway Companies affected have not behaved fairly to their 3ervants in refusing to make conces- sions. The chef point at iasuel—the pivot it may be said upon wlich the whole matter turns—is the determination oi the part of the men to have ten hours fixed as tie working day, with overtime to be paid them afier 60 hours per week have been worked. We donot, for our own part, see where there is room to trgue as to this being a reason- able basis—that is, looking at the matter from the Railway Directors' point of view. They know perfectly well that the average work- ing hours of the various trades of the country are not ten but line hours per day; and they ought to jump st the offer now made to fix the railway day atten hours. How can they keep a conscience, and nsist that ten hours a day is too little for a railway servant to work P But let them mind what they are about, for even if they succeed in defeating the. Scotch strikers they will find that the -end of the matter is not yet. The public will want s word upon the subject, and they are entitled to have a word. Experience has Shown that the longer the hours of tailway tier- 'vents the greater ii the percentage of railway acci- dents. Even if vorkmen had nothing to urge upon the subject, the time has arrived when the Community should say—" We will not allow un- necessary risk to be incurred .through working People when they are not as fit to work as they ought to be." Beyond this. working-men of all classes are interested in reducing the hours of railway servants, for they may be quite sure that 8° long as these unreasonably long hours are per- mitted in one branch it will be difficult to get a reduction in ,other branches. This is evidently being recognised, for the subscriptions to the men out on strike come from Trades Unionists of almost every class. The miners, in particular,have zhown themselves • active in their sympathy, and hey are taking steps for extending the strike to other branches of labour, if the Railway Com- Panies persist in their present course. The situa-

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
"John Gandy" and " Qui Vive."—Next week.

The latest news as to the distress in the West of Ireland is that the extreme limit of destitution has been reached. Are the people of this part of the country going to give help? What say the authorities?

There has been another delay at the Warring- ton Police Court through the absence of maa°is- trates. It is not that Warrington is short of magistrates, but short of magistrates who suffi- ciently recognise that the honour of the position involves the duties of the position. There ought to be a stipendiary magistrate ; this would get rid of "waits" which are too common, not only at Christmas, but at other times.

The Rev. John Yonge had an admirable topic, on Sunday evening, in preaching to young men on "The Peril of Pleasure," and he made good use of it. Seed sown in this way must bear; it cannot all fall upon stony ground. The reference to science and art classes was pertinent; it will set some of the young men thinking about the proposed Technical School. Balls and Billiards are something,but they aro not everything in life.

Scotchmen from neighbouring cities and towns had a gay good time of it on Saturday afternoon in curling on Newton Lake. How they do love the game ! Life is certainly worth living when anybody can enjoy anything as " Sandy " enjoys curling. It is undoubtedly a fine healthy pastime —a sort of game of bowls on the ice, with sliding " stones " instead of rolling "woods." The various clubs play for cups; and after the game the cups are filled—occasionally.

The "Sheffield Telegraph" gives currency to a rumour that Mr. Parnell is obstinate about the leadership because, if he were to withdraw, the extremists who are now on his side would form an Assassination Club to destroy all who had been to the front in compelling Mr. Parnell to retire. This is not mid-summer, but mid-winter madness. It is a tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing.

On all hands there is evidence of distress as a consequence of the unusually hard winter, but the funds to relieve the sufferers are not always forth- coming; so it has happened in several cases that victims of poverty and frost have relieved them- selves by dying. Yet there is no lack of money, for do we not hear that one of the Rothschild's has given £12400 for a picture ? We don't know how many guineas an inch this represents; but it occursto us that somebody or something ought to be hung besides that picture.

The Depots have been under the noses of a large pottion of the inhabitants of Warrington for a long time; and they are now to be kept under the noses of the Town Council. Notice of motion for an inquiry has been given, and will, in due course, come before the Council. A Committee of In- quiry of one kind or another ought certainly to be appointed ' • and the Sanitary Committee will do well to fall in with the proposal. The policy of keeping everything and everybody in the dark never was, and never will be a good policy ; for that which is done in secret is at length pro- claimed from the house-tops.

It is not yet proclaimed from the house-tops, but it is no longer a secret, that there has been a breakdown of two gas engines employed in deal- ing with the manure. Such things will happen at times. Then again, it is all abroad that the price of the manure manufactured at Longford has gone down from £6 10s. per ton to £5 per ton. It is rumoured that there is a stock of no less than 700 tons ; and this would mean a loss to the ratepayers, through a falling market, of £1,050. It is quite time an inquiry was instituted —an inquiry that shall be searching, thorough, and impartial.

Admiral Jones-Parry, who presided at the Thel- wall meeting, on Tuesday, would appear to be a Tory of the old-fashioned type. As he seems to be in love with the Disraehan tradition, somebody should ask him to explain, if he can, what wily Benjamin could have in his mind when he said "a Conservative Government is an organised hypo- crisy." Hr. Disraeli junior—the Juvenile Plunger —exposed himself, as usual, by dwelling on the enormity of the alliance of the Liberals and the Nationalists. When was he born to know nothing of the alliance of the Tories and the Nationalists in 1885?

There are clubs and clubs. A Knutsford publi- can has been applying for an extension of licence for what he called a Swearing Club. This sounded very shocking until it transpired that what he really xneart was an Anti-Swearing Club. It seems that at his house there are fines for swear- ing, and that the fines are spent in providing for a supper at the end of the year. It is in this way that the puniahed.sinners are consoled, and en- couraged to stick to the club, and find a more excellent way. The need for an extension of time is suggestive of large accumulations of fines; but perhaps the members of the clnb spend a little time in drinking as well as in eating.

The Rev. C. F. Aked, of Liverpool, and formerly of Earlestown, caused a scene on Tuesday at a meeting of the Young Men's Christian Association. He objected to the military element in connection with the Boys Brigade which the Association is supporting, and desired to submit an amendment. The -Bishop of Liverpool, who was in the chair, ruled the amendment out of order, and there was no small uproar when Mr. Akod sought to justify the course he was taking. We cannot understand why the amendment should not have been put; and, without expressing any opinion on the issue, we must compliment the Baptist minister upon having the courage of his convictions.

According to a letter sent by Mr. A. Fletcher, Chief Inspector under the Alkali Act, Widnes is suffering at present from an emission of sulphu- rotted hydrogen—a most poisonous gas. There is, in his judgment, "an offence being committed against the Publia Health Act"; and he thinks it is for the Local Board to take proceedings to hate the nuisance abated. On the other hand, the Local Board seem to be looking to him to take action ; so between the two it is just possible that the air of Widnes will be poisoned for some time. The odd thin(' is, that this new source of danger has arisen out of an attempt to get rid of the nui- sance of the heaps of alkali waste; but the cure is, so far, worse than the disease.

The Warrington School of Art waft fortunate in getting Mr. Walter Crane to present the prizes on Tuesday evening, and give an address. Mr. Crane is an artist, designer, fend illustrator of no mean order, and speaks therefore with authority. Students will do well to read and re-read what he had to say, for they may rest satisfied that his advice is good and practical. He hit the nail on the head when he said the capacity of a nation was not to be measured by the amount of goods it produced. We must look to our goods and see that they are good, but tho motto should be "good men "rather than "good goods "; and "good men" means capable men—men who develop the talents they posses in the School of Art, the office, and the workshop. •

There was a singular collapse at St. Helens, on Monday, of a series of Government prosecutions against the St. Helens Collieries Company. Pro- ceedings were taken for alleged breaches of the Coal Mines Regulations Act, as revealed in evi- dence given at an inquest; but when the wit- nesses were questioned in the Police Court they declined to answer. They were acting, of course, under instructions, in order to defeat the prosecu- tions, and the successful plea on their behalf was that they could not, according to English law, be
LOCAL NEWS.
FATAL ACCIDHNT TO A CHILD.
Walter Outran', a little boy, aged three years, whose parents live in Hope-st., died on Thursday from injuries received a week previous by falling from a chair.

THE FROST AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES Has continued during the past week, with one or two brief periods of thaw, and the skaters have taken full advantage of their opportunities. The Bridgewater canal is still impassable and traffic is at a standstill. CONVIVIAL GATHERING AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening a convivial gathering was held at the Railway Hotel, Runcorn, when Mr. and Mrs. Griffiths placed a capital spread on the tables. The usual toasts were honoured, and songs were given with much effect by the company.

div.head: SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSICIAN.
div.p: SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSICIAN.

At the recent examination of the National Society of Professional Musicians, held at Liverpool, Miss Jessie Cecilia Smith, daughter of Mr. W. H. Smith, Greenway- road,Suncorn, successfully passed the first examination in pianoforte playing. Miss Smith has studied under Mr. E. France. SOLT-IVESTF.R ROOF PLATM—.T.S. Garland, Builders' Iron moup,or, 51, Bridge-at., Warringtou.—Aeirt. VISIT OF THE Ray. HUGH PRICE HUGHES TO RUNCOI2N: In aid of the'London Miesion,sermons will be preached in St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday, January 25th, the minister being the Rev. W. D. Walters. On the following (Monday) afternoon the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes will preach and in the evening will be the prin- cipal speaker at a great meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD,
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery Office on Wednesday. The Secretary (Mr. W. F. Salkeld), reported that during the nine months ended December 25th, there were 355 interments against 287 correspond- ing period last year ; increase 68 ; the fees received dur- ing the same period amounted to £321 19s. 2d. ; last year £244 13s. 61., increase £77 ss. Bd. The Finance Com- mittee reported that the receipts amounted to £209, and the payments £176 193. 3d. The balance of £32 is. was paid into bank. The Committee recommended accounts amounting to £6 4s. 3d. for payment. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canaga, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Z-aland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Oniou, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsey-ist.. Warrington.—.Advt. TEMPTATION TOO STRONG AT WIDNES.

Mary Jane Riley, a young woman, against whom 21 convictions are recorded, was brought before the Widnes Bench on Monday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly on the previous Saturday. The prisoner said it would be better for her to leave the town alto- gether, and asked their worships to send her somewhere for seven years. A fine of £1 and costs was imposed, and Mr. Timmis remarked that it was very sad to see such a young woman there so often. In default of paying the fine, the prisoner went to goal for a month. A charge of breach of the peace was withdrawn. . _
ANNUAL SALE now on, at J. ,S; W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. SUDDEN DEATH OF A RUNCORN MAN.

Mr. John Williams, aged 42 years, of Bra ckley-st., Run- corn, died suddenly at Widnes on Monday. The deceased was employed as storekeeper at Messrs. Hutchinson's Works, and while at work on Monday, he became unwell and started for home. In West-st. he fell down and he was carried into Mr. McKenzie's shop, when he almost immediately expired. Dr. Robinson having given a certificate of the cause of death an inquest was unnecess- ary. The funeral took place at Runcorn Cemetery on Thursday afternoon, the deceased being followed to the .grave by many members of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, with which he was actively identified.

div.head: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART COMMITTEE,
div.p: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART COMMITTEE,

A meeting of this committee was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon—present, Messrs. J. Mor- rison (in the chair), H. Wade Deacon, J.P., S. Sadler, W. C. Cal!ander, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. J. T. Allen (clerk). Accounts amounting to £33 6s. 9d. were passed for payment. Mr. Joepli Shone was appointed caretaker of the school in the place of his wife (de- ceased). The Clerk stated that he received an inquiry from the County Council, in reference to technical edu- cation, and he had sent them the statistics of the school for last year.—The Chairman : I suppose they are see- ing what they can give us.—Mr. Deacon: They will not give us much.—The Chairman : No, I think not. We have applied for £5,000.

div.head: WOUNDED BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES.
div.p: WOUNDED BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. S. Timmins and Mr. 11. Wade-Deacon, Rose Ann Mooney, 30, Nelson-st., was charged on remand with having unlawfully wounded Michael Costello,a, labourer. Costello and his wife and daughter lodged with the pri- soner, and on Saturday night, the 27th December, a dispute arose berween the prisoner and prosecutor, and bad language was freely used. The prisoner took from the mantlepiece a brass candlestick, and with this struck 'Costello several times on the head and face causing half a dozen wounds, which penetrated to the bone. The in- jured man lost a large quantity of blood, and Dr. Hut- chinson ordered his removal to the Accident Hospital. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: ACCIDENTAL DEATH OF A BOY.
div.p: ACCIDENTAL DEATH OF A BOY.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. W. T. HuSband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Widnes Police Station, on the body of Richard Davies, aged 6 years, son of John Davies, of 9, Kent-st., who died on Tuesday after- noon last. On Wednesday the boy complained of a pain in his shoulder and said he had been sliding in the yard at Simm's Cross School and a boy named Jackson had knocked him down. He, however, went to school in the afternoon, but at night he was much worse, and was taken to Dr. McCambridge's surgery, where Mr. Burgess saw him and set his collar bone, which he found was broken. On Sunday inflammation of the lungs super- vened, and he died on Tuesday. Dr. McCambridge gave a certificate to the effect that the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. H. Wade Deacon. It was decided not to discuss the suggested opening of the Library on Sundays until due notice had been given.—The Librarian (Miss Proctor) reported that during December the attendance at the reading room had been 12,431, giving a daily average of 497; corresponding month last year 522. The number of books isstied during the month was 4,770.—Mr. Robinson, upon a report from the Librarian as to the working of the branch libraries at St. Helens, suggested that branch libraries should be established at Farnworth and West Bank.—The Chairman thought it was premature to bring this subject forward at the pre- sent time, as after paying all expenses, there was only £l2O available for books, which were much needed.— Several members concurred. Eventually a sub-committee was appointed to consider the suggestion of the Librarian to have a room set apart for boys.

div.head: ROBBING A PAUPER AT RUNCORN,
div.p: ROBBING A PAUPER AT RUNCORN,

At Runcornletiy —Ses-sio—n-s, on Monday, Daniel Massey, (13), was charged with having stolen 3s. 6d., the moneys of Elizabeth Johnson, on the 10th inst.—Susannah John- son, a married woman, living at 80, Cooper-st., said that she was living at the house of the prosecutrix, who was related to her by marriage. Prisoner was her son by her first husband. On Saturday morning he was sent as usual to the office of Mr. Ward, relieving officer for the township, for Elizabeth Johnson's relief-3s. 6d. He did not return, and witness made enquiries, and ascertained that prisoner had received the money. On Sunday night she saw him near to home, and he admitted receiv:ng the money, stating that he had spent it in sweets and pies.—Mr. Wm. Howard deposed that he was in Mr. Ward's office when the prisoner received the money, and Inspector Bowyer said he apprehended the prisoner, who said he had spent the money in cakes and sweets at a shop in Percival-lane.--Prisoner, who:pleaded guilty,was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod, to be administered by P.C. Crowder.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891.

Moult COAL STEALING AT WIDNES. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Catherine Cafferty and Agnes Ryan, women, were charged with having on Friday stolen a quantity of coal belonging to Hutchinson's trustees, from a siding at West Bank Dobk. Cafferty was fined £l, or a fortnight's improvement. No evidence was offered against Ryan, who was dis- charged.—Mary Ann Keogh, aged 16, was fined ss. for stealing, from the canal bank, coal belonging to the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company. The girl Keogh was again brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursday, charged with stealing 73 lbs. of coal from the canal bank, at Widnes, the property of the London and North Western Railway Company. P.C. Robinson on Tuesday saw a woman carrying a bag of coal away, and when she observed him, she dropped the bag and ran away.—Superintendent Noblett said he was sorry the mother was not charged instead of the daughter, as she was more to blame.—Tho Bench imposed a fine of ss.,and informed the prisoner she would be sent to prison next time. ACME Doos CHECKS SPRlNG9.—Garland, Ironmonger, Earlestown and Warrington.—Adrt.

FATALITY T; A SHIP CANAL NAVVY. Shortly before midnight on Saturday, whilst a navvy named Robert Fisher, fifty years of age, who lived at the New Huts, Ellesmere Port, and who was employed on the Ship Canal works, was walk- ing home along the London and North-Western Railway, near Ellesmere Port, he was knockad down by an express goods train and killed. HOT WATER HKATING.—Garland sends estimates free Warrington.—Advt. REMOVING A PIG WITHOUT A LICENSE. At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, William Birchall, collier, Rainford, was sum- moned for moving a pig without a license out of St. Helens into the infected district of Rainford. In reply to the chairman, defendant said he did not know he was doing anything wrong, The chair- man said that defendant had rendered himself liable to a fine of £2O, but as no harm appeared to have come of the occurrence, he would only be fined ss. and Costs. ANNUAL SALE LIONV on, at J. & W. Ihrrrox's Bankey-st., Warrington.—ddrt.

INQUEST ON A MINER, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lanca- shire, held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley Cross, on Saturday, touching the death of James Harrison, 18 years of age, of 49, Gerard-st., who died in the Cottage Hospital on %Wednesday night, from injuries received earlier in the day. Deceased was a driver in the Little Delph* mine of the Crop Pit, of the St. Helens Collieries Company, and was injured by some rubbish and stones which fell from the roof. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned. NOW OPEN' FOR TUE EIRABON.—STRatt and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at Mr. Chtntry's, 13 Sankey-st.. Warrington. Open every Tuesday from 3to 9 p.m. Writing: Gentlemen are taught a fine bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and flow- ing style. Terms for the complete course, One Guinea. Book- keeping : Pupils are taught how to open, keep, balance, and close a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certifi- cate for proficiency is given to each pupil. EXCHANGR OF PULPITS AT RUNCORN. On Sunday last the annual interchange of pulpits amongst the Nonconformist ministers took place at Runcorn, and proved a great attraction at the vari- ous places of worship in the town. On Monday evening a united service was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, and the Rev. H. Harries, M.A., of Stockport, preached the sermon.

Doc} A iTJZZLING IN LANCASHIRE. The Town Clerk of Bolton has received a letter from Mr. Chaplin in answer to a request that the dog muzzling order should be relaxed as far as Bol- ton is concerned. Mr. Chaplin points out that, at Salford, ten miles from Bolton, a case of rabies occurred in October last, and he cannot repeal the order at present.

A WIDNES SCIENTIST, AND GAS MANUFACTURE. The current number of the "Gas World" states that Mr. John Hornby, P.1.C., of the London Gas Light and Coke Company, is contributing a series of articles to that journal entitled "Chemistry for students in gas manufacture." It also states that a former series of articles by the same gentleman upon "Chemical analysis for gas managers" are be- ing reprinted, and will shortly be published in book form. Mr. Hornby, who is a double medalist in gas manufacture, obtained his preliminary scientific education at the Widnes Science Classes, of which lie was one of the first members, joining at their commencement in 1874. THE WOOLTON WILL CASE. The hearing of the extraordinary action, Hemp- son v. Guy and others, generally referred to as the Woolton will suit, again came on for hearing before Mr. Justice Butt in the Probate Division on Mon- day. The action has been brought to test the vali- dity of a will under which an elderly lady named Hampson left about £B,OOO to the superioress of St. Paul's Convent, Woolton. Witnesses were examined, and the further hearing was adjourned. On Thurs- day the jury found that when the wills of 1886 and 1887 and the codicil of 1889 were executed the de- ceased was of unsound mind;• farther, that the documents were procured by undue influence, and that she did not approve the contents. His lordship pronounced against these three testamentary docu- ments with cobts against the defendants. THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER AT NORTHWICH. On Saturday, at North wich Police Court, before Mr. Lea Jones, two girls, named Ellen Lyden and Elizabeth Carles,were charged with the manslaugh- ter of Sabina Naughton. Mr. Bancroft represented the prisoners. P.C. Wharam stated that on Decem- ber 25th the two girls were in Sheath-st., North- wich. They had been quarrelling with a woman named Tunney, who lodged with Timothy Naugh- ton. About nine o'clock they went into Naughton's house, knocked his wife down, and she died on the folio wing Sunday. On the 30th ult. an inquest was held,when the jury returned a verdict of manslaugh- ter against the prisoners. Ile subsequently appre- hended them.—lnspector Johnson asked for a further remand until the Petty Sessions, to be held on Tuesday.—Mr. Bancroft said he had no objection to the granting of the request. He hoped Mr. Brunner would be present on Tuesday, as he had apparently taken a decided stand in the matter, —The girls were then remanded to Knutsford gaol.

div.head: LOCB-OttT AT GIRSTOg.
div.p: THE LOCB-OttT AT GIRSTOg.

The necessitous families a-de—dock labourers hi Garston were on Saturday provided with coals and provisions by the Garston relief committee. A small amount of money was also given to the men by the Dock Labourers' Union. Several lock-out men who were sent to other towns to get work by the Garston relief committee have come back again. These men state that there was no work at the places they were sent to, and others say that they could not obtain lodgings. The statements of the men are being investigated by the relief com- mittee. The bulk of the men, however, sent away by the committee have found work in Wigan and elsewhere. ANNUAL SALE now on, at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it.. Warrington.-41044.
THE WINSFORD BRANCH OF THE CHESHIRE LINES.

The application of the Windsford Local Board for an order requiring the Cheshire Lines Committee to resume running passenger trains over their branch between Cuddington and Winsford was dis- posed of by the Railway Commission on Wednesday, the result being in favour of the applicants. In an- nouncing the dc,cision of the Court the President (Mr. Justice Wills) said that the Act of 1854 seemed to compel railway companies, whether they liked it or not, and whether it was profitable or not, to give reasonable facilities for traffic generally. Tly., question of profit could not be overlooked, but as soon as it had been shown that there was a serious and substantial traffic to go over a line a case had been made out for requiring reasonable facilities - .

---------- " OH, YR3!' Cough Mixture, Chiretta Balsam. Relief in three minutes. Cures Bronchitis. Hope. late Methuen, Deansgate, Manchester, and all Dealers.—Advt. ALTERATIONS AT EARLESTOWN RAILWAY STATION.

During the past week, building operations on a small scale have been in progress at Earlestown station. These consist of a ticket collector's hut, and a new entrance to the station. At present the entrance to the platform is by a double door, but it is intended to do away with this,and erect a sliding door, some ten yards further along the platform, and at the foot of the bridge which crosses the lines. At this door the ticket collector's office will be stationed, and the intention is that none but pas- sengers will be allowed on the platforms, and, with the exception of the Manchester platform, only by the bridge. This will undoubtedly be a great im- provement, as all danger of crossing the lines by the level crossing at the end of the platforms will be obviated, and many parents will be relieved from anxiety by reason of their children getting on to the platform, as they at present are able to do. ANNUAL SALE now on, at J. a W. DurreN'a Sankey-at., Warrinirton.—Ad.

NARROW ESCAPE OF A ST. HELENS TRAIN. On one of the foggy mornings of last week, the nine o'clock express passenger train from Manches- at to St. Helens, had a narrow escape from collision at St. Helens Junction. The train was signalled to cross the up-line—Liverpool to London—on which a heavy goods train was travelling. The passenger train, well filled with ".commercials " and busi- ness men, was right across the main line when the goods train came down the Sutton bank. All steam was put upon the passenger train, and fortunately the main line .vas cleared,some say by a few inches, and some by a few yards, when the " goods " came thundering past. A few seconds delay and in all probability a most disastrous accident would have had to be recorded. It is stated to be a ques- tion of whether the driver of the goods train or the signalman was to blame, and the matter is being thoroughly, investigated by Mr. James Shaw, the district superintendent. Alertliti. BALE now on, at J. A. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Adrt. CHARGE OF CHILD STEALING. _

At the Police Court, on Wednesday,Elizabeth Big- gins, a married woman, hailing from Sheffield, was charged with feloniouslytaking away a child named David Grundy, two years and nine months old, son of Francis Grundy, of Sandfield-crescent,St. Helens. It was stated that prisoner arrived in St. Helens, on baturday, and took lodgings in the house of Robert Bradley, in Sandtield-crescent. The child's mother, who is the daughter of Bradley, also lives with her husband in the same house. On Monday afternoon prisoner left the house and took the child with her. She did not return at night, and Mr. Bradley went in search of the woman. lie found her in bed in a lodging house in Prescot, and she then had the child with her. Information was given to the police, and she was apprehended by the Prescot authorities. In answer to the charge the woman said sbe did not take the child with the intention of keeping it. She had a" sup o' drink and lost her way." Chief Con- stable Wood informed the magistrates that he was not prepared to go on with the case that day, and the prisoner was remanded until next Monday. TaE RAINFORD TRAGEDY : LETTER FROM PICEAVANCE. Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, editor of the "St. Helens Lantern," and who was instructed for the defence of John Duckworth Pickavance in the Rain- ford murder Case last year, has published the follow- ing letter:—" Mr. J. D. Pickavance tried for and (on the grounthof insanity) acquitted of complicity in the Rainford murder,writes from Broadmoor, under date January 1,1891, to his uncle, Mr, John Preston, as follows I received your welcome letter and was glad to hear that you are all in health and that you have had a good Christmas . . . . Con- sidering where I am I have had a good Christmas and New Year . . . . On Christmas Eve we had half-ounce of tobacco; and currant bread and roast beef and plum pudding on Christmas Day • • • • Last night we all had currant bread and ' tea and half-ounce of tobacco and an orange each . Rainhill could not be better than this • • . • I get a shilling a week spending money when I work a full week. lam buying a violin and to take lessons . . . . please give my best wishes to all my friends and hope you will enjoy a happy New Year.'" div.head: EIGHT MH:711,8 QUESTION':
div.p: THE EIGHT MH:711,8 QUESTION':

On Wednesday night there was a crowded atten- dance at Earlestown Baptist Improvement Society, to hear and to take part in a debate on the eight hours question. Mr. Swarsbrick opened with a paper affirming that the question was rapidly ripening, both in our own country and also in America, while in some cases it had been tried in Australia with beneficial results to both capital and labour. In working out the scheme it was seen that foreign competition would damage otherwise bright prospects, and therefore, he argued, for in- ternational labour boards. Besides the increased leisure coining from the adoption of an eight hours working day and a consequent rise in general intel- ligence, the additional employment of hands, now idle, would create a demand for more manufactured articles with consequent larger incomes for the capitalist and of necessity a rise in wages all round. Mr. E. Ecker4ey read a paper contending that the eight hours day had a selfish basis, and was. not practicable. Mr. Evans contended that as the nine hours movement had not achieved all the boasted good results neither would an eight hours working day do so. Mr. Shaw vigorously upheld the idea of an eight hours day. Mr. Harri- son thought that things good in themselves were often bought at too great a cost, and this remedy for the distress caused by numbers of unemployed might and probably would tend to increase that number. Messrs. Morris, Sirett, Limond, Mellor, and Holdsworth, together with Ntr. Gilmour and several other visitors took part in the debate. No. 1 CONVENTION OF GOOD_ TEMPIAES.

The usual monthly session of No. 1 Convention, (South-West Lancashire) Good Tempiars was held at Widnes on Saturday afternoon. The Session opened at four o'clock, Bro. G. Clarke C.C.T., Earles- town, presiding, supported by a good staff of officers and representatives from various parts of the Convention area, including Warrington, St. Helens, Earlestown, Golborne, and Ashton. Soon after the opening Bro. Morris, D.0.T., of Liverpool, arrived and • was received with the usual honours, and invited to preside over the business of the Session. After the appointment of the credential and report- ing committees, the report& of the officers were received and adopted, an application from the Hope of Wigan Lodge, to join the Convention being agreed to. It was decided after a general discussion, to have a series of papers and essays at the close of the monthly Sessions, on the educational and other ' aspects of the temperance question. Several reports of deputations which were appointed at the last meeting to visit various places, where lodges might be opened, were received, and two of them were so satisfactory that it was thought possible to open lodges within the next two or three weeks. Warrington Barracks, and St. Helens were nomin- ated for the next place of meeting. An address was given by Bro. J. Harris, temperance missionary, of Wigan, indicating the rapid progress of the lodge there, and ,of the Temperance cause generally in thatdistrict. Bro. Morris Jone's, D.0.T., also gave an address, and thanks were tendered to the Widnes friends for the arrangements of the Session, and to, the visitors for their presence and addresses. A goodly number afterwards sat down to a first-class tea, a public • meeting following, which was .well attended. The Rev. T. Law, of Widnes, presided, and addresses were given by the Chairman, and Bros. M. Jones, D.C.T., and G. Clarke, p.c. During the evening, several anthems and glees were sung by the Baptist choir, and readings and recitations were given by members of the Order.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Col. Ashton. Present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Fisher, J. Hall, Pickering, Bran- dreth, J. Whitlow, W. Whitlow, 11. G. Linaker (deputy clerk). Mr. James Williams, the county auditor, wrote, stating that upon examining the claims in respect to the Union, it appeared that the undermentioned sums were the several amounts which weuld be paid by the County Council of the County of Chester in aid of the following :—Medical officer and inspectors of the Rural Sanitary Authority district £l3O ; registrars of births and deaths £18; pauper lunatics chargeable to the Union £376; cost of Union officers and drugs and medical ap- pliances £1,416 ; total £1,940.—1n answer to questions, the Clerk said this was about the same amount as was received last year, and there were no further comments. —On the recommendation of the Finance Committee, accounts amounting to £53 3s. 9d. were passed for pay- ment. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £1,474 17s. Bd. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Marsden for giving a treat to the inmates of the House on the 6th Inst.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

There were present Messrs. J. W. Wareing (chairman), W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Leatherbarrow, NV. Middle- hurst, NV. Daine, G. Davies, W. Ranson, J. Ellison, J. Burchall, J. Kenwright, Jos. Bircball, J. Mercer, J. Peover, J. Whalley, W. B. Longton, N. Lows, H. Hulme, and 8. H. Hartley (clerk.) RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 601 inmates this week, 606 last week, and 602 in the cor- responding week last year. Girl's—The Chaplain acknowledged the receipt of parcels of books and periodicals for the use of the in- mates from Mrs. and Miss Gaskell (Huyton), Mrs. Par- rington (Roby), and Mrs. Crook (Huyton). RESIGNATION OP THE WIDNES RELIEVING OFFICER.— The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Joseph Treacev, re- lieving officer for Widnes,stating that he gave a month's notice of his intention to resign the office. Be added that after reading the directions given by the Board to the clerk at the last meeting he felt it his duty to make room for some man who would need no pressure to en- able him to fulfil his duties.—The Chairman, as a Widnes Guardian, who had been brought a good deal into con- tact with Mr. Treacey, expressed his opinion that Mr. Treacey had always done his work well and had been a painstaking officer. He was personally sorry that he had taken the course he had done, but under the circum- stances he thought the Board had no course but to , accept the resignation.—Mr. Tyrer moved, and Mr.
Lowe seconded, a motion to that effect, wiZich was carried. _

—ITITITSION OF WIDNFS RELIEF DISTRICT.—The Cfork reported that the sub-Committee appointed to consider' the proposed rearrangement of the relief districts had passed the following recommendations :—(1) That a new relief district be formed consisting of Much Woolton Little Wooßon, Ditton, Hale, Halewood, Speke, and the West Bank end of Widnes (bounded by the low level railway). The Widnes district to consist of the remain- ing portion of Widnes with Bold and Cronton ; and that a portion of Eccleston including Burrows Lane, Oilers Green to Catchdale Moss, Eccleston-Lane-Ends, Portico, Seddon's Brow, and the whole of Eccleston now included in the Prescot Local Board district, he added to the Prescot district. (2) That the salary of the Relieving Officer to be appointed commence at £lOO a year.—Mr. Merebr moved the adoption of the minutes, and said he thought the division of the Widnes district as proposed, would be a satisfactory solution of the difficulty they had been so long troubled with.—Mr. Middlehurst seconded the motion which was carried.—lt was also decided that the new district should be called the Ditton district. This was the principal business.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD,

The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Public Offices, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. Gossage (chairman), Dr. O'Keeffe, Hargreaves, Taylor, Wright, Mid wood. Neil, Cook, Sadler, Brown, Houghton, Liddell, Heyes, Timmis ; J. T. Allen (clerk) and other officers of the Board. THE POLLUTED ATMOSPHERE.—IMPORTANT LETTER.

The Clerk read a letter that had been received with regard to the escape of noxious gas at works in Widnes, from Mr. A. Fletcher, chief inspector under the Alkali Act. In this communication Mr. Fletcher said that he could not feel surprised at the complaint the board made made of the increased discharge of sulphuretted hydrogen into the atmosphere of Widnes. It had for a long time caused him great anxiety. The source of it was, they were aware,-the Chance-Claus process for the recovery of sulphur from the alkali waste. The pro- cess was hailed as one which promised to relieve the neighbourhood of the nuisance which had been long experienced from the heaps of alkali waste. Unfortu- uately, the process was itself the scource of a greater nuisance still. The difficulties that had arisen were un- expected, and had cnly gridually been developed. Un- fortunately, the evil did na arise from one works ,only, but from several, since six manufacturers had almost simultaneously started the new process in Widnes. Efforts were being actively made to discover methods to arrest the noxious gases which were the ground of complaint. Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Company, had adopted a satisfactory method, but it was one which was only applicable to their own works. Messrs. Sullivan and Co. were trying a method which would be more generally applicable, but its success was not established. A method for preventing the nuisance was successfully carried out at Gateshead for about six weeks. He at once invited their resident inspector, Dr. Afileck, to meet him there in order to study it. That method, however, had failed, and was at present abandoned. In order further to stimulate effort in this direction he had issued a circular letter to all the manufacturers who carried on the Chance-Claus process. Further, he was suggesting a means that would, at any rate, diminish the nuisance now experienced. He would remind them that the Widnes Sanitary Authe,rity had more power to suppress the nuisance complained of than had the irlepector under the Alkali Act. The emis- sion of so poisonous a gas as sulphuretted hydrogen was clearly an offence against the Public Health Act, whilst it was not a contravention of the provisions of the Alkali Act except in cases whare that gas was discharged from a process carried on at the alkali works. This was not universally the case in Widnes. The process was in use at one works that was not an alkali works, and there he , had no power to interfere,and at any of the works where the apparatus for the process is detached from the alkali works proper his right to interfere might be successfully challenged. He would assure them, however, that no effort on his part was or had been wanting to combat the great and suddenly increased evil complained of. He had closely studied the subject, and done all that seemed possible to stay the nuisance short of attempting to stop the process in all the works where it was carried on. That step, he reminded them, could at once be taken by the board ; it was in their power to remove the nuisance by stopping the process throughout Widne,s: as an indict- able offence under the Public Health Act. It was also reported that copies of this letter had been sent to various works in the town, and to the United Alkali Company. Messrs. Sullivan and Co., of the British Alkali Works, wrote that in their works means had been taken to prevent any nuisance arising from working the Chance-Claus process. With regard to the general ques- tion they understood that the chief inspector had had an interview with the chairman of the United Alkali Com- pany. The reply from Messrs. John Hutchinson and Co. was to the effect that they were delaying the com- pletion of plant until the best means had been ascer- tained for dealing with the escapes complained of. The Liver Chemical Company said that they were giving their careful attention to the matter, so as to avoid all cause of complaint. Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. replied that as they had not yet worked the Chance process they were not in a position to offer any practical suggestion; and Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co. wrote that they would continue to use every precaution to prevent the escape of sulrhuretted hydrogen from their Chance plant. So far as they knew, they were not allowing any of this ' gas to escape into the atmosphere. The secretary of the United Alkali Company (Mr. E. Carey), wrote inform- ing the board that the company were appointing an , engineer of great experience in this (the Chance) process ' to investigate the method of work at each Oat he estab- lishments in Widnes, and to pint out in whal way any escapes that might have occurred could be prevented._ In the course of some conversation, Dr. O'Keefe re- marked that the nuisance had been in existence a long time, and pointed out that the' board seemed to has more power in the matter than had the chief alkali inspector himself.—The Chairman said that the United Alkali Company had appointed an engineer to report up- on the nuisance, and after that report had been sub- mitted it was expected that they would appoint inspectors to prevent any escapes occurring inthe future. —Dr. O'Keefe expressed himself satisfied with what the United Alkali Company were doing. He was prepared to leave the matter in their hands for the present.—The Chairman added that the company were taking imme- diate action, and the nuisance would no doubt be remedied as soon as possible.—The consideration of the subject then dropped.

div.head: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Committee contained the follow- ing :—Resolved unanimously that the tenders of the Wigan and Whiston Coal Co. Ld. be accepted for the year 1891, delivered at the pumping stations—Stock's Well :Coal. us. 6d., burgy 10s., slack Bs. 6d. ; Notherley : 10s. 10d., 9s. 4d., 7s. 10d.—The Engineer's report read as follows :—Stock's Well—Deepening Borehole in No. 1 Well—The contractor's workmen have sunk this hole 72 feet deeper, making the total depth from the ground line 422 feet. Up to the present the boring has not raised the level of the water to any appreciable extent, but the nature of the rock now being penetrated is very hard, and it is hoped that when the soft rock below this is reached additional water will be found. A certificate for £l6B, the amount now due to the contractor, is submitted. Fence and gates at Pex erection of this work has been completed with the exception of the painting, and the raising of the road and footpath. Oxide of Iron —Messrs. Nelson and Co. have delivered the contract quantity of natural oxide of iron, and a certificate for -062 10s., the sum now due, is submitted. New Dins- more Plant—The valve boxes on the new Dinstnore plant, alluded to in my last month's report, became practically unmanageable, the valves getting so fast with pitch as to render working wittiout risk of burning the men, and loss of gas, impossible. At a consultation with my Cnairman, I suggested that the boxes and "ducts" should be taken down until the heavy part of the lighting season was over, and then re-erected in a position further from the front of the bed where the pitch would be less liable to accumulate,and if it did, the clearing of it could be carried out without interruption to the ordinary .working. The beds are now connected and working. as ordinary retorts. Purifying House Ex- tension—This work has been further delayed through the severe weather, but the lime shed has been roofed over, and the first of the new purifiers was put to work yester- day. 91n. Gas Slain along Marsh-road—The laying of this main has been stopped by the severe weather. A letter, dated 24th ult., is submitted from Mr. J. C. Rout- ledge, granting permission from Hutchinson's trustees to open up 9ic road and cross their bridge. Permission to lay the pipes across the Railway Co.'s bridge has not yet been obtained. Sulphate Plant—This plant has worked 25 days during the past month ;no sales have been made ; present stock 40 tons.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

The following items were included in the Surveyor's report to this Committee :—" The sewer in Ditton-road has been cleaned out. I received a complaint from the manager of the Co-operative Stores that the cellars in Ditton-road branch were flooded. I had the drains and sewer examined 'at once, and found that the cause of stoppage was the leakage from the chemical waste form- ing a deposit in the sewer, and I recommend that the. Committee order the hydrants suggested for flushing purposes, in my report of 2nd October last, in Ditton- road, Violet-st., and Ann-st.' to prevent these sewers filling with deposit. Mr. E. Wood has paid a deposit of 7s. for connecting sewer in Albert-road. I submit plan and estimate for sewering, curbing, channelling, metal- ling with slag, &c., Lowerhouse-lane from Birchfield-road to Steward's-lane. I wrote to Mr. Carr on the 17th inst. calling his attention to the fact that since Oct. 2nd he had not sent any notices re breaking up streets, although several streets had been broken up, and I informed him that he must take the responsibility until these trenches were put in repair. I should like the Committtee's in- structions on this matter. I have served notices on Messrs. Evans, Lockett, and Co. and C. H. Cotsworth to lay ow a new street off Peelhouse-lane 36 feet wide, and to remove the fence defining the width of street 7 feet 6 inches wide. I have also served notices on the following:

I—Job Stott, to provide access to ashpits at the rear of new houses at Upton; J. Shaw, to fix ventilating pipe at his house, Albert-road; E. Williams, to alter ventilating pipe ; Sayce and Randle, to provide intercepting syphon and disconnecting gulley at Baptist Chapel, Deacon- road, and to uncover drains which have been covered without inspection." The Committee recommended that, before breaking up any streets or roads for gas or water trenches, three days' notice be given to the Surveyor, or, on special occasion, such shorter notice as the Gas and Water Engineer and the Surveyor may from time to time agree upon. Building Plans: Undertaking, dated 19th Dec., from D. Cohen, to remove the theatre after the 31st July, 1891, within one month from notice so to do, sub- mitted and approved; plans for the following submitted and approved: Two houses, Federiek-st., for T. Sadler; stable and storeroom, West Bank-st., for the Globe Chemical Co. Recommended that legal proceedings be taken against the following :—Evans, Lockett, and Co., or other person or persons in default, for street off Peel- house-lane not laid out in accordance with deposited plans. Sayce and Randle, for covering drains without notice to the Surveyor, and for not draining in accordance with the approved plans, at the Baptist Chapel, Deacon-road; J. Shaw, Albert-road, unless a ventilating pipe is fixed as per deposited plan; E. Williams, Albert-road, unless the size of the ventilating pipe is altered as per deposited plan; the owner or occupier of No. 2, Norland-street, unless the erections in the back yard are removed.—Mr. Sadler moved the confirmation of the minutes, which was seconded by Mr. Taylor.—Mr. Hargreaves called atten- tion to the need of more lamps at Simm's Cross, and Mr. Sadler replied that the matter would be brought before the Committee, and he also withdrew for further consid- eration the minute with regard to the breaking up of the streets.—The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: *THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: *THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.

-- - The Assistant Inspector reported to the Health Com- mittee that durina the month of December there were five deaths from whooping cough and one for diarrhcea. During the same period 1101bs. of onions and 2761b5. of apples had been destroyed as unfit for food. The com- mon lodging houses had been inspected and found in order. The Committee recommended that Walter Lowe be appointed Nuisance Inspector at a salary of £llO per annum, this appointment to include. the inspection of canal boats and alkali -waste deposits. Recommended that the Surveyor have charge of all the horses and carts and the removal of the nightsoil—the Nuisance Inspector to report to him. Recommended that the Medical Officer of Health for the district be empowered to serve notices under Seection 6 of Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890, that is, as to the disinfection of bedding, &c. Recommended that the nuisance inspector be empowered under seal to in- spect premises for the purpose of carrying out Section sof the Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890, that is, power of entry upon premises to see that disinfec- tion has been attended to. Plans for the following had been approved :—Two houses, Frederick-street, for T. Sadler ; and stable, &c., West Bank-street, for Globe Chemical Co.—Mr. Wright, ix moving the confirmation of the minutes. referred to the loss the Board had sus- tained by the death of the late Mr. Dickson. Mr. Dick- son had at one time been a member of the Board and then its chairman, and he had also for a long number of years been inspector. He suggested that the Clerk should write to the wife and family of the deceased ex- pressing the sorrow of the Board at his death.—Mr. Timmis seconded .—Dr. O'Keefe also spoke in complimen- tary terms of the services the late Mr. Dickson had ren- dered to the town and the Board. He had now gone to the majority, and they wished him all the happiness he could enjoy there.—The Chairman likewise cordia,By endorsed the remarks made with respect to Mr. Dickson, and said the Clerk would write a letter of condolence to the widow and family.—The minutes were then agreed to.
GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTER.

The minutes of this Committee contained as follows t —Letter, 31st December, from the Clerk to the County Council, iatimatin,g that a proposal will be made to give to Widnes an additional member for the County Council purposes, and that it will be necessary to divide the township so as, if possible, to give a representative to art equal number of inhabitants. Recommended that scheme No. 4 (six wards) be adopted. This will allow for the following electoral divisions :—North Division, to comprise Nos. 1, 2,and 3 wards.with 2,282 burgesses ; South Division, to comprise Nos. 4,5, and 6 wards, with 2,820 burgesses. Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Liddell and Wright, and the Clerk, appointed to wait upon Lord Cross and Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., to ask them to use their influence in support of the application for a Charter of Incorporation.—Dr. O'Keeffe, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the scheme that was receMmendet fi'n• the division of the town into wards, would suit very well, both for the purposes of the cOunty Council election and for municipal elections afterwanlZ' There would be no sub-divisions and no two booths erected in one ward, by adopting the scheme. The de- putation mentioned had seen Lord Cross and Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., with regard to the application for a Charter of Incorporation, and they could give a very satisfactory report as to the courteous manner in which they were received, and the promises that were made to support the application.—The minutes were then passed.

div.head: PUBLIC HEALTH.
div.p: THE PUBLIC HEALTH.

On the motion of Mr. Sadler, it was decided to adopt the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, 02 and after the 16th February, 1891.—0 n the motion of Mr. Wright, it was decided that measles should be included as one of the diseases to be reported under the Act. The Board then went into Committee.

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT MOORE.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT MOORE.
DAM AGE OVER £l,OOO.

A destructive- fire broke out late on Wednesday night in tht farm-yard of Mr. Thomas Percival, of Moss Side, Moore. As soon as the fire was noticed a messenger was sent off to Warrington in great haste for the Fire Brigade. Shortly after eleven o'clock the alarm bell of the town was rung, and was heard in the stillness of the night over almost the whole of the town. The firemen quickly res- ponded to the call, and were soon in attendance at the fire brigade station. Horses were speedily har- nessed to the engine Nile, and in about ten or fifteen. minutes from receiving the alarm Superintendent Turner and his firemen were on their way • to Moore. The scene of the conflagration was reached in quick time, and it was there found that a large number of bays of wheat, oats, and straw were on fire, as well as one or two of the outbuildings. The flames could be seen for miles around the district. Fortunately, there was a good supply of water to be obtained from a pond in the farmyard, and no time was lost in commencing operations, although l it was evident from the- first that all the sacks which were on fire were doomed. No exertions which might be put forth could save them, and the energies of the firemen were directed to preventing- the flames spreading to the other stacks in the yard, and their efforts in this direction were successful. Shortly after the arrival of the Warrington Fire Brigade, the Wilderspool Brigade, under the direc- tion of Mr. Superintendent Thomas Ince, put in an appearance with the new engine Empress. which was on this occasion used for the first time, and rendered valuable service. Mr. Ince was accompanied by seven men. For a time both engines were kept busily at work, but at half-past three in the morning Mr. Turner and his men re- turned to Warrington, leaving the Wilderspool Fire Brigade on duty. The two brigades had, however b'y their joint exertions succeeded in saving a number of other stacks of wheat and oats. The Wilderspool brigade remained on the spot all night. Several farm building were completely gutted, and a large quantity of agricultural implements, in- cluding chaffcutters, mowing machines, as well as three carts, were so damaged that they will be unfit for further use. The damage altogether is estimated at from £l,OOO to £1,200, and is accounted for by the destruction of three bays of wheat, two bays of oats, six bays of straw (all of which were in a wooden building with a slate roof), a stack of straw and a stack of hay in the open air; a cart house, a barn, and two adjoining bays. Fortunately, eleven other stacks of wheat, oats, and straw, which were in dangerous proximity to those on fire, were untouched by the flames. The loss is covered by insurance in three fire offices. It is not definitely known what was the origin of the fire, but it is surmised that it was caused by a tramp, who had intended to sleep near the stacks, throwing a lighted match among a quantity of loose hay and straw.
ASIATIC CHOLERA IN SIBERIA.

div.head: THOUSANDS DYING,
div.p: THOUSANDS DYING,

The black death,or Asiatic cholera has reached Tobolsk,_ Siberia. The whole of Asiatic Russia from Samarkand in the south to the mouth of the river Obin, in the ex— treme north, is suffering under the awful scourage, especially in the town of 019dorsk. Thousands are dy- ing, and as there is only one doctorin the whole district, there is no hope of checking the fast spreading disease.
