div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. I
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. I

THEFT OF BOOTS IN HORSEMARKET-STREET. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wed.. thy, Thomas Hawthorne and Thomas Holden were charged with stealing,the previous night, about nail pa 7 o'clock, from the shop of Samuel Hamer, toot and shoe dealer, Horsemarket-st.—Detective Sergeant Monaghan said he was on duty about ten minutes to seven on Tues- day night, and saw the prisoners loitering about the prosecutor's shop. They went away,and came back,and- one prisoner handled some boots which were at the door, and the other put them under his coat. They. went to Town Hill and he followed them, and Holden ran away. Be took them both into custody, Holden being captured at Daley's lodging-house in Scotland-rd. 'Hawthorne said he was guilty,and Holden said he met with Hawthorne in a public house, and had a walk with him.—Annie Ashley identified the boots as those stolen.—Hawthorne now pleaded guilty, but said he was drunk at the time of the theft. Holden pleaded not guilty.—Detective Ser- geant Monaghan said both men worked together, and lived at the same lodging-house.—They were sent to for 14 days' hard labour each.

div.head: VISITORS WHO ARE NOT WELCOME.
div.p: VISITORS WHO ARE NOT WELCOME.

A Ship Canal navvy, named John Clement, was on Saturday at Warrington Police Court, charged with being drunk and disorderly in St. James's-st., on the previous night, and with assaulting P.C. Clarke whilst in the execution of his duty. P.C. Clarke said he was on duty in St. James's-st., on Friday night, when he saw the pri- soner lying drunk on the footpath, and using very abusive language. He picked the prisoner up about half a dozen times, and told him to go home, but he refused to do so. He eventually took him into custody. The prisoner became very violent, kicked witness on the legs, and stamped upon his foot. Two young men volun- teered witness assistance, and they had to carry the pri- soner all the way to the Police Station. The Prisoner: I don't know what the man is talking about. I know nothing about it. I had a drop of drink. A man of the force gave me some whisky. I only started work on Wednesday, and had not any drink before.—ln reply to the Chief Constable, the prisoner said he thought the man's name was Cooper. He used to work with pri- soner.—The Chief Constable: A man reeently joined the force from the Ship Canal.—Alderman Burgess: You will not allow that sort of thine, to be done ?—The Chief Constable: No. I will work' it out.—P.C. Corbett: Cooper was not on duty at ten o'clock last night.—P.C. Clarke said he locked the prisoner up at 10.30.—Alder- man Burgess: You will be fined ss. and costs for drunk- enness and ss. and costs for the assault. It is quite intolerable to have men like you coming to the tow u and creating disturbances like this. -We have much tiT3uble with our own people.
MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Alderman Harrison, Alder- man Davies, Dr. Gornall, and Major Pickmere. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick M'Guire, drunk and disorderly, in Bridge-st., on the 27th of May last, was fined 7s. 6d. including costs, in default seven days' hard labour.—Joseph Bate, Mary Bate, and Jane Lee were summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Rose Yard en the Ist inst. Joseph did not appear. They were fined ss. each, including costs or seven days.—Patrick Mitchell, drunk and disorderly on the 2nd inst., in Ship Yard, was fined ss. and costs, in default seven days.— Richard Warburton, hawker, 19, drunk and disorderly, in Ceckhedge-lane, on the 4th inst., was let off with a fine of ss. including costs, or seven days, on his promis- ing to sign the pledge.—Mary Travis, was charged wfth being drunk and disorderly, in Stephenson-st., on the sth inst., also with assaulting Police-Sergeant Jones on the same occasion.—Mr. Whittle appeared for the prose- cution. He said the defendant was the wife of George Travis, living in the neighbourhood of Battersby-lane, a hardworking artisan. The wife of the complainant and defendant had been known to each other for some time, but, owing to the behaviour of the defendant some six weeks ago in following the complainant's husband into his bedroom she told her never to come to the house again. Ever since then the defendant had persisted in going tothe house and annoying Mrs. Jones. Mr. Whittle then detailed the circumstances of the assault, stating that she had so injured the complainant's hand that he had to be off duty for a short time.—Police-Sergeant Jones stated that about half-past five p.m. on Monday, on his return home he found a crowd about his door, and the defendant there very drunk and using filthy lan- guage. He requested her to go home, and she said she would not for him or any other policeman in the force. He got hold of her by the right hand, and she fell, and he picked her up. She got hold of his left hand and bit it. He had a stick in his hand, and he struck at her, with it and broke it. She threatened to get him dis- -charged if she could, and to take the lives both of him- self and his wife before very long. She was taken away by her lodger and her son.—Alice Hannah Walker and Mrs. Rawlinson, gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant said Mrs. Jones had been circulating about that she and Sergeant Jones had been unduly intim- ate, an allegation which she denied, and she there- fore went to ask for an explanation. The com- plainant used foul language to her.—The defendant denied that she was drunk or assaulted the Sergeant. —John Travis, a boy, the defendant's son, said the Sergeant knocked her down, and knocked her teeth out saying "Go home, you drunken ." She was not drunk.—Agnes Hartley, gave evidence to the like effect. —The defendant was bcund over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months, in default a month's hard labour.
Armown,ro A HORSE TO STAND.—William Bottomley, for allowing his horse and cart to stand in the Market Place longer than necessary on the 3rd inst., was fined 3s. 6d. and costs.
CHIMNIES ON FlRE.—Nathaniel Fairbrother, Thomas Lynch, and William Thompson, for having their chim- nies on fire were each fined is. .

AN OBNOXIOUS LODGING BousE.—Ann Farrell, lodging- 'muse keeper, was charged with allowing a quantity of solid and liquid refuse to stand on her premises.—Mr. Whittle appeared for the prosecution.—Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, proved the case, and said the woman was perfectly unfit to be in charge of a lodging- house, in which opinion Superintendent Hunt concurred. He asked the Sanitary Committee to disqualify the pre- mises as a lodging-house.—The defendant was fined 6s. costs.

NON-ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.—The following persons were prosecuted by Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, for not sending their childrenregularly to school: —Wm. Carney, forgeman, Crossley-st., two children, fined 10s. Peter Smith, factory hand, Titley-st., ss. ljlomas. Bate, labourer, Old-st., 55. Thomas Berry, tabourer, •Haydock-st., ss. John Clare, forgeman, Win- -wick-st.. ss. Henry Jewess, forgeman, Guardian-st., ss. William O'Connor, cabinet maker, James-st., ss. 'Thomas O'Rider, forgeman, Bewsey-at., ss. WEDNESDAT.—Before Alderman Holmes and Mr. J. Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.—Hannah Holmes, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., the previous night, was impel ss. and costs. VAGRANCY.—Elizabeth Lawrenson, of St. Helens, fcr vagrancy in Naylor-et., this morning, was sent to jail for 14 days' hard labour. FRlBAT.—Before Mi. J. White, Alderman Harrison, Dr.

Gomel!, and Major Pickmere. HAVING A CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Thomas Littlewood for having his chimney on fire was fined is. and costs. MALTREATMENT OF A HORSE.—John Jackson, was charged by Inspector Brown, agent to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, with working his horse while in an unfit state on the 7th inst. _ Inspector Brown said he saw defendant in Buttermarket-st., in charge of the horse, suffering from strained tendons, which were enlarged and inflamed. The horse kept lift- ing up its foot as if in pain. The defendant told him the horse had been lame a week, and that he had just been to the station with a lad for flour.—A Police-constable and another witness corroborated.—Mr. Fairclough, miller, said he examined the horse at defendant's request, on the day in question. It was quite fit for light work, such as drawing a load of flour. Had the animal's leg not been bandaged, the Inspector would not have noticed anything particular about the horse. He considered the case a most paltry one.—The defendant was fined .55., including costs.

ASSAULT OiV:AN ELDERLY LADY.—John Warburton was charged with assaulting and beating, on the 13th inst., Mary Walton, aged 69, residing in Monk-st., Lovely-lane. He was also charged with stealing a looking glass and a , table from the complainant's house on the same occasion. There was a cross-summons by which Warburton charged Thomas Walton the husband of Mary Walton, with assault. Mr. Unsworth appeared for the Waltons and Mr. Browne for Warburton. From the solicitor's statement and Mrs. Walton's evidence, it appeared that the defendant came on the day in question to her house and demanded the articles, which had been there 12 months, and had been given by him to her daughter, Mrs. Atkinson, a nurse at the farm of Mrs. Warburton, the defendant's wife from whom he is separated. Mrs. Atkinson was not in, and witness refused to give • them up without written authority from her. The defendant pushed her in the face against the wall, rushed upstairs, and brought down the articles, carry- ieg them off in a cart. The coinplairiment sent for a policeman, but he arrived too late. Witness's husband, aged 70, followed the defendant upstairs, and remonstrated with him, when he. threw Mr. Walton on the bed, and assaulted him.— Rachel Woodhead, granddaughter of Mrs. Walton, Wm. Lowe, her son-in-law, and P.C. Amson gave corrobora- tive testimony. Mr. Browne,vihose client did not appear, stand that he was absent through sudden illness, and characterised the case as a most trumpery one. He ad- mitted that Mr. Warburton pushed Mrs. Walton aside, but said she was merely the bailee of the goods, which were his. The parties had been hitherto on perfectly friendly terms, and he used to call at Mrs. Walton's to see Mrs. Atkinson, to hear accounts of how his children were doing with their mother. He merely went with the idea of getting the things back in a friendly way.—The Bench fined Mr. Warburton £3 and costs, and Mr. Uns- worth withdrew the charge of stealing the goods, while the charge of assault against Thomas Walton was dis- missed.

- SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A GIRL.--qhomas Rosvere, Mel- ton-road, was charged with committing an aggravated assault upon a girl named Emily Hettie Vause, aged nine years.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty and wa*defended by Mr. J. W. Knowles. The girl described the prisoner's conduct towards her while in. the house, and the mother who entered the house when the offence was 14,eing com- mitted also gave evidence in support of the charge,—Mr. Knowles argued that as no evidence of violence or abuse had been adduced, the Bench could not convict.—The magistrates reduced the the charge to a common assault, and imposed a fine of 40s. and costs or a month's im- prisonment.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. WIDNES OLD BOYS IsT. —Played at Widnes, on Saturday. The visitors winning the toss, the home team kicked,off, the game continuing to be evenly contested up to half time, when the score read, Rangers 3 minors,Old Boys, nil. Upon the re-start the visitors pressed heavily, and Massey opened the scoring account with a splendidly-dropped goal, which was quickly followed by tries- from Welsby, Savage, Molt, Bradbury, and Garrity, Cook placing a goal in one instance, the Rangers eventually retiring victors by 2 goals, 4 tries, 7 minors, to Old Boys nil. RUNCORN v. SALE.—These Cheshire teams met at Run- corn on Saturday. The ground had been well proteeted, making it in playing condition. Hunt kicked off on behalf of Sale, and Williams charged his kick down. Some passing amongst the Sale backs passed Runcorn. The home forwards now broke away, and dribbled grandly to the Sale quarters, Runcorn pressing hard, Abrams eventually getting over, no goal resulting. Kick- ing out, Cookson was prominent with a fine run. Cromp- ton took the plai to the centre. Stephens got well off, but Houghton was safe. Some grand passing between Faulkner, Crompton, and Davies almost had the desired effect, Crompton at length getting an opening run. in. Houghton with a splendid kick landed a goal. From the kick off Abrams threw to Faulkner, who got over, Crompton adding the major point. Half-time result.—Runcorn, 2 goals, 1 try; Sale, nil. Faulkner restarted,and dribbled brilliantly to the Sale lines. Cook- son intercepting a pass, raced to the centre, Houghton bringing him up. Davies from a pass by Adams ran strongly along the touch, getting over at the corner flags Resuming, a grand burst of passing between Abram. Faulkner, and Crompton resulted in Davies again getting over, Crompton kicking a goal. Final result.—Thancorn, 3 goals, 2 tries; Sale, nil. WARRINGTON v. PENYGRAIG.

The'Penarth match having been scratched,the Warring- tonians played the second match of their Welsh tOur on Tuesday, playing Penygraig. The ground was covered with snow, and rather than disappoint the fair number of spectators that had' assembled to witness the game, the Warringtonians played an exhibition match, tackling being dispensed with. Rees kicked off,and for the first few minutes play was of a give-and-take nature. Fine dribbl- ing by Ashton and T. Jolley and a couple of huge kicks by Webster gave Warrington a footing well within the home 25, but by strong rushing, regardless of the danger attending such tactics, the oval was worked to near the Warrington line, but Boscow repeatedly elicited cheers with his fine kicking. The game now settled down into a mere farcical exhibition, and after Penygraig had forced aief ouple of minors, the result of long kicking, the Lancas- trians, in a movement initiated by Ashton, worked the oval through the opposing defence and Mather scored. Webster failing at the place, a minor to Warrington was all that was scored during this half, and the second half was an uninteresting medley, the dispensing With the tackling process rendering the game anything but pleasant to witness. However, summarizing this half, the Warringtonians had a trifle the best of it, scoring three minors to one, the final score reading as Warring- ton 0-1-4, Penygraig 0-0-3. Teams—Warrington : Bos- cow, back; Daniels, Webster, Barnes, and Massey, threequarters : Jas. Bate, and J. T. Bate half backs; ,H. Ashton W. Povey, J. Jolley, T. Jolley, Mather, T. Donohue, J. Holmes, and J. T. Thornily. Penygraig: B. Philips, back; W. Phillips, D. Lloyd, T. Jones, andJ. P. Evans, threequarters ; M. Rees, and D. Forster, half barks; Casey, R. John, J. Green, L. M. Green, D. Evans, J. T. Davies, Watts, and Ellis. WARRIN3TON v. LLANELLY.

The Warriogtonians opened their Welsh tour at Llanelly on Saturday. Our local club made the journey on Friday, commencing at twelve o'clock, arriving at the Welsh town a little before eight o'clock. They travelled minus the services of the Brothers Turner, Evans, and Berry. A severe frost occurred on Friday evening, and although the Llanelly executive had taken precautions, the ground was so hard at the time an- nounced for commencing hostilities that it was very doubtful whether the match would take place. How- ever, a " gate " had been taken, and Warrington, •rather than disappoint the a.siembly, consented to compete. An arrangement had been arrived at between the rival skippers, and whatever the final score was, it was agreed that the meta should be styled as a draw. As will be seen the Llanelly men had made a special whip for the occasibn, their team including no fewer than seven internationals, although the last-named fact does not count for much in Wales, only four clubs forming the international team.

At three o'clock W. H. Thomas started towards the town goal, and a spell of exchange kicking between Barnes, Massey, Jolley, P. Lloyd, and Bowen marked the opening items, half way being the scene of opera- tions. By smart passing the homesters obtained well within the Warrington 25, but its stay here was of short duration, for James Bate foiling " Gitto ", Griffiths, im- proved Warrington's position. By lucky. fly kicking Warrington quarters were again invaded, and a spell of passing between the Welsh three-quarters was neutra- lised by a similar effort on the part of the two Bates, Barnes' and T. Jolley. Ashton and J. Jolley were pro- minent in an attack on the home goal, and J. Bate, with a dribble down the open, was at fault near the line. Lovering getting the oval away, Warrington would not be denied, and a line passing movement amongst the backs ,was frustrated by A. C. Davies. A penalty kick, which should never have been allowed, gave the visitors relief, but the combination of the War- rington lads served them in good stead, and again Llanelly defended. T. Jolley burst through and had extremely hard lines in not scoring. Another fine dis- play by the Welshmen changed, the venue, but Boscow was safe, and no liberties taken. However, the ." wire- pullers" had to adopt defensive tactics, and a rush by .the Welshmen was saved by Barnes. The Warringtonians were having an anxious time of it at this juncture, but the forwards wheeling a pack in smart style took the leather beyond the half-way flag. Llanelly still persevered, and :as a result of a passing movement P. Lloyd ran in, Lovering fail- ing at an easy place. A minor followed directly after, but on the drop out Webster was loudly applauded for a beautiful piece of work, and although the play was taken direct to the line, the Warringtonians failed to score up to the call of half-time, when Llanelly led by a try and a minor to nil. T. Jolly re-started, and Llanelly were compelled to defend at the onset. Short passing movements by the Warringtonians were freely indulged in, James Bate being specially prominent. " Gitto " Griffiths ran well, but BOSCOW tackled effectively. The finest piece of play throught the match was now wit- nessed. Bate got extremely quick away from the grasp of Evan Lloyd. and, passing finely to Barnes, the latter threw to Webster. The lengthy three-quarter took the pass splendidly, and being on his running in a moment ran through the thick of his opponents, but finding his

div.head: THE, EXAMINER,: SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891. WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: THE, EXAMINER,: SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891. WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.

caeeer barred by Lovering and Bewen threw to Barnes, I and the latter handed the oval over to his skipper, who failed to grasp the opportunity, and the chance was hopelessly lost. John Bate tried ineffectively to trick his opponents, but a moment later T. Jolley-, by a powerful punt raised the hopes of the Warringtonians, though- fortune was not theirs,at least not for the time being. A long kick by James Bate forced Lovering to save. A drop at goal by Webster from beyond the half-way flag fell un- der the bar. Despite the ill-luek which had attended the efforts of the Warringtonians, they played with surpris- ing energy,and J. Jolley almost got in after a strong run. The Warrington forward was tackled, however, and although a splendid chance was here presented the visi- tors, they failed, to grasp it. Donohue, Holmes, and Povey were prominent in effecting a relief after Llanelly had threatened the visiting citadel. Again Warrington were at fault in a final touch,and J. Jolley made another rum towards the close, passing to Barnes, the latter tak- ing his drop, which grazed the post on the outside. Bowen made a run alohg touch near the close, and play being at half-way, the whistle brought a:good fast game to a close, the result being, as arranged, a draw, the final score reading as Llanelly 0-1-1 ; Warrington 0-0-3. ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The annual prize distribution in connection with the Warrington Sahool of Art was held on Tuesday evening in the Lecture Room, at the Museum, the prizes being distributed en this occasion by the well-known artist, Mr. Walter Crane. Mr. John Rylands presided, and -amongst others present, be- sides Mr. Walter Crane, were Messrs. Jno. Crosfield, F. Monks, R. Garnett, W. Owen, J. White, W. Darbyshire, C. S. Burgess, and C. B. Aylward (head master), Councillors Shaw Green and F. W. Monks.

A FAVOURABCA RhPORT. The HEAD "MASTER, in his-report for the session ended June 26th, 1890, stated that the number of students on the school register was 239, 68 attending the day classes and 171 the evening classes. The only session reaching a total comparing favourably with this was that of 1886, when the total was 230; the day class numbering 54 and the evening class 176. For the current session, September to .December, 203 students had entered , their names, as compared with 185 in 1889, and 126 in 1888. Out of 200 candidates promised, 197 presented themselves at the science and art examinations. In the second grade art examinations the successful papers worked were 129, 22 being excellent, as compared with 12 in the previous session. In the third grade art exam- ination there were 22 successes in the first class. The passes in the science drawing subjects—practical plane and solid geometry, machine drawing, an.l building con- struction—were nearly° double those of the previous year. In November the school was visited by Mr. Eyre Crowe, A.R.A., Science and Art Department inspector, who presented a favourable report of the work of the students. At the termination of the session, Miss Mary Burgess, Miss Annie Chrimes, and the headmaster were granted, by the Science and Art Department, an extended course of study at the National Art Training Schools, South Kensington. With the assistance of Mr. J. Dooley, an art class had been conducted by the headmaster at Penketh. He (Mr. Aylward) was anxious to encourage practical results from the School of Art training, by getting its advanced students to be regular exhibitors both in sculpture and painting at the public exhibitions. and by providing trained teachers for private and ele- mentary schools. Certain handicrafts, such as decorative painting, stencilling, embroidery, tile and glass painting, wood carving, wood etching, modelling and casting in plaster and modelling and glazing in local clay—all those, which required only a little technique for art ex- pression, could be conveniently carried on in the school and undertaken by the students. In conclusion, he wished to express his indebtedness to the assistant teachers for their co-operation in the work of the school. (Applause.)

the CHAIRMAN said he was sure it must be a matter of congratulation that they could have a report like that. That was not the annual meeting, and therefore they had not a financial report, but he was sure that that would be equally favourable. They might now con- sider thay had got over their difficulties, and hope that the School had commenced a prosperous career. (Ap- plause.) Referring to what had taken place at the last meeting of the Town Council with regard to the Corpora- tion taking over the School of Art, he said that for many years he had argued that it was the duty of the Corpora- tion to take over the School of Art, and at one time it would have been of very great assistance to them if they had done so. They had had to fight for their existence, and it had been a very uphill fight, but he was glad to say they were now independent. They felt that they could go on without the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) But he still thought it the duty of the Corporation to take the School of Art. They did not know what might happen. The town was growing, and clearly it ought to be out ot the range of possibility for the School of 4rt to fail. It ought to be absolutely certain that as long as a School of Art was required, it should be there. It was for the Corporation,to take possession of the School of Art bodily, and see that it was always Maintained. He was in hopes that would take place, and he should be very sorry if it did not. They should then look forward with confidence to the future. (Applause.) Mr. WALTHR CRANH was received with loud applause. He congratulated them on the very favourable report of the head master. He was particularly interested in that part of the report in which he expressed the opinion that it was very desirable to turn attention to certain handi- crafts. He might claim to have called the attention of the Department to that desirability himself, and he was glad to see that the advantage of it was so thoroughly re- cognised. Mr. Aylward mentioned certain arts which he said required only a little technique, but they must after all remember that it was simplicity .which was the most difficult thing to attain success in. It took a really clever and learned man to write a really good school primer, and it took a very able designer to design under simple conditions and with simple materials. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Aylward had shown him some stencil patterns done by some of his younger students, and they seemed to him fork the most part very well cut steacils. The designs were constructed quite on the right lines,and he did not know any better exercise in the way of general teaching of design in its primitive elements of line and VMS:— Thisrwas done by young men who work in the day and come to the school in the evening, and he thought it was very creditable to them. It fulfilled the design' of the department in their •scheme of such schools which were to begin with being called " Schools of Designs." If after working at their calling during the day-time men could go to a School'of Art in the evening and do so well,it suggested how much better they could do had they more leisure. All this pointed to the desirability of shortening the hours of labour generally. The true wealth of a nation was not in the amount of goods it put out,but in the capabilities of its people. Wealth could be built up and destroyed again;but,if they hada strong, gifted, and capable nation, and the sense of art was well diffused among the people it meant an immense deal—it meant that they lived under good conditions and that they were in every way strong as a working people. (Applause.) They all knew there was no monopoly of talent. They uever knew where an artist would spring from. They had come out of all order. (Hear, hear.) The Sugges- tion of turning attention to the arts and crafts of design in a school was a good sign, because it indicated the growth of a wider view of art. The idea of art must not be limited to the painting of easel pictures. /t never had been so limited before our century. The public had been for some time industriously cultivating painters of pictures, and he thought this country might fairly claim to have a great number of very clever painters; but, after all, there were many who could make a very clever sketch from nature, but when it came to designing any- thing, it was found that therewere only a few who could design a- decent looking stove or a tolerable coal box. (Laughter.) Those might seem to be very common things, but it had always been true that if one wanted to know how a nation stood in art, the commonest objects were the surest index. Ornament, if found in the wrong place, was certainly one of the most inartistic things in existence. The designer of things ought not to be disso- ciated from the actual maker of them. To that cause were due fanciful designs for objects which did not suit them at all, and there was an absence of simplicity and directness about the work. The suggestion that local clay should be used' might be acted upon with advan- tage. One of the things which had to be counteracted in these days was centralization—having everything directed from the centre. 'His own feeling was very strongly in favour of local development in art as in other things. It was worth consideration how far the School of Art could be connected with the industries of the town. (Hear, hear.) Amid the uncertainties of life there was one thing which seemed to him quite certain —labour always told. The more thought, feeling, and attention were put into a work the better it was sure to be. A student might become a great artist, but the greatest artist could never cease to be a student. (Ap- plause.)

After the distribution, Mr. F. MONKS moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Crane. Speaking on behalf of the Com- mittee which was likely to take in hand the work of the technical school, he said their object would be to give increased facilities for studies in art, and also to iievelope local talent as much as possible. As far as he knew the mind of the Committee, it was to give every young man and young woman an opportunity of developing what- ever talent they might possess. Mr. C". S. BURGESS, in seconding the vote of thanks, said that if the School of Art was to be no better under the Corporation than it was now, and was to receive no funds from the Corporation or ratepayers he could see no good to accrue either to one party or the other from the schools being transferred. (Hear, hear.) The vote of thanks was then heartily accorded. A similar vote to the Chairman, moved by-Mr. CRANE and seconded by Mr. R. GARNETT, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: TEE BAZAAR FATALITY.
div.p: TEE BAZAAR FATALITY.

The coroner's inquiry as to Ihe death of the nine victims of the tire in the New Wortley bazaar was resumed and concluded on Wednesday. The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death," but censured several persons con- nected with the entertainment which resulted so disastrously,and made some suggestions to public bodies with the view of mitigating risk in the future.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY COLLISION AT
div.p: FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY COLLISION AT
BOLTON.
OVER 40 PERSONS INJURED.

- - On Saturday at midnight a disastrous collision oc- curred at Trinity-st. Station, Bolton' which resulted in injuries to over 40 persons. Owing to the fog the traffic at Bolton had been greatly delayed throughout the whole of Saturday, and the Preston train due at Bolton at 11.47, did not arrive until 12.23. A large number of gentlemen who had been visiting a Bolton political club were waiting to depart to Manchester, and had taken their seats in the Preston train, which had just arrived, when a Scotch relief train from Hellifield for Manchester due at Bolton at 11.27, dashed into the station round a curve,and collided with the Preston train. Wm. Holland, night foreman at the station, who was attending to the luggage, was thrown to the ground, sustaining injuries to the shoulders and head; and twenty-five passengers who were amongst the injured had to be medically at- tended to. Two passengers, Arthur had, designer, of Chorlton-on-Medlock, and John Calland, of Strange- ways, Manchester, were the most seriously injured, both suffering from concussion of the brain. They were re- moved to the Infirmary at Bolton. The other passengers who complained were conveyed in a train specially made up of first-class carriages to Manchester, and two Bolton sufferers were removed to their homes. As to how the accident occurred, Thomas Pottstpoints- man who was acting as signalman at the Blackburn Junction cabin, states that all the signals were against the driver of the Scotch train. The signalman at the Johnson-st., fork junction cabin, named Edwin Dodgin, also states that the signals were against the driver of the Scotch train, which was proceeding very slowly, other- ' wise the result would have been more disastrous. There was no damage caused to the permanent way, but two or three carriages of the Preston train were slightly damaged and the coupling of the Scotch train. The injuries sustained by the Manchester passengers were chiefly cuts and bruises about the head, through being prvelled from their seats by the collision. Much excite- ment prevailed for a time, until the extent of the disaster had been ascertained.

All the injured passengers at Bolton are progressing as well as can be expected. " In the cases of Arthur Webster, of Molyneaux-st., Chorlton-in-Medlock, and John (or Thomas) Callam, of Julia-st., Strangeways, Manchester, the two men who were most seriously injured, are now lying at the Bolton Infirmary under treatment for con- cussion of the brain.

div.head: CHARGE OF FIGHTING. UNFOUNDED ACCUSATION AGAINST CONSTABLES.
div.p: CHARGE OF FIGHTING. UNFOUNDED ACCUSATION AGAINST CONSTABLES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor, Aldermen Harrison and Davies, and Dr. Gornall, Martin M'Guire was sum- moned on a charge of fighting in Tanner's-lane, on Sunday night last.—P.C. Amson deposed that he and P.C. Davis found the defendant fighting with another man at a quarter past tenon Sunday night in Tanners's-lane.—P,C.Davis corroborated .-4ohn Troy deposed that he was talking with the defendant at his own residence, three doors from witness's, up till ten minutes past ten.—The Muror : There was time for a fight afterwards.—Witness said he knew the defendant was never out that night.—Mrs. Hughes gave corrobmative evidence.—JohnM'Guire, defendant's brother, said he spoke to the two con- stables about 1020 o'clock on the night in question, and they were very far gone in drink that night.— )P.S. Bowen deposed that he saw them about eleven o'clock, perfectly sober.--P.c. Amson said the de- fendant would have been locked up but that wit- ness heard he was subject to fits.—The Mayor, ad- dressing John M'Guire, said he had made a very serious charge against the officers. If it was sub- stantiated, they would both get into serious trouble.—The witness replied that his statement was true.—The defenilant's mother said P.C. Davis lost his cape in the passage.—LP.C. Amon: I can answer for myself. I had not tasted that day.— Chief Constable Hunt: They would have both to go through their parade and examination, and, if they had been tainted with drink, they would have had to fall out,—Alderman Davies said the Bench were perfectly satisfied that the officers were sober, but in jus- tice to them, that they might have an opportunity to clear their characters, he would ask that the case might be adjourned for them to call witnesses to dis- prove the charge.—At the, request of Chief Constable Hunt the Bench decided to allow him to send for these, and to adjourn the case till they cqme. Alßout half-an- hour later Inspector Cox and Sergeant Rowbotham made their appearance, and both said that the con- stables were on parade at a quarter to ten p.m., and were not in the slightest degree under the influence of drink, and that they saw the officers at different times between eleven and twelve that night, and they showed no signs of drink. The witnesses further said they had never known either of the constables to be under the in- fluence of drink.—John M'Guire was then re-called, and the Mayor told him that the Bench thought that by making such charges against the two officers he had committed a most unwarrantable offence.—M'Guire. I don't think so.—The Mayor said the Bench felt so satis- fied on the point, that if they had the power they would send him to prison for perjury.—M'Guire said the officers had had a lot of beer when they spoke to him.—Alderman Harrison said M'Guire had committed a deliberate perjury in making such a charge against the constables. The police had plenty to do to keep themselves clear from persons who were ever ready to scandalize them on the slightest pretence. This was a deliberate attempt to injure these two officials, and he only wished the Bench could commit him for a month: he would hold up both his hands for it.—Major Pick- mere asked the Clerk whether there was a case for pro- secution for perjury, but the Clerk advised that there was not under the circumstances.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months; in default seven days' hard labour.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

FOOTBALL —RUGBY. Football is being completely upset by this trying weather. There is a constant doullt about engagements being fulfilled, and one can hardly remember the time when officials had such a long and anxious spell. The frost has virtually been master of the situation since the end of November, and such matches as have been pos- sible during the past few weeks have been contested' under very disagreeable conditions. Even in cases where the utmost vigilance has been displayed and every pre- caution adopted, the grounds have been unplayable, and affairs are in a state of chaos. Skating has been the only enjoyable outdoor sport, and football fixtures are being abandoned on the wholesale scale.

It was almost annoying to the Lancashire authori- tiesito be kept in suspenSe up to the very last as regards their journey into Somersetshire. It was a poor excuse to say that the team could not be summoned together after receiving back word, as a telegram would soon have found the players. However, the substitution of the Devonshire for the Somersetshire match was a good move under the circumstances, so .that the Lancashire fifteen were given something to do,and thus add another wreath to their laurels.

A victory by two goals and five tries to a couple of tries is pretty substantial, and the difference would per- haps have been still greater with a decent turn to operate upon. Every game serves to establish the excellence of the Lancashire team this season. They are strong in scoring, this being plainly demonstrated by the fact that they crossed the Devonshire line no fewer than seven times. Pity Coop was not more successful in his place kicks, as two goals out of seven attempts is nothing to boast about. Lancashire were the better team indivi- dually and collectively, and the experiment of playing four three quarters was justified by the results. Miles made a very respectable debut for the winning county.

Yorkshire are having a large share of disappointments, and they will have to wait for a more favourable oppor- tunity for bringing off their contests with Middlesex and Kent. These should have been disposed of on Monday and Tuesday, but the keen frost made play in each in- stance quite out of the question. The composition of the Middlesex team, by the way, is somewhat of a curio- sity. Seven of the players are Scotchmen and me a Welshman, and the ground on which the game should have taken place is in the county of Surrey. A strange combination, surely.

The recent scene on the field of the Wakefield Trinity F.C. had a parallel on Saturday at Askam. It was a match between the home side and Kendal, and a member of the last-named was ordered to leave the ground for insulting the referee. He flatly refused to obey the order, the game being abandoned and declared a win for Askam. It is such occurrences as these that tend to bring football into disrepute, and it is to be hoped that due notice of the affair will be taken by the authorities.

ASSOCIATION'. Everton had their caleulatioUS Xll4O-37,, day. They had counted their chickens before they were hatched, and are now in sackcloth and ashes. They had only to beat North End at Anfield Road and they would be hailed champions of the League. But the apparently easy thing did not come off. On the other hand, the Preston team added one more to their long list or suc- cesses in their engagements with their Liverpool rivals. Crossans, the newest acquisition, whom Scotch writers pronounce to be far below first-class, scored about twenty minutes after the start what proved to be the only goal of the afternoon. As may be imagined the chagrin of Everton was very manifest. They may still attain to the championship, but they will be kept wait- ing for a definite settlement until March 14, when they play their last game at Burnley. North End alone have been able to beat Everton in both their League fixtures this season. Their defence on Saturday was magnificent, the backs playing so resolutely that Trainer had com- paratively little to do.
rupacit...an Snt,l-

The failure of Everton gives the Blackburn Rovers a chance of winning first place in the League race. Their 'second victory over West Bromwich Albion gives them the best average of any of the twelve clubs, and if they maintain their present form to the end they may take the cup from the Nprth End.

The extraordinary collapse of the Wolverhampton Wanderers at Derby has knocked them out of the run- ning. It is almost impossible of credence that a team can be beaten by eight goals and then go and take down such a club as the • Wolves by nine goals to none. No team in the League does such remarkable things in this line as Derby County. They have establisb,ed a record so far as scoring in League games goes.

MISCELLANEOUS. A letter has been received in Manchester from the famous Lancashire wicket-keeper, who has been sent out to Australia for the benefit of his health by the County Cricket Club. Writing at Sydney on December 6th, Pilling reports a great improvement in the state of his health. He is living in the mountains, and finds so much benefit from the invigorating climate that he expects to be able to leave the colony in April, and arrive in Man- chester about the middle of June.
AN AMUSING INCIDENT AT ASHTON.

A most amusing occurrence, in which a local doc- tor, and a couple of policemen were the victims, happened on Friday. On that day a man, who re- sides at Ashton, was found lying on the roadway,in a helpless condition, having been knocked down and run over by a cart, during the fog, and had one leg broken. A messenger hurried to the man's resi- dence, and informed his wife of the accident, and she, grasping the seriousness of the case, hastened to obtain medical assistance. A local doctor, to whom she went, gathered together his splints, bandages, and other- appliances, and made his way to the man's house to wait his arrival. Meanwhile the police had been apprised, and, taking the Ambu- lance stretcher, they proceeded to the spot where the man lay. They gently picked him up, and as gently laid him on the stretcher, and then betook themselves with all speed to his home. They car- ried him in, but on the doctor preparing to set the injured limb, the patient quietly informed him that it was his wooden leg which was broken. This proved to be the case, and it is hardly necessary to say that law and medicine made a rapid exit, in a frame of mind which boded ill for somebody.

div.head: CENTENARIAN.
div.p: A CENTENARIAN.

Sarah Hayter, a widow living in Frowde's Alms- houses, Salisbury; died yesterday morning at the age of 103. Her sight and hearing were somewhat defective, but her intellect was clear. She had been compelled to keep her bed only for the past few days. Her custom was to go to bed very early in the evening, and to rise at about half-past seven in the morning.
INCREASE OF GLASS BOTTLE MAKERS' WAGES AT ST. HELENS, &c.

Durincr the past year a great improvement has taken place in the glass bottle trade; work has been brisker, and then has never been anything like the quantity of bottles turned out that are being made at the present time. As a consequence of the great demand prices are understGod to have very greatly increased. Taking these facts into consideration the Glass Bottle Makers' Trade Protection Associa- tion decided to apply to the masters for an increase of wages, and accordingly, in December,. they sent in an application for an advance of 3s. per week, and for some alterations in the list of prices. They re- ceived a reply from the employers to the effect that they would meet a deputation of the workmen to discuss the, questions, and the meeting was arranged and held at the Raven Hotel, St. Helens, on Satur- day last. The representatives of the eMployers were Mr. E. Cannington, Mr. A. Cannington, Mr. Shaw, Mr. F. R. D. Nuttall, and Mr. 'Borron, of Newton-le-Willows ; while the deputation from the workmen consisted of Messrs. John Rigby, pre- sident of the society : James Hunter, William Brogan, William Makin Gladdle, Richard Rigby, Edward Mercer, William Gee, George Wilson, John George Wolfe. James Marshall, and Robert Hunter, general. secretary. The various questions in which both sides were mutually in- terested were discussed at some length, and ultimately the employers offered an advance of sixpence per gross on overwork on all class of bottles up to imperial quarts. The workmen's deputation _retired and went to their head-quarters where they reported to the committee, who were in waiting. Eventually it was resolved to accept the advanceoffered. This advance will be quite equal to the advance of wages asked for and the bottlemakers in St. Helens are now, in as good a position as they have ever been before.
It should be added that the agreement affects'all the glass bottle makers in the St. Helens and Newton-le- Willows districts.
THE CATHOLIC PHILANTHROPIC SOCIETY.

On Monday evening the annual dinner of- this society was held at the Wagon and Horses Hotel, Warrington. Father K W. Sumner, 0.5.8., rector Of St. Mary's and Chaplain of the society, occupied the chair. Amongst those preseut were Father Feeney Father Myerscough, Father Hennelley, Lieut. Clarke, and Messrs. John Caldwell, Charles Green, Kiernan, Thomas Mather (treasurer), J.Eccles (secretary), J. Simons (president) R. Lowe (vice- president), John Burrows, A. Marsh, W. Dilworth,J. Eckersley, R. Hind, Alban Boyle, Henry Houghton, James Boyle, Alban Stirrup, Peter Langley,. R. John Son, Martin Lyons, Jones, Richard, Jackson, and others. An excellent banquet was placed upon the tables by Mrs. Jones, and afterwards the toasts of " His Holiness Pope Leo XIII." and" Her Majesty the Queen," were drunk with musical honours. The other usual toasts of" The Bishops and Clergy of the dioceses of Liverpool and Shrewsbury," "The town and trade of Warrington," "The Army and Navy," &c., followed. The health of the chaplain, Father Sumner, was proposed by Mr. Kiernan, who said Father Sumner had won the esteem of the townspeople by the work he had done since he came into the town. Father Sumner said he thanked them very sincerely, and his stay of eight years in Warrington had been a happy time for him. and he had been enabled to do something towards the completion of St. Mary's Church. He hoped to stay in the town many more years, if he was spared and permitted by his superiors. He would continue to work towards finishing the church. The priests retired at ten o'clock, and afterwards songs were contributed by the members of the club. Letters were received from the Mayor and others, apologizing for non-attendance. The compfkilyseparated at one o'clock, after singing "God save-tire queen." The society which has been in existence since 1823, is now worin zooo,-- and is -a sick and burial society for the Catholics of the town.

div.head: MR. MORLEY AT NEWCASTLE.
div.p: MR. MORLEY AT NEWCASTLE.
Mr. John Morley addressed his constituents at New-

castle on Tuesdai night. He said that whatever hap- pened at the next general election it was certain that the Liberal Unionist party would cease to exist. The next election would be a clean-cutting election between Liberals and Tories. As to the future of the great ques- tion which Liberals had at heart, all depended not upon them but upon Ireland herself. Referring to Mr. Par- nell's speech at Limerick, he had direct authority to say that after reading that speech Mr. Gladstone maintained that not a single proposal was made at the Hawarden meeting—that was to say, that no proposition was men- tioned to which assent was asked. Mr. Morley denied that the proceedings in Committee-room No. 15 and at the Kilkenny election showed the unfitness of Ireland for self-government, remarking that he had seen no better sign of there being a political opinion and a moral courage among the Irish than this latter event, when the people voted by two to one against the man whom they .had revered for ten years. He charged the opposition to Home Rule upon the enemies of democracy and those who desired to see ill-feeling between the peo- ples of England and Ireland, quoting in support of the latter contention Mr. Howorth's letter to the "Times," and declaring that the phrase quoted by that gentleman ----"ro hell with the Irish "—was the watchword of the Tory party. He denied that the violent and extreme men in Ireland were the dominant force; but if it was desired to turn them into a master force we had only to refuse them, as the Unionists wanted to do, a fair and constitutional settlement. Replying to Mr. Chamberlain, the right hon. gentleman paid that upon the Irish land ' question he stood where he had always stood. He thought it would be best that that question should be solved at Westminster concurrently with the establish- ment of a legislature in Ireland. He had seen. wonder expressed whetker Home Rule was to be dropped. Libe- rals had entered into a solemn engagement with Ireland, and they were bound by every consideration of honour and policy to redcem that engagement; and he believed that the party stood as firm as ever they did to the con- , victions, to the principles, and to the professions which bad been growing and strengthening for five years. All depended upon Ireland. It was for Irishmen to choose; if they were true to themselves the Liberal party would never betray them.
SHOCKING DISCOVERY AT ST. HELEN.
A BODY IN A SOAP BOX;

A shocking discovery, the particulars of which caused some excitement was made at the old St. Thomas's Church burial ground, off Knowsley-road, St. Helens, on Sunday afternoon. The cemetery in question is situated about a mile away from the church, and is some 300 or 400 yards outside the borough boundary. It appears that about noon on Sunday, Joseph Gregson, the caretaker of the nice- tuary chapel at the burial ground, visited the build- ing in order to prepare for a funeral in the after- noon. He stayed about the place for some time,and on leaving locked up the chapel. After dinner he again proceeded to, tho cemetery, and a few min- utes Yater Thomas Dadge, the sexton of St Thomas's Church, arrived. The men subsequently found a wooden box, measuring about 18in. in length, 6in. wide, and about 6in. in depth, in a closet inside the chapel. The lid, which had been tacked down, was immediately opened, and the body a newly-born female ' child was discovered. rhe body was wrapped in two .pieces of old calico, and did not appear to have lain in the box many hours. Appearances indicated that the child was stillborn or of premature birth, and the body with the box, which had been formerly used for " Hud- son's Dry Soap," accordine, to the labels on the outside, were conveyed to the Griffin Inn at Eccleston. The countylipolice authorities were informed of the circum- stances, but up to Wednesday all inquiries into the matter had been unsuccessful. . INQUEST.

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on the body at the Griffith Inn, Eccleston, near St. Helens, on Thursday. The Coroner stated that Dr. Murdoth, of Rainford, had made a post-mortem examination and found that the child was stillborn,and had not had a sep‘arate existence. That being so there was practically nothing for the jury to do but to say that the body was found. If there had been any concealment of birth it was for the police to investigate the matter. Thomas Dadge, the sexton, Jos. Gregson, caretaker, and Dr. Murdoch then gave evidence. There was no evidence how the box was conveyed into its hiding place. The jury recorded the fact that the body had been found.

HARTLEPOOL ELECTION.
MR. GLADSTONE ON THE IRISH PARTY AND LEADERSHIP.
. The "West Hartlepool Northern Daily Mail" says the following letter has been received by Mr. C. Furness, Liberal candidate for the Hartlepools, from Mr. Glad- stone :

Hawarden Castle, January 8, 1891. Dear, Sir, I have already signified my cordial hope that, with your character, abilities, and local position. you may so commenß yourself to the constituency of Hartlepool that it may add itself to the long list of places in all quarters of the country which have reversed the hasty verdict of 1886. But the particular circumstances' of the last few weeks may perhaps warrant my going beyond this general expression, and adding a few words on the political situation. The Irish party has vindicated itself by putting an end to the leadership of Mr. Parnell, and has left us prepared to pursue as hereto'ere the duty of denouncing the principal of unequal lawsand the odious system of coercion, not for crime, but for combin- ation apart from crime which has been adopted by the present Govefument, and Parliament, and made a portion of the permanent law of the land. The Liberal gain of seats, constantly repeated during the last four years. have meant much more than the mere success of a party. They have declared the union for the first time effected between the British and the Irish peoples. That union aims at closing a controversy which I notice that your opponents seek indefinitely to prolong at the cost of national reputation,of Imperial treasure, of inextinguish- able discord, and of the gravest injury to every interest of the country, especially to its interest in the steady march of good legislation. The People of Ireland have put their trust in the people of Great _Britain to deliver them from bad laws, made worse by harsh and insulting administration, and it rests with each constituency as occasion offers to show the sister nation that confidence has not been so reposed in vain. The views of the Liberal party on general legislation have been expressed by you in your excellent address, and still mere largely by the Federation at Sheffield. They longed for the time when by the settlement of tbe Irish question fuller opportunity will be afforded for giving to those views adequate effect. The powers of an Opposition in this respect are very small, especially under. a Government which has done so much by excer tional restraint to reduce or extinguish all ParliamentarY action except its own. Still I think that the time has come when we should endeavour at least to supply a sample of our practical intentions. And this may perhaPS be done by a Bill to clear away the obstacles which hin- der or delay qualified voters from coming upon the re- gister, and to limit the register of every single citizen to a single vote.—l remain, my dear sir, yours faithfully. W. E. GLAngroNE.

C Furness, Esq. The Mayor of Hartlepool on Tuesday received the for the election of a member of Parliament in the rooel of the late Mr. Thomas Richardson. He has fixed the nomination for to-day (Saturday), and the polling for Wednesday next. A Hartlepool Correspondent describes the peculiar conditions under which the election there is being Con- ducted. Fathers and sons are fighting in opposlte. camps, publicans and teetotallers are working peacefullf together, and Church and Chapel are for the time goirg hand in hand. The Dissentients are making despente efforts to secure the working-class vote. The West Hartlepool branch of the Sailors' and fire" men's Union, which commands about 150 votes, decided on Wednesday to give undivided support to Mr. Fulness% as he promises to employ none but union men m his vessels. This Sir William Gray would not promiso.

FAILURE OF RAILWAY CONTRACTORS.
LIABILITIES £400,000, ASSETS £1,000,000

The 4, Daily Telegraph" says:—Some of the after effects of the Baring catastrophe are new being felt, and the failure has been noticed on Wednesday of Messrs. J. E. and M. Clark and Co., railway contractors, of New nroad-st., who were established in 1882. The liabilities are roughly estimated at £400,000, against assets worth 41,000,Q00, subject to realisation.

div.head: THE. RUMOURS OF DISSOLUTION.
div.p: THE. RUMOURS OF DISSOLUTION.

• Sir William Hart-Dyke writes to a correspondent : "There is not a shadow of foundation for the rumour that I have intimated to anyone, directly or indirectly, that there was a prospect of an early dissolution of Par- liament." . Sir George Trevelyan, replyingto a correspondent who 'wrote on the subject of an early dissolution, says :—" I never felt less certain about the immediate future. On the other hand, I never knew the Liberal party in the North of England sounder and more hearty than at the Present time, and if there is a dissolution now or here- after, it will clearly show itself."
A WOMAN FOUND DROWNED NEAR
OLD WARPS.

An inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse, coroner, at the Police, Station, Warrington, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of Ann Bond, aged 5/, who was found drowned on Sunday morning, at Warrington Lock.—Thomas Bond, son of deceased, said the deeeased was the widow of Peter Bond, and had resided at Barton-on-frwell, near Man- chester. She left him on the 4th September last, a little before dinner time, and told him she did not know where she was going. He never saw her again until he saw her dead on Monday morning. He never heard from her. She led an unsettled life at times, and had no fixed residence. Ann Hansbory, 13, Furness-road, Warrington, said the deceased had lived at her house some time back. They took her in as a matter of charity. The deceased left witness's house about half-past nine on Friday night, -to go to Ship Yard, she said, Vrhere she lodged.—P.C. Blackburn deposed to find- !rig the body about eight o'clock on Sunday morn- ing, at Warrington Lock, where he lived. The body Was about sor 6 yards from the river. Ile helped to get the body out.—P.S. Rowbotham said he was informed that the deceased had been turned out of ".her lodgings on Saturday night because she could not pay the rent. She bad lived with Mrs. Ward, 26, Ship Yard. Witness found 4d. and a quantity of miscellaneous articles in the deceased's pockets. —The jury returned an open verdict.

THE CHARGE OF ROBBING A FARM LABOURER OF £l5. Am SHE SWALLOW SOME OF THE SOVEREIGNS? At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, the three women Harriet Cooper, Catherine Bowden ,and Sarah O'Brien, were brought up on remand 'charged with stealing on the Thursday previous, from John Phillips, farm labourer, employed by Mrs. Davies, of Helsby, near Frodsham, Cheshire, a calico bag and its contents, "Steen sovereigns.—John Phillips deposed that he came into Warrington about half-past 2 p.m., on the Ist inst. lie had the bag containing, fifteen sovereigns in his in- side pocket. He had a drop too much before he came. Ile went to the Rose Inn. He was not sure whether he took a whisky bottle in • his pocket. While he was at the tee the three prisoners came in, and he stood them -some drink. Two of the women took hold of him and the other took the money out of his pocket. They. went -cut immediately after, he did not know where to. He shouted out that he was robbed, He did not remember anything that happened afterwards until he found him- self at the Police Station.,-o,'Beien denied that any one of the prisoners ever put her hand on Phillips, and said it w,as a question whether he ever had the money.—Mary Jackson, daughter of Thomas -Jackson, of the Rose Inn, deposed: The complainant came in first about a quarter past two p.m., and the Prisoners about two minutes after. They had some beer and Phillips paid for it. They complained that it was lia,ucldri and called for a quart of the best mild. O'Brigin oa. out of Phillips's hand • and paid far it. Vie Prisoners sat down beside him, and presently ran out, Cooper exclaiming" Come on; I've. got it, we'll divide." Witness saw her put her hand into'her breast. Witness Galled her father down.—Joseph Bate, said be was Passing the Rose Inn in company with his wife, when he saw the prisoners rushing out of the inn, and looking behind them. Mary Jackson told him they had robbed a men. Witness followed the women to the Mersey Hotel in Mersey-st., and went in as if he wanted a glass of ale. The landlady was serving the prisoners with a glass of ale each, and witness saw Cooper pull a bag out and "team" sovereigns from it into her hand. She was all in a tremble likeia leaf. She ripped the end of the bag open, and threw:it under the seat. There seemed to him to be about thirteen sovereigns in the bag. Cooper gave Bowden some gold, and O'Brien four sovereigns. O'Brien seemed very. dissatisfied. He accused the women of having robbed a man in the Rose Inn. Cooper burned to him, and offered him two sovereigns, and said "keep still." He refused to take them. Bowden said "have a drink," and he refused. There were no other witnesses in the room. He stood there with the door in his hand, till Mr. Jackson, the landlord of the Rose,came in. Witness left him there and brought Police Sergeant el:Hinder, and he took the women in charge.—Mary Bate, wife of the previous witness, partially corrobrated her husband's evidence, and said that at his request she , Went to the' Mersey Hotel and brought the bag away from, under the seat; and she handed it to *tweet Chantler. Elizabeth Bailey, landlady the Mersey Hotel, said about 20 minutes to three on the Thursday afternoon previous the Prisoners came to her, house, and Joseph Bate eame in soon after. Cooper put her hand towards him ad he said "No, I shan't take it." O'Brien as she was drinking her beer, put something in her mouth as if she waa taking pills and every time she did this she washed it down -with beer. She did so about three times.— O'Brien: Do you think I drank pills with beer? What a dish it would be !—P.S. Chantler deposed to Phillips identifying the women at the police station, and said dn his (the Sergeant's) asking them to put out on the desk all they had upon them, Cooper put down 2d., O'Brien 6d., and Bowden is. Wild. Whilst Bowden was subse- quently being searched by the female searcher—witness . being then behind a screen in the room—something like Ingney dropped, and a sovereign was picked tip.-80W- den: I got that at the post office bank in the morning. —Wheless proceeded: He asked Bowden to account for the sovereign, and ehe.said she had got it out of the post office bank that morning. Witness said "Very well, we Witt go to the post office, and find out whether that is true. She said I did'nt say the post office; a little men gave me it at Bank Quay Station •, I don't know his name. Witness took the prisoners into the charge room and charged them, and they all said they knew nothing of the matter. They were making use of bad language all the time in the office. They were searched a second time by a female searcher, but nothing was found:—The prisoners, whose demeanour throughout showed them to be thorough blackguards, said they had nothing to say in answer to the charge; and werecommitted for trial to next Liverpool Assizes. COOPER AND BOWDEN CHARGED -WITH ANOTHER THEFT. At the Occasional County Police Court on Monday, before Mr. John Marson, two of the prisoners in the case above reported, Annie Cooper and Catherine Bowden, were charged with stealing at Arpley, oh the 14th inst., aa overcoat, value 305., the property of Peter Williams, labourer, of Phillip-st., Warrington. The foNowing is the substance of the evidence adduced. The prosecutor 'went with a woman named Emma Howard to Arpley, about half-past ten on Sunday evening. They laid down .on his overcoat on the grass, and were there for about a 'couple of hours. Two women and a Man came to them, and the man struggled with Williams, who got away, leaving his overcoat on the ground with Howard. The two women got hold of her and subsequently ran away, 'With the man. Williams came back with two or three !nen from the Spelter Works, but no one was about, and the overcoat had disappeared. The two prisoners came to Spencer, the night watchman at the works, about three o'clock the next morning and asked whethei they 'could lodge there the remainder of the night, Bowden carried a bundle. He gave them permission to stay,and woke them about quarter to six, and they went away, leaving the bundle. He examined it and found an over- coat in it, but allowed it to remain there, and did not inform the police. The following night the prisoners ctline again, and asked for permission to remain a second tine. They enquired whether he knew anything about pie coat. They remained that night, and went away , !n•the morning with the bundle. Bowden pawned e coat at Mr. Orton's the pawnbroker's on Tuesday !corning. The women were subsequently given into cue- ;°dY, and Bowden on being charged said the coat cad been given to her the previous morning about half Past six, by a man at Bank Quay Station. The prisoners were committed for trial.

div.p: NOW READY. FLETT'S CELEBRATED MARMALADE.

THE WARRINGTON EXAMINER SAYS.:— " THE MARMALADE TRADE.—The severe" "weather we have recently experienced in" "this quarter has extended as tar south as." "Seville. It is In the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the °canes best suited for*" "marmalade making are grown. A recent" "frost (the like of wh,ch has not been ex-' perienced for ten years), has played havoc." "with the fruit, and, although though the" " full extent of the damage is not yet" "known, it is believed that fully one half " "the orange crop has been destroyed." "Luckily one shipment has been made to" "Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" "SS " Zurbumn," which has just arrived." "The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett." "Limited, have been fortunate enough to" "have a large consignment on Board this" "vessel, but they do not anticipate getting" "nearly sufficient to meet the demand for" "their well known marmalade, the sale of" " which is fast increasing."

A CORRECTION.

Sir,—Referring to your report of the Aged People's Treat held at the rublic Hall on New Year's Day, I am credited with being the father of the'" Precocious Child Actress" who sang "Cookies and Mussels." I beg to inform you that the child in question—Miss Tissy New- all—(not Miss Minnie Ashton as stated in your valuable paper) is the adopted daughter and late pupil of the latc Brinsley Sheridan, Esq., whom I accompanied on the piano atthe time above mentioned. I should•feel obliged if you would correct this error, as it is only justice to the child and her relations, and at the same time remove any erroneous idea that your readers may form with regard to the same.—Sincerely yours, E. A. ASHTON. General Manager, Theatre Royal., Warrinkton.
(In justice to ourselves we should explain that the in- formation as to the name in our report was given by an official in connection with the Aged People's treat.—ED. Er.]

PUBLIC CHARITY DINNERS AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—Pursuing this subject as promised last week, I must say that the system of public dinner giving to the poor, well meant though it is by its benevolent pro- moters, might very well be superseded by a more excel- lent way. It imposestoo much humiliation on poor peo- ple,and it appears to me that it must leave many de- serving persons unrelieved, because the most self-sup- porting and independent of them will be the least disposed to betray their distressed condition to the, outer world. The feelings of the poor are as susceptible as those of the rich, and ought to have equal considera- tion shown to them. Almshouses are built for decayed gentry, but we never hear of decayed gentle-folk being invited to partake of a charity dinner, tinder the eyes of numbers of the gazing public. Christmas, moreover, of all periods is the time sacred to domesticity 4 and,it seems to me, the time when the poor as well as the rich like to realise the comforts of their homes and their own firesides in one common circle. Why should not the charity given to them at Christmas assume the form most calculated to encourage and meet this natural and laudable wish? .

Then again, by the giving of a dinner or tea at Christ- mas, it is implied that the only or the chief want of a poor person at that season must necessarily be that of .a plentiful meal. Well, this is probably the great need in most cases, but in many instances it is not so. A supply of coal or of clothing, the payment of rent, or the redemption of a. useful or much-prized article from the pledge may be the most immediate want, Would it not be better in future to devote the .amount usually spent in these public Christmas dinners and teas to supplying the poor with meals in their own houses, or relieving them in other ways? It would not always be advisable to distribute cash, I admit, as this might only be spent in drink in many cases ; and I quite understand that it would be much more expensive to supply meals to a number of familes individually than to contract with a caterer for supplying them all to- gether. Ido not deny that there are difficulties in the way ; but it seems to me, that there are considerations nvolved of greater moment than the mere financial question; and considerations that are not to be dis- tainfully put aside on the mere plea of being sentimen- tal. Ido not say a better plan than the existing public dinner system can be devised without some little deliber- ation and care, but I invite our local philanthropists to lay their heads together and see whether in the Christmas of 1891 an experiment cannot be tried in the direction I have indicated.—Yours truly. Warrington, January 14th, 1891.
THE QUESTION OF INSPIRATION.

div.head: MANLIUS.
div.p: MANLIUS.

Sir,—Mr. Peers divides men" in regard to the Bible into four great classes, I. Believers, 11. Reconcilers, 111. Mutilators, IV. Rejectors." He himself manifestly be- longs to class IV, of whom he says that" finding they cannot accept the whole, feel logically and conscienti- ously compelled to assume an attitude of entire non- acceptance." Now•what I want to point out to Mr. Peers is this, that his awn proudly intellectual class IV., and the much despised class I—the Believers "who in the innocence of their hearts and the emptiness of their heads accept without question or inquiry the Book in its entirety as the word of God," stand upon exactly the same footing logically with regard to the total inspira- tion of the Bible. Extremes meet. The Believer (I adopt Mr. Peers' very disputable classification) primarily it may be, convinced of the deity of Christ, and perceiv- ing Him to be the centre of the vast circle of history, law, and religious and ethical teaching contained in the Bible, accepts the whole as transfused by the central life. The Rejector, finding in modern science what con- futes the cosmogony of Genesis, makesit his centre and concludes that all the radii from it to the circumference must pass through unsafe ground. Or, to vary the figure, both Believer and Rejector hold that the part and the whole are made up of similar constituents. No doubt. But the question is, which is the whole, and what is a part ? It is just here that the question of in- spiration comes in. And it is because no theory of inspira- tion has ever yet satisfied, or is ever likely to satisfy even Christian men, that ever), seeker after truth is bound to be a law unto himself in the matter, and ac- cept what commends itself to his spiritual—or if Mr. Peers likes it better—his moral sense. fhe intelligent believer has, however, one great advantage over the rejector, in that he is sure of his centre, and hi g uncer- tainty relates merely to the circumference of eternal truth—a circumference which now expands, now con-

tracts, as science r And spiritual discernment bring forth will ml bGeoadb'lse ttreea, Airy things new and old. Such a man events, of' e knit together for himself many, at all woven .nt threads of divine truth which are inter- It; : the texture of scripture. ip perfectly futile to attempt to settle the question of " AAration by logic, or to make a logical classification of *Wen in regard to it. For in which division of the four ; attempted by Mr. Peers could he himself be classed ? Of him Logic says, " As an Agnostic he is ipso facto disqualified for the task of deciding what is or is net a Divine revelation. If he doubts the existence of God, he puts himself entirely out ot court in the discussion of questions which depend utterly upon a belief in Him." It may be interesting to Mr. Peers to have put before him the view taken of the cosmogony of Genesis by the best Christian thinkers and writers of the day :—" It embodies the beliefs current in the time of the writer, or writers, coloured by the monotheistic convictions of the Israelites."—l am Sz.c.
