div.head: HOT-WATER SYSTEMS OF HOUSES, AND
div.p: THE HOT-WATER SYSTEMS OF HOUSES, AND
THE FROST.

Sir,—Reading of the recent melancholy results that have occurred through the bursting of kitchen hot-water boilers through the frost, and having been several times asked if it was advisable to keep up a fire in the kitchen during the frosty weather, and thus risk an explosion, led me to think that a few remarks explaining the cir- culating system of an average-sized house might be acceptable by giving the uninitiated an idea of the prin- ciples upon which the system is based, and the danger that may be run into through a little want of knowledge in this department. The circulation-of hot water in pipes is caused by the unequal density of the fluid arising from the difference in temperature in the ascending and descending columns Of waterconnectcd with the heating reservoir, and its velocity is governed by the height of the columns and the heat of the water. Bearing this principle in mind will 'help to make my remarks clearer. Somewhere in the roof or oonvenient position a supply cistern is fixed, fed from the -water company's mains 'through a ball tap. From this cistern the water is con- veyed through a pipe by the quickest route possible to the bottom of a copper cylinder placed in the bath- room or other convenient position, and from thence to a , boiler (this should be of copper or wrought welded iron) conical, saddleback, or otherwise, fixed generally behind the kitchen fire-place, where it is heated, and as it be- comes warmed rise • and passes out through a pipe called the 'return" pipe tothe before-mentioned copper cylinder. The colder portion of it comes back again through what is termed the " flow" pipe to the boiler, which it enters at the lowest part, to be re-heated, to rise, flow and return as long as the fire is kept up. The above-men- tioned self-supplying cistern must be placed above the highest level to which the hot water is desired to rise, so as to give a sufficient pressure to carry the water to its various destinations. From the top of the copper cylinder a pipe is taken, termed the exhaust pipe, which pipe is carried through the roof some short distance, and turned down at the end; this pipe acts as a safety valve for any steam that is generated when the water reaches boiling point. Now, as water will always find its own level, the water in this pipe will necessarily rise to the level of the water in the supply cistern, and, as the hottest water will always be found uppermost, the hottest water will be found in the exhaust pipe. From this exhaust pipe con- nections are made and pipes are laid to the various posi- tions where hot water is required in the house. When this arrangement is carried out, viz., taking the supply pipe from the exhaust pipe, as above mentioned, a good fire may be kept up during the frosty weather, and the chances of an explosion aro reduced to as low a point as possible, for, should the self-supplying cistern in the roof become frozen and refuse to work, the cylinder will still be full of water, which cannotbe drawn off, if the supply is taken, from the exhaust pipe, this pipe being above the cylinder. Should the supply system refuse to work by reason of frost or otherwise,the hot-water taps in the house willthen simply stop their supply,as the main feed is cut off, and as the only drain upon the water in the cylinder generally contains from 30 to 50 gallons, I need hardly say it will take some time for it to be emptied. Should the above happen, viz., taps stop their supply through the main feed being cut off, it is advisable to leave these taps turned on full, so as to allow of any steam that may be generated to pass away through them, for it sometimes happens that the end of the exhaust pipe it- self becomes frozen up through the drippings of the con- densed steam, and this being the case, the steam gene- rated has no means of getting away except by the taps. Having now explained the main principles of the sys- tern, I will endeavour to point out one or two defects which, I regret to say, are all but too common in houses which are professedly fitted up in the best manner. One of the chief dangers is in taking the supply pipes to the various positions in the house from the circulating pipes, instead of from the exhaust pipe. This is more particu- larly done in the case of the scullery slopstone supply, and which is, perhaps, the most dangerous ease, as more hot water is drawn from this tapthan any of the others, it being often in constant daily use. By doing what I have mentioned, the cylinder can be syphoneedry, also the flow--and return pipes down to the level of the tap, pro- viding the self-supplying cistern in the roof refuses to work, through frost or otherwise. This defective arrange- ment is adopted to save the extra length of the pipe that would be required to track all the way from the exhaust pipe ; but, as I have pointed out, it would be much safer to take the supply from the exhaust pipe. Another defective arrangement is the filling of the supply cistern in the roof by means of a force pump from a tank from, say, beneath the scullery, as this necessi- tates constant pumping to keep the cistern full, and this pumping is not always sufficiently attended to. Should the cistern be allowed to become empty and the supply pipes be taken from the circulating pipes instead of from the exhaust pipe, the cylinder would be emptied as before mentioned, and in case the pump was then used and cold water pumped into the cistern whilst a good fire was burning, steam would be rapidly generated, and the ' danger of an explosion might be run into. A point that it is advisable to attend to where practicable, is- to carry all piping on inside walls,not outside walls, so as to keep them as warm as possible, and reduce the chances of freezing to a minimum. Another precaution of encasing the pipes, particularly the exhaust pipe, with felt or otherwise, may be adopted to render additional security. I have not gone into the question of double circulation whereby hot water may be obtained immediately the taps are turned, thus avoiding the delay of emptying the length of pipe of cold water, but have confined myself to a simple single system to be found in an average clam house,arri should my remarks be of use to anyone, my object will be accomplished. Of course, any and all precautions taken in perfect- ing this system are always liable to be deranged by a severe and long-continued frost; as even the bet system may give way at one point or another. In conclusion, I should particularly advise householders to have the hot water system of their houses thoroughly examined by a competent plumber,and see that all precautions are taken to avoid the danger and expense of any mishap that might occur through faulty or jerry construction.— Yours, &c.,
PERCY SILCOCK, Architect. Egypt-st., Warrington, Jan. , 'lB9l.

div.head: RUNCORN RELIEF 'FUND.
div.p: RUNCORN RELIEF 'FUND.

As announced last week a relief fund for reliev- ing the distress caused in the town by the long and severe frost, has been formed in Runcorn, and Et Committee,with Mr. S. Taylor as chairman, is carry- ing out this scheme of relief. The extent of the relief given in individual cases is 45., and tickets have been printed as follows: " Runcorn Relief Pund;lB9l. Supply the bearer with meat or groceries Is," or supply the bearer with one cwt. of coal." Tickets are also distributed for soup, which is daily dispensed at noon, at the toulhouse of the Town Hall. This is an important and arduous part of the undertaking. Sitting accommodation is provided for nearly.6o persons in the place, and all those in need are supplied.with nutritious and savoury soup, and a large slice of bread, while large numbers carry the soup away in cans to their families at home. Mrs. Jackson, caretaker, and Mr. Percival, inspector, are the principals in-- making the soup, and several gentlemen daily take an active -Dart in its distribution. On Thursday at noon, no fewer than seven hundred were fed, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldri and Mr. Taylor waiting upon the hungry folk.who seemed deeply grateful for the meal pro- vided. On Tuesday afternoon the large quantity of sand wiches.,currant breedokc. left from the aged persons' treat, ware distributed to several hundreds of men,women,and children. In fact it may be pointed out that in the dis- tribution of the soup the children received the first and most patient care. Mr. W. Shaw, the Mersey Missioner, also provides soup daily as does Mr. Jonathan Horsefield for his boat-people at his house in Canal-st. The response for subscriptions has been very generously responded to, and several of the large firms have guaranteed a consid- erable sum of money for each week while the distress prevails, and Mr. P. Speakman C.C., has promised £lO worth of coal.

Details have been received of the piratical seizure of the British steamer Nam° near the coast of Hongkong by a nnmber of Chinese robbers who had taken passage on board. The captain and two of the crew were mur- dered, and the passengers were maltreated and robbed by the pirates. A British gunboat has been sent in pur- suit, but no captures have been effected. Mr. Gladstone, speaking on Thursday night at the annual dinner to the tennantry on the Hawarden estate, said he rejoiced that the condition of the masses of the population was far better now than fifty years ago. He aerwards dealt with agricultural depression and the great abatements in rent, and expressed the opinion that the period of difficulty had tended to unite more closely the various claws interested in the cultivation el the soil,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1891.
THE DUKE OF AOSTA.

The Duke of Aosta in his time played, though but for a brief period, the important part of a King ' of Spain. He was the second son of the late Victor Emman- ual, King of Italy, and was born May 30, 1845. After the revolution in Spain in 1868, Marshal Prim, offered the Spanish crown first to the King of Portugal, next to the Duke of Genoa, and after- wards to the Prince Leopold, all of whom refused it. Finally he fixed on the young Duke of Aosta, who was on the 10th of November, 1870, elected King of Spain by the Cortes by 191 votes against 120. The young king landed at Cartagenan on December 30, the very day Marshal Prim expired from the wounds received at the hands of an assassin a few hours previously. His reign was a brief and troublous one. Ile was unpopular with the masses of the Spanish people, whose dislike to foreigners is a marked trait in their character, and his position. which had never been secure, became extremely dangerous in the summer of 1872, when a Cariist rising took place in the northern provinces, and an insurrection broke out almost simultaneously among the sailors and the workmen in the arsenal at Ferrol, who hoisted the red flag and for son-e time set the Government at defiance. On the 19th of July in the same year, an unsuccessful attempt was made to assassinate the King and Queen. Amadeus then thought it prudent to be a King of Spain no longer, and he declared his abdication on February 11,1873. He left the country the very next day. From that time till his death, which took place on January 18th, last year—a victim to Russian influenza—he lived in his native country as a private Italian citizen.
MR. JOSEPH GILLIS BIGGAR, M.P.

Mr. Joseph Gillis Biggar, M.P. for West Craven died sudd, ,f heart disease in London on the 19th February last. Mr. Biggar was born at Belfast in 1828, and was educated at the Bel- fast Academy. It is said that the House of Commons in ;hese later days would have )een quite a different place ithout the familiar figure of

Mr. Biggar. It was at West- minster that he earned the distinction of being the "champion obstructive." He was for many years a member of the Belfast Corporation, and it was not till 1871 that he transferred his attentions to Parlia- ment. The Government, it has been remarked, always showed its regard for him by saving him from the fate of so many of hiscompanions-in-arms —the plank bed and prison gruel. Mr. Biggar's advocates used to declare that his somewhat harsh exterior hid as kindly and generous a disposition as there was in the House of Commons, and that when Lord Beaconsfield asked in surprise," What's that ?" on the first occasion of Mr. Biggar rising to address the House, he might truthfully have been told, "A body like an oyster shell covering a heart like a pearl."
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."
That the caustic men out on strike at Messrs. Pilkington's chemical works, Widnes, have returned to work on the old terms after losing their wages for two months. _ _ _ _

That the men have returned on the advice of Mr. King, the organiser of the Chemical Workers' Union. Pity the advice was not given sooner. That the application of Widnes Local Board for a Charter of Incorporation will be considered by the Privy Council in February, and there is no doubt of a favourable reply. That the action of the Board in dividing the town into six wards, instead of four, will meet with the general approval of the ratepayers. That the sulphuretted hydrogen nuisance of Widnes travelled on to Runcorn during the early part of this week, and was not welcomed very heartily. In fact, for several mornings the ground was covered by a very objectionable deposit. That the letter of Mr. Fletcher, the chief inspec- tor under the Alkali Acts, has shown the Board their power in this matter, and although there is no desire to harass the manufacturers, the nuisance ought to be stopped altogether or very much abated. That the aged persons' treat was a very successful and pleasant gathering, and it was a sight worth seeing to witness the grey-headed old men and women enjoying themselves so heartily, That the annual report of the Runcorn Savings Bank, on Tuesday. shows that there is a widespread spirit of thrift in the town, and the figures pre- sented by the actuary are very interestiug reading. That an expression of regret at the discontinuance of the penny bank will be generally echoed by those interested, and it would be a good thing if the idea thrown out by Dr. McDougall could be carried out. That the Relief Fund Committee of Runcorn is carrying out a very useful and necessary work, and the gentlemen connected with it are deserving of the thanks of the community.

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINerS BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINerS BANK.

The 48th annual meeting of the trustees and managers was held at the bank, on Tuesday. under the presidency of Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P. The secre- tary (Mr. W. Handley) having read the circular convening the meeting, and the minutes of the last meeting of the trustees and managers having been confirmed, submitted the following epitome of the business of the bank f)r the past year: -There were 2,301 personal deposits to the amount of £5,356 10. id.; the penny banks, £9 2s. sd. ;71 charitable societies, £3Ol 18s. 10d. ; 125 friendly societies, £1,812 Os. 2d.; total deposits, 2,503; amounting to £7,479 11s. sd. There were 716 withdrawals of personal deposits, amounting to £6,403 9s. 6d.; the penny bank, £3 195.; 13 charit- able societies, £291 38. 9d. ; friendly societies, £2,386 Os. lid.; total deposits withdrawn 844, amount £9,084 13s. 2d. These figures showed a total number of transactions of 3,347, and a turnover of £16,564 4s. Bd. Owing to the activity of the building trade in the neighbourhood, a larger amount than usual had been withdrawn and invested in either the purchase or mort- gage of property; these amounts were being gradually replaced by the continued savings of, in many cases, the same depositors. The average personal deposit had been £2 6s. 60., and withdrawal £8 18s. 101 d. The number of open accounts at the close of the bank year was as follows: personal accounts 963, amount £23,668 Bs. 9c1.; penny bank 1, amount £l7 7s. 5d.; charitable societies 16, amount £498 Os. id.; friendly societies 49, amount £5,713 9s. 5d.; total open accounts, 1,029; ledger balances, £29,381 18s. 2d. This was an increase of accounts, as compared with last year of 28; and 518 of these accounts or more than one half of the , total number consisted of balances under £lO each. The interest allowed the Bank by the National Debt Commissioners during the year amounted to £BOl 15s. 6d.; dividends on consols held for depositors £lB us. 3d.; commission allowed the bank on purchase of stock ss. 7d. ; sale of pass books £1 Bs. 4d. ; total income £822 Os. Bd. The interest paid and credited to depositors was £699 18s. id., dividends on stock £lB us. 3d.; expenses of management £92 16s. 4d.; total payments £Bll ss. sd. ; leaving a surplus for the year of £lO 15s. Adding to this amount the surplus at the close of the previous year, gave a total surplus over liabilities of £B7 14s. 11d. During the year 5 depositors had through the bank invested £5OO in Government stock at an average cost including commission of £96 193. 3d. The amount of stock held by the National Debt Commissioners through the agency of the Bank was £900.-The Secretary also submitted the certificate of the auditors (Messrs. J. H. Salkeld, Ed. Marwood, Wm. Williamson, and C. Pownall), and the -certificate of the National Debt Commissioners.

The President expressed the pleasure it gave him to propose the adoption of the report. As they all knew he took, and had done so for many years, a great interest in the welfare of an institution which in the past had done so much good to the town and neighbourhood, and indpced so many to commence and continue saving,and which was rapidly approaching its. jubilee in vigorous life and greater usefulness. He had noticed, during the reading of the report, that there was now only one Penny Bank and that at Weston, and though he knew that the number of small depositors had largely increased at the Savings Bank he greatly regretted that the Penny- Bank which for so many years had usefully and success- fully been carried on at Runcorn had been given up. At the Savings bank the smallest depositthat could be taken was sixpence, while a Penny Bank appealed to the chil- dren to gavel their pence and thus inculcated habits of thrift and providence from infancy; and as a matter of fact he had known as many as 7,000 deposits in a single year. He mentioned this in passing, as he was sorry that such a useful institution no longer existed in the town; but he was especially pleased to see that the Savings Bank was increasingly appreciated as testified by the report just read, and he had very great.pleasure in proposing that the report be adopted. Dr. McDougall seconded the proposition. He had ob- served with great satisfaction that so large a number of the accounts were fof small sums, 518 accounts being for sums under £lO out of a total number of 1029. He this spoke well for the institution as fulfilling its purpose of a Savings Bank. The President had drawn attention to the closing; of the Penny Bank, and he snggested that the jubilee of the Savings Bank 'might be suitably recog- nised by doing something in the way of re-establishing such a useful institution. The report was unanimously adopted. The Rev. Dr. Preston moved that the best thanks of the trustees and managers be accorded to their treasurer Mr. J. Simpson, for his services during the past year. They all knew what an excellent treasurer they had in Mr. Simpson, and how careful he watched over the financial interests of the bank, and he trustedhe would long be spared to serve, and that the approaching Bank Jubilee would find him in full vigour as their treasurer. Mr. S. Taylor cordially seconded the proposition, and said he was sure that it was impossible for the bank to have a more worthy or more respected treasurer. The proposition was unanimously carried. In acknowledgement Mr. Simpson stated the greats pleasure it gave him to fill the office, and to do all he could for an institution with which he had been so long connected. _

Mr. T. Handley proposed the re-appointment of the auditors, Messrs. J. H. Salkeld, Marwood, Williamson, and Pownall, and bore testimony to the carefulness of of their audit as he knew that not only did they thoroughly examine the accounts at the close of the year but at the close of each quarter they audited the deposits and withdrawals.

Mr Whittaker seconded their reappointment. Mr. Lake proposed that the best thanks of the trustees and managers be tendered to the President for the interest he took in the welfare of the Bank. The propo- sition having been seconded by Mr. A. Salkeld, was carried with acclamation.

Mr. Brundrit thanked them for the way in which they had received it. As had been remarked he had been con- nected with the Bank for many years and he thought he was the possessor of the most unique if not the oldest account in the Bank Ledger, for about the year 1847 he became a depositor for the sum of £5 which sum had remained untouched except for the addition of the annual interest. It would' be interesting to know how much that £5 now amounted to (on reference to the Ledger it was found that it had nearly quadrupled itself.) It would always be his pleasure to do all he could for an institution with which he and so many whom he had known and honoured had been connected.
The annual returns to the National Debt Commis- sioners were then signed and the meeting separated.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY,

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Co!onel Ashton presided, and there were present, Messrs. Molntyre, Aaron, Pickering, Heywood, Brandreth, W. Whitlow, J. Whitlow, J. Hall, and 11. G. Linaker (clerk.)
FEVER IN THE DISTRICT'.

The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams), reported that six cases of typhoid fever had occurred in the township of Appleton, and also one case of scarlet fever. A case of typhoid fever had also taken place at Frodsliam. Five cases of diptheria had also occurred at Stretton, and sanitary defects at one residence ought to be remedied. —The report was approved. The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Farrington), reported that he had received complaints of a nuisance arising at Stockton Heath through the deposit of tannery refuse i a disused sand hole In the early morning and late at night the nuisance was abominable. The Sanitary Com- mittee of the borough of Warrington had prohibited the deposit of the refuse in their district. The subject was referred to tbo Medica) fl2er for his report.

div.head: AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUN CORN.
div.p: AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUN CORN.

A most interesting gathering took place in Run- corn Public Hall on Wednesday night, when the aged people of the town were entertained to tea. Some years ago, when the Y.M.C.A., was in exis- tence, the annual aged persons' treat was an event in the local calendar, anxiously looked forward to by the old, who derived much happiness from the reunion. ' When the Association closed its doors un- fortunately the treat became a thing of the past, and it was not uutil a few weeks ago the idea of resuscitating the treat was conveyed to Mr.S.Taylor, the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners. Act- ing on the requisition presented,Mr. Taylor called a public meeting to consider the subject, and it was determined to join in an effort to throw a " ray of sunshine and a gleam of happiness" across the paths of the old folks. A committee was appointed with Messrs. J. D. Jones,H. Wright,and W. IL Frith,as tieevetaries,and the ready response to the appeal sent out was vet?, grati_ fying. On Wednesday, five hundred of the oldest inhabi- tants gathered in the Hall, which had been decorated by Capt. Le Couteur for the occasion. They were provided with a capital tea, in which ham and beef formed a not unimportant part, and there were also fancy breads pro- vided. The oldest person present was Mrs. Edwards of Rutland-st., who had attained the age of 87 years. Born at Astmoor, she had spent the whole of her life in Run- corn, the furthest distance she had travelled away being Liverpool. She had also present a brother aged 76, and and a sister 73, their united ages being 238 years. The wants of the guests were attended to by a host of willing workers, and after tea an entertainment was provided. Mr. S. Taylor presided and amongst the large number on the platform were the Revs. Canon Wood, Dr. Preston, Dr. Gastaldi J. Holden, A. J. Jame- son, G. H. Kingston, G. B. Seeley, W. Burson, J. Simp- son, and A. Finch; Dr. Steele, Captain Le Couteur, Mr. P. Speakman C.C. Messrs. John simpson, F. J. Norman, J. J. Howitt, H. J. Grice.—The Chairman after giving all a hearty welcome, said they were not to be troubled with a lecture, nor a sermon, nor a speech, but they might expect him tosay a word or two. He might tell them that it was intended to make the treat to the aged people of Runcorn an annual affair. (Applause.) He owed his position of chairman that evening to the fact that he was Chairman of the Commissioners, and the treat was now established on such lines that it would be impossible , for it to fall through. It had not been an easy matter to organise the treat, and those who had taken part had had a great deal of hard work to do; it had proved a much more gigantic affair than he had at first antici- pated. The response of the people appealed to had been most gratifying, and whoever occupied the position of Chairman of the Commissioners in future would feel bound to carry on the treat. (Applause.)—The pro- gramme was then proceeded with. The Volunteer band performed several selections of music, and Mr. J. Woods gave a cornet solo on "Welsh airs" in clever style. Mr. C. Pownall sang "Tom Bowling" with appropriate ex- pression; Mr. T. Clegg was encored for his rendering of "Simon the Cellarer " and in response gave "Tit- Willow," from the "Mikado." Later in the evening he caused much merriment by his humorous sketch "Julius Ccesar's visit to Runcorn." Mrs. J. Leach contributed two songs, which she rendered in her well-known finished manner, and Mrs. Tait rendered "Home sweet home "with charming Expression and effect,and acknow- ledged a recall by singing " On the banks of Allan waters." Mr. J. H. Harrison gave "Off to Philadelphia". with much effect, and Mr. T. Wilkinson sang "True as Steel" with considerable force. Mr. David Billington sang the comic song "She was" in character and created much laughter and earned an encore. The Parish Church Choir rendered in capital style the part songs "The Old Brigade" and "The Village Blacksmith" and brought the concert to a close by singing "Auld lang sync," in which the audience heartilyjoined. During the interval each woman was presented with a mince pie, an orange, and two ounces of tea, and each man a mince pie. A vote of thanks was accorded to the donors of the treat on the motion of Mr. William Bonken, 70 years of age. The treat was an unqualified success from every point of view, and it was a pleasing sight, enjoyed by a large number of townspeople who occupied the gallery to see the bright and happy faces of the old folks.

div.head: MIDI.
div.p: MIDI.

CONGREGATIONAL .BAND OF HOPE.—The Rev. Charles Clay presided over a public meeting in connection with the Congregational Band of Hope on Monday evening. in attractive programme was submitted, and many of the members recited in a pleasing manner. Several dialogues were also given. The Wesleyans held their usual meeting the same evening. PRESENTATION TO A SHEPIIERD.—At a meeting of the Shepherds by Night Lodge, Lymm (Warrington District A.U.), a very interesting ceremony took place on Satur- day. at the Lodge Room of the above society, at the Nag's Head Hotel, when Bro. William Ratcliffe was pre. seated with a beautifully framed emblem of merit, in recognition of faithful services rendered by him to his lodge for several years. Bro. Robert Ditchfield, of Thel- wall, made the presentation before a full lodge. WF,SLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The annual social tea meeting and entertainment in connection with the above school took place oft Tuesday evening. A large number sat down to tea, after which a public meeting was held, presided over by Mr. C. Brown, the superintendent of the Sunday school. The Rev. Thomas Ross, of Warring- ton, also delivered an address. Several songs were given and recitations delivered by some children from the Boys' Refuge, Manchester. Miss Greeb, R.A.M., played several pianoforte solos beautifully. A museum of art was also on view, containing microscopical illustrations and foreign curiosities. THE POPULAR CONCERTS.—The second of a series of popular penny concerts to be held during the winter months took place on Saturday evening in the Bridge- water Rooms. There was again a capital attendance, Mr. Richard Dutton occupying the chair. Songs were given by the Misses Boyds (Stretford), Mr, D. Ellison (Latchford), Mr. Jones (Lymm Grammar School), and Master Arthur Astley. Mr. W. Leather and Misses Dot-

div.head: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYMM PETTY SESSIONS.
FRlDAY.—Beforeiie;sis: T. P. Norris (chairman), and
Dr. Brabazon.
TILE DEATH OF MR. BARTON.—The Chairman said before the business of the court commenced he should

Eke to say a wcrd of sympathy with the widow of the magistrate who had died during the past week, and the oldest magistrate in that division with the exception of Mr. Jones, Mr. John Barton. He was well-known in that court and also at Altrincham, and he (the Chair- man) was quite certain no gentleman ever carried out his duties with a better conscience and more carefully than the deceased gentleman always did. He was sure the court would concur with him in offering condolence with the widow.

BRGGING.—Thomas Smith was charged with begging at i Eagle Brow,Lymm,on the 15th inst. It appeared that he 1 was going from shop to shop asking for coppers, though he ha.cl upon him a quantity of currant bread, half a threepenny loaf, some pork, some sausage, and 6d. in copper. The defendant was evidently imbecile, his com- ment on the evidence of each witness being "I have nothing to say to him; he is a man." He was sent to prison for seven days. DOGS UNMUZZLED.—Thomas Griffiths, for allow- ing his dog to be at large unmuzzled at Little Legh, and without having a collar on it with his name thereon; Thomas Massey, for having his dog out unmuzzled at Lymm, on he 31st ult., Joseph Priestner for a similar offence on the sth inst. at Warbur- ton, were each fined 3s. 6d. and costs.—Ezekiel Ball, of Warrington, was charged with having - his dog at large unmuzzled, on Sunday last, at Little Legh. A constable haying given evidence against him, the defendant pleaded that he had had a temporary muzzle on the dog, just before the officer came up to him, but the animal was crossing the road, and a bicycle came past and caught the muzzle and broke it. He produced a chain, and said that was what he had used to muzzle the dog. The case was dismissed. DISCHARGING e. Gott IN rue HIGHWAY.—Wm. Bowden, of the Ship Canal Huts,Thelwall, was charged with firing off a gun in the public highway atthe same place, I on the 17th ult. The defendant said he fired at two sparrows. He was ordered to pay the costs, ss. 6d. DRUNK, &c.—Martin Ward drunk on the 10th ult., at Lymm, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—William VV hiteway, charged with being drunk on the 31st ult., at Lymm,was dismissed.—George Frederick Goole, charged with being drunk and disorderly at Lytnvn on the 31st ult., was dismissed. A TRACTION ENGINE CAlil3.—John Hugh Simpson was charged that on the sth inst., he allowed a tKaction en- gine to be used on the highway, at Lymm, without hav- ing some one in front to drive or conduct it properly. The case was proved by the police, and the magistrates imposed the nominal fine of is. and costs. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LlCENSE.—Theodore Smith was charged with keeping a dog without a license at Heatley on the 29th ult.—The defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING LAST NIGHT AT LYMM.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING LAST NIGHT AT LYMM.

Last evening one of a series of meetings that are being held in the Altrincham Division of Cheshire, in support of the candidature of Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, who hopes to succeed Sir W. C. Brooks, as the member for that part of the county, was held at the Plough Hotel, Lvmm, under the chairmanship of Mr. Peter Stubs. He was supported by Mr. Raikes, M.P., the Postmaster- General, by Sir W. C. Brooks, the sitting mem- ber, by the candidate, and by many other local Conservatives.—The Chairman, having briefly referred to the campaign now being conducted in the division,—Sir W. C. Brooks, proposed a motion ex- pressing full confidence in the Government, and con- gratulating her Majesty's ministers on the success of their home and foreign policy.—Mr. Coningsby Disr- aeli was the next to address the meeting. The Union- ist Government, he said, had been for the past four years undermining the power of secret societies in Ireland, and had accomplished their purpose. He seconded the resolution, which was carried with applause—. Replying to it,. Mr. 11. C. Raikes said that the friends of the Government remained well united. He proceeded to reply to Mr. Morley's speech, and to refer to the split amongst the Home Rulers. The meeting Closed with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT THEL-
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT THEL-
WALL.

Under the auspices of the Altrincham Division Conservative Association, a public meeting was held in the Temperance Hall, Thelwall. on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied bx Admiral Jones Parry, and among the audience were Sir William Cuuliffe Brooks, Bart. M.P., Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, the Conservative candidate for the divi- sion; Mr. Peter Stubs, Major Pickmere. Mr. A. W. Callender, Mr. William Tinsley, Mr. Colin Mclver, Mr. L. W. Reynolds, and Mr. F. R. B. Lindsell (sec- retary to the Altrincham Division Conservative Association). Several ladies, including Lady Brooks, occupied seats on the platform. There was a good attendance of the voters in the district. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman apologized for the absence of Mr. R. A. Naylor, who he said, was not quite well, but it was hoped his trip who, Colwyn Bay would restore him to health and strength again. (Ap- plause.) Since their last meeting in that hall, they had lost an excellent neighbour by the death of Mr. Henry Stanton, who had been a good friend to the Conservative cause. He had, indeed, been a staunch Conservative, and he was sure every one in the room would have heard of his death with the deepest regret. kHear, hear.) With reference to Sir William Brooks, they were all sorry he had decided to retire from the representation, of the division, but in the present state of affairs, they could not ask anyone to remain a member of the House of Commons if he wished to retire. The position of a mem- ber of the House of Commons was not a bed of roses, and they had often heard that "evil communications corrupt good manners." (Laughter.) He contended that in Mr. Coninesby Disraeli they had a good candidate. (Hear, hear.) In choosing a candidate they must not ask "What are your ideas about Home Rule, disestab- lishment, the abolition of tithes ?" &c. These were simply political fads, election cries. They should select a man who "feared God and honoured the King." (Applause.) They wanted men in Parliament who would not be ashamed of history, but who would carefully study it as they would the Bible— as a guide to them. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Major Pickmere proposed "That this public meeting expresses its full confidence in the Unionist Government, and congratulates her Majesty's Ministers on the success of their home and foreign policy, and trusts that the beneficent legislation already affected, and now being, proceeded with, will secure the continued union and pros- perity of the nation." (Applause.) With regard to Mr. Disraeli, he felt that even if he had been a Liberal he could have voted for him, because he held such an hon- oured name. He was, however, a good Conservative, and he hoped that on the day of election the electors would vote for him, and return him as their representa- tive by a large majority.. (Applause.)—Mr. William Tinsley seconded the motion.—Addresses were next given by Sir W. C. Brooks, M.P., and Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, the Conservative candidate.—The resolution was then put to the meeting, and carried with one dis- sentient.—The Chairman said he had forgotten to apolo- gize for the absence of Mr. Bleckly.—Mr. Thomas Cooke proposed a vote of thanks to Sir William Brooks and Mr. Disraeli for their addresses. Mr. John Houghton seconded the motion, which was heartily agreed to.—Sir William briefly returned thanks, and proposed a vote of thanks to Admiral Jones Parry for presiding over the meeting.—This was seconded by Mr. Disraeli and carried, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
COVENANT SERVICE .A.T.THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

On Sunday afternoon, in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel, the annual covenant service was held. The service was conducted by the Rev. T. Ross, and afterwards the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper was administered. There was a large atten- dance.

div.p: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
H. Gorse of the abovii school has been elected— after open competion, to a Minor Scholarship of the value of £4O per annum at Queen's College, Cam- bridge.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNITED TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNITED TRADES COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this council was held on Tuesday at the Horsemarket-st., Cocoa Rooms. After the routine business, a communication was read from the organising Secretary of the Winsford branch of the Women's Association, requesting the assistance of the Warrington Trades Council to form a branch of the Women's Association in War- rington. As the General Labourers Union had pre- viously taken the matter in hand, it was ultimately decided to work in co-operation with them. A meet- ing will, therefore, shortly be held to try to orga- nise a branch in Warrington. The question of hDld- ing a trades demonstration during the, present year was again brought forward. Delegates attended the meeting for the first time from the Plasterers Society, who in response to appeals have joined the Council. It was decided to alter the name of the Council to the " Warrington Trades and Labour Council."
FORMATION OF A TRA.DESMEtT'S ANGLING CLUB.

On Thursday evening the first meeting of the Warrington Tradesmen's Angling and Social Club, which was formed the previous Thursday night,was held at the flop Pole Inn, Rorsemarket-st. Mr. W. Mawson, presided. Mr. James Bancroft, one of the best local authorities on angling matters, was appointed secretary pro tem., and Mr. Harry Dale. landlord of the Hop Pole, treasurer. The members number already between 20 and 30, and include Mr. Wm. Bolton, of the Royal Exchange Inn, said to be the champion angler of Warrington.

div.head: LAT EST NE WS.
div.p: LAT EST NE WS.
ANOTHER CREMATION.
The remains of the Duke of Bedford were yesterday morning removed to Woking to be cremated.
FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.
Yesterday a destructive fire occurred ai..a hatter's shop in Islington, London. A girl, aged seven years, was burnt to death. THE IRISH DISTRESS.

The " Freeman's Journal " says that letters and reports continue to arrive from all parts of the western districts of Ulster, Connaught, and Munster, testifying that the extreme limit of destitution has been reached. MR. PARNELL'S RETIREMENT CONFIRMED.
The new anti-Parnellite states that the retirement of Mr. Parnell has not merely been determined on, but consented to. Mr. Parnell's voluntary abdication is being rapidly arranged.
THE CONSUMPTION CURE.

PARIS, FRIDAY.—The members of the medical profes- sion in Paris hold that Dr. Koch's account of his dis- covery is incomplete as to the quantity of the dose, and the substance, of which the liquid is composed are not indicated.

div.head: ARRESTED FOR MURDER.
div.p: ARRESTED FOR MURDER.

A Castleisland correspondent -telegraphs that the Castleisland police on Thursday night arrested five young men on the charge of being concerned in the murder of Cornelius Hickey, at Crinna, near Castleisland, six years ago. DEATH OF THE EARL OF DEVON.

Edward Baldwin, the thirteenth Earl of Devon, died in London late on Thursday night. The deceased succeeded his father on November 18, 1888. His Lordship was attacked with paralysis on Saturday last, and never rallied. The late earl, who was born in 1836, was never married, and is succeeded by his uncle, the Rev. S. H. Courtenay, prebendary of Exeter Cathedral, and rector of Powderam. MURDER AND SUICIDE AT NEWBURY.

Mrs. Chamberlain, wife of a cattle dealer residing at a farm on Welsh Common, Newbury, was sitting at her home with her husband and brother named Heath, on Thursday night, when she told the former that she wished to speak to the latter privately. The husband retired, and during his absence she shot her brother with a gun and killed him. When her husband was attempt- ing to take the gun from her she was shot. It is sup- posed she committed suicide.

div.head: SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE.

There was a decided improvement in the arrival and departure of trains at Waverley Station yesterday morn- ing, otherwise there is no change in the position of the strike. The engine of the passenger train broke do% n at Cartsdyke. A railway man has been arrested for intimidation but subsequently released. A Glasgow cor- respondent telegraphs that the North British superintend- ent reports that the railway police are being annoyed at Parkhead by the crowds as they go to work. The police had to interfere at Glasgow, and a South-Western engine driver on returning from work yesterday morning was knocked down and had his head cut and lip split.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCITESTKR TRADE, PRIDA.Y.—There is not much buoyancy in any department of this market, and not a very large nor very satisfactory business going through. Cotton, however, seems buoyant; the estimate has improved from 8.000 to 10,000 bales. Spinners are to-day willing sellers of yarn at quotations, but manufacturers are not in a position to operate for quantity, and little is going through. In cloth a moderate miscellaneous trade continues to be done for the Levant, and also for Egypt and the Soudan. LONDON PRODUCE, PRIDA.Y. Sugar: Pieces in fair demand at firm rates; dry goods and crystals quiet—Lvle's third crystals 16s 9d and Tate's first crystals 19s 3d ' • foreign dull; beet slack—January buyers 12s 51d and sellers 12s 61d, and February buyers 12s 6d and sellers 12s 7id. Coffee quiet but firm; Rio—January 775, March 745, and May 735. Tea firm. Rice steady. Jute and hemp still dull. Linseed oil, 21s 6d to 21e 9d. Turpentine, 28s 9d to 295. Petroleum un- changed. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, PRIDAY.—The beef and pork markets exhibit but a slow demand; prices however, are wuthansted. Bacon generally rules quiet with an easier ten- dency, though there is no quotable alteration in values. Hams still meet an active demand at steady price.. Shoulders show no alteration. Cheese rules quietly steady. Butter remains firm with yesterday's currencies repeated. Lard is firmer in tone, but not quotabl* higher.

A CHESHIRE BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.

J. Tatlock, Acting Under Sheriff,was engaged on Thursday with a jury at Chester, in assessing the damages in an action for breach of promise brought by Margaret llardcastle, formerly a lady 'S maid, and the daughter of a gamekeeper at Run- corn, against Dyfrig Davies, builder, of Wrexham. The parties became acquainted while the defendant was carrying out some alterations at a house where the plaintiff was in service. They arranged to be .married, but the defendant failed to keep his pro- mise. The facts of the case were no less extraor- dinary than painful, the plaintiff's story being borne out by a series of letters written by the de- fendant, in which free use was made of quotations from the Scriptures. The plaintiff was awarded £l5O damages and costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.
div.p: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.

THE CHALLENGE SHIELD COMPETITION. WARRINGTON VICTORIOUS. Last evening a team of eight representatives of the Warrington Gymnasium travelled to St. Helens to compete with a team selected from the St, Helens Y.M.C.A. G 3 mnasium Club, in the first round of the competition for the national challenge shield. This is the first year in which the St. Helene athletes have entered the competition for the shield, but it will be remembered that last year the Warrington team,although the local Gymnasium WO at that time quite a new organisation, made a bold bid for at least the second place in the final round. In the course of the contest last year, the Warrington "gymnasts" met and defeated teams representing the Exeter Hall (London) Gymnasium( and Bournemouth, and as a result of these achieve- ments they were one of the three " lots " who ree in the final at Liverpool on the 12th of April last. Their opponents were the Liverpool and Dundee teams. The result of that contest was a rather easi victory for the unrivalled Liverpool organisation+ who scored 303 i points. The interest of that event really lay iu the severe struggle for second place between the Warrington and Dundee teams. The contest was indeed a " neck-and-neck " affair Dundee, however, ultimately running out with a lead of four points-2721 to Warringcon's 264 The defeat of the local team was largely due to tbe superior performances of the Scotchman on the parallel bars, in which exercise they scored 7.51 points as compared with Warrington's 67. In the competition which took place last night Warrington was represented by the following team: —Messrs. J. Podmore, G. Vernon, A. Vernon, Joh!! Holmes, D. Walsh J. E. Warren, James Holmes, Oa T. Locker. The St. Helens team was as follows Messrs. G. Ashcroft, G. Butcher, B. Lightfoot, Marsh, W. H. Pollitt, H. Twigs, E. F. Thilwynd, ase J. B. Wilcock. The judges were as follows: For Warrington. gr F. Gelling,North Liverpool, Y.M.C.A., for St. HelenS,. Professor Renshaw, of Manchester. The contest took place in the large and well-appointt gymnasium of the St. helens Y.M.C.A., se' at the time of commencing—eight o' clock-; there was a large attendance of spectators. Mr. 0 E. C. Else presided. There was a fair numbst of visitors present from Warrington, most of thegl having travelled with the team in conveyances hi road. Amongst these were Alderman Wrigbt+ Councillor Hutchinson, Mr. T. Morris, Mr. Hesketh' und Mr. Ferguson. The teams, as they filed int° the hall, were loudly applauded. The merits of the competitors were tested in three exercises, namellf. horizontal bar, high jump, and rope climbing. Tll° following are the results : WARRINGTON.

PRESCOT UNION, APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICERS. The Guardians are prepared to receive applications from married persons for the offices of Relieving' Officer for the Widnes and Ditton Districts. The Widnes District comprises the townships of Bold and Cronton and a portion of the township of Whines. The Ditton District con- sists of the remaining portion of the township of Widnes and the townships of Ditton, Hale, Halewood, Speke, Little Wootton, and Much Wootton. The salary of each Officer will commence at £lOO per annum, The persons appointed must reside within their respective districts, and devote the whole of their time to the duties of their office. Applications stat- ing age, and present occupation with copies of recent testi- monials (which will not be returned) to be sent to me not later than 10 a.m. on Monday, the 26th January. Bond re- quired through a Guarantee Society for the sum of £l5O for each District. The appointments will be made subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. Canvassing the Guardians will be a disqualification. S. H. HARTLEY, Wnion Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 15th Jan., 1891.
